en: The *Dharmasaṃuccaya*, proclaimed by the bhikṣu Avalokitasiṃha,
is here first [presented as] an *udāna*.
The sections on the Conquered Dharma-body, Impermanence, Heedfulness, Sensual Craving, Women, and Alcohol— these constitute the ten [chapters].
(1) The Chapter on Victory;
Auspicious Invocation.
Om. Homage to the Buddha.

I bow to him, the supreme among the three realms, whose stainless glory has abandoned all outflows, and who, through his equal quality of compassion, lifted up the world submerged in the mire of afflictions.
From the ocean of the extensive *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*,
I, intent upon being an eye for the world, shall extract these verses. (Dhs 1.2)
There are six bases for liberation:
vigilance, as well as faith, the exertion of vigor, steadfastness, the practice of knowledge, and constant association [with the wise]. These are the six bases for liberation.
There are nine causes for the attainment of peace:

generosity, ethical discipline, self-control, patience, loving-kindness toward living beings, non-violence, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; these are the causes for the attainment of peace.
The primary causes of hell are restlessness, attachment to evil, cruelty, false speech,
wrong view, and negligence; these are the primary causes of hell.
Among the hungry ghosts (pretas), there are six causes for rebirth:

stinginess, envy, harsh speech, indulgence in negligence, abstaining from virtue, and a mind intent on malice toward the principles of reality; these are the paths that lead to birth among the pretas in this world.
The causes for rebirth in the animal realm are:
indulgence in ignorance, dullness of intellect, the destruction of the true Dharma, and a fondness for sexual intercourse.
They declare that a powerful capacity for food and sleep is the cause for rebirth in the animal realm.
Having performed the three kinds of unwholesome fruits of action through body, speech, and mind,
one is seen to be bound ever further by that very karma.
Even for the foolish, that [virtue] is indeed connected in a continuous succession;
and by performing the three kinds of merit, the virtuous go to nirvāṇa.
Therefore, understanding the fruit of karma and abandoning negligence, one acts for the sake of spiritual welfare through the intellect; this is the unsurpassed happiness.
For one who is constant in generosity and morality, and who has compassion for all sentient beings, all accomplishments are equally attained; therefore, one should be devoted to morality.
For whom does the accomplishment of one's purpose occur?
For that embodied being who is endowed with loving-kindness and compassion, who is free from longing,
and who is intent on benefiting others— for such a person, the accomplishment of their purpose is established as certain.
For one who is contented, vigilant, desirous of the welfare of all beings,
and liberated from passion and hatred, the accomplishment of his purpose is certain.
For the embodied being who has abandoned both friend and foe, whose mind is equanimous,
and who is freed from the lower realms, the accomplishment of his purpose is certain.
And thus, for that steadfast one who delights in the gift of Dharma and is liberated from stinginess and envy, the accomplishment of his purpose stands as certain.
For one who abides in restraint, who is peaceful, who delights in honoring the guru,
and who knows the rules regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done, the accomplishment of his purpose is certain.
For one who is free from deceit, exceedingly skillful, always speaking kindly,
and capable of meditation and study, the accomplishment of their purpose is certain.
For one who knows the place, the time, and the method; who discerns what is achievable and what is unachievable;
and who knows the methods for feasible means, the accomplishment of the task is certain.
The determination of the true nature of reality by means of the method for conquering anger and other afflictions:
Anger is slain by non-anger; cruelty is conquered by forbearance;
unrighteousness is defeated by righteousness; and darkness is overcome by light. (Dhs 1.19)
Truth and the like are praised; false speech is overcome by truth, and slander by meditative concentration.
Harshness is conquered by gentleness, and idle chatter is conquered by restraint.
Taking life is always conquered by loving-kindness, and theft is always conquered by acts of giving;
improper mental attention is always conquered by that which is born of right reflection.
Ignorance is conquered by knowledge, as night is by day;
and the dark fortnight is entirely conquered by the bright fortnight.
One who has not been conquered by false desires through the investigation of reality with the intellect is always conquered by the noble eightfold path born of right application.
By means of the four grounds of self-confidence, that stinginess is utterly conquered;
and forgetfulness is destroyed by mindfulness, along with the self itself, in an instant. (Dhs 1.24)
Men who have conquered the power of passion through their commitment to dwelling in the forest have surpassed Mount Meru; they are like a grove of trees that has eclipsed a forest garland.
All sacred fords originating in water have been conquered by the ocean;
and all planets and stars have been surpassed by the splendor of the sun.
The eternal has been conquered by the impermanent; poverty has been overcome by the perfection of generosity;
deceit has not been conquered by mildness; and the liar has been struck down by truth.
The unreal was conquered by the real; the abundance of trees by fire; thirst was overcome by waters, and likewise, the desire to eat by food.
The praise of vigor:
By means of vigor, the lion has conquered all animals and those beings who are superior;
likewise, it is constantly proclaimed that through austerity, great desire is overcome. (Dhs 1.29)
Compassion is always praised; lack of compassion is never praised at all.
Through vigor, all laziness—which increases delusion—is utterly conquered.

Praise of the person who perceives reality: By those men who perceive reality, who are ever self-controlled and preeminent in knowledge, those men of cruel deeds and excessive false speech have been utterly conquered. (Dhs 1.31)
All the heretics who propound crooked doctrines have been conquered by the Buddha;
the asuras were defeated by the gods—this is the established order of dharma.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on Conquest.
(2) The Section on the Instruction in Dharma: What kind of person should be a teacher?
He who indeed teaches the Dharma that leads to security and Nirvana.
He who cuts all bonds becomes a teacher for embodied beings.
He who, having severed the snare consisting of delusion, teaches what is auspicious,
is declared to be the teacher of the true path and the one who wards off the evil path.
The preeminence of the Dharma is such that by means of this Dharma, human beings cross the ocean of existence;
it is called the most excellent of true Dharmas, for worldly dharma is not that.
For that embodied being who possesses these four fields,
this birth is said by the teachers of the path to be fruitful.
Having attained the integrity of all his faculties and having received the teaching of the Buddha,
that mortal who does not delight in the Dharma later comes to regret it.
For embodied beings whose minds are constantly attached [to worldly things], who perpetually seek after their desires, and who are devoted to children and wives, the Ender approaches. (Dhs 2.6)
The mastery over the mind—[which is] agitated by various defects due to the faults of volitional construction—leads the mind through skillful means; for embodied beings are bound by the mind.
Especially for one who is difficult to tame, extremely fierce, and desirous of attaining accomplishment, one must not come under the sway of the mind; for that [mind] is an enemy to human beings.
Through the Dharma— well-heard, well-expounded, and cultivated many times— the mind is pacified, just as a horse is controlled by a bridle.
The fruit of hearing the true Dharma: having heard the true Dharma, a person desists from evil and constantly applies himself to what is beneficial. (Dhs 2.10)
Having listened to the true Dharma, the mind attains great joy; and for such a person, vast merit awaits at the moment of transition.
By hearing, one becomes righteous in nature; by hearing, one does not commit evil;
by hearing and knowing the fruit of karma, one attains nirvāṇa.
Having heard it, one understands the Dharma; having heard it, the wise person gains faith in the Buddha;
having heard the Dharma, the wise person strives for liberation.
Having heard [this], a person becomes a knower of the reality of the characteristics of phenomena;
therefore, having heard it, one should diligently apply the intellect with great effort. (Dhs 2.14)
Having heard the discourse taught by the Sugata which turns one away from saṃsāra,
one abandons manifold craving and proceeds to the imperishable state.
Having heard the fourfold conditionality of phenomena and their arising and passing away, a person who has cultivated faith comes to know them all.
Having heard these two characteristics of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, all of that is understood; therefore, one should be devoted to the Dharma. (Dhs 2.17)
Those three powerful defilements, which are the bonds of the entire cycle of existence,
are indeed destroyed without remainder through the hearing of the true Dharma.
One who possesses sacred learning understands the entire characteristic of worldly involvement as well as that of renunciation in its entirety; therefore, sacred learning is unsurpassed. (Dhs 2.19)
For an embodied being who has encountered the time of death and is afflicted by pain,
not even the slightest distress arises in the heart when one takes refuge in what has been heard.
For those by whom the trees of the afflictions have been completely burnt away on all sides by right knowledge,
their re-emergence is never again observed.
For learning refined by heedfulness brings about all forms of happiness;
moreover, learning is the root of the highest good. Therefore, one should be devoted to learning. (Dhs 2.22)
Having heard the true Dharma and having honored the elders, the wise person proceeds to the unsurpassed state, which is free from old age and death.

Having heard [the Dharma], one conducts oneself according to the Dharma and is indeed liberated from suffering; having heard it, one becomes characterized by loving-kindness. Therefore, hearing is the supreme good. (Dhs 2.24)
The wisdom of body, speech, and mind arises in embodied beings after hearing [the Dharma];
therefore, one who desires right understanding should listen with reverence. (Dhs 2.25)
Having heard [the teaching] and relying upon it with firm vigor and prowess,
people swiftly cross over the vast and great triple existence.
The wise declare that man who, having heard [the teachings], is born wealthy in all respects, is truly rich; whereas one who lacks the wealth of the meaning of what has been heard is called poor.
The fruit of the destruction of the True Dharma belongs to one who has lost the wealth of the True Dharma, who is abandoned by the Guru,
and whose life and efforts are rendered fruitless, being struck down by evils.
Negligence and the like are the means for achieving undesirable results:
"The life of an embodied being who is negligent, indolent, and possesses evil friends is seen to be fruitless, like seed sown in saline soil. (Dhs 2.29)
The wise declare that the authority of the treatises concerns matters beyond the reach of what is heard or seen;
it is not said to concern matters beyond the reach of the eyes. (Dhs 2.30)
Attachment to the practice of unrighteousness: for he who abandons the Dharma and practices what is contrary to it, abandons medicine and pursues only disease. (Dhs 2.31)
For those men who practice it again and again, dharma arises in manifold ways,
just as a garden flourishes through the convergence of the rainy seasons.
In this world, the ground of the vajra-seat does not exist otherwise than in saṃsāra; likewise, the arising of the thought of awakening and the attainment of supreme awakening occur here. (Dhs 2.33)
One who practices the Dharma, whose self is tranquil, who rises from the body [in vigilance], and who is concentrated,
will certainly partake of the auspicious, even if he has been deceived by negligence.
Therefore, having reflected upon the qualities of knowledge, the wise person should cultivate knowledge with devotion; for no man can ever become truly great while joined with ignorance.
Faith that follows the Dharma, faith that follows the Dharma, brings happiness as it proceeds; it is utterly free from miserable rebirths and is a great strength amidst calamities. (Dhs 2.36)
Like a lamp in the darkness, like medicine for the diseased, and serving as eyes for all matters, it is a great strength for the poor. (Dhs 2.37)
For those being carried away by existence and its causes, it was formerly a bringer of happiness;
for those intoxicated by negligence and pride, it is now the destroyer of that negligence.
The fruit of attaining the state of peace is that he, preceded by right knowledge, reaches without weariness that very state of peace, Nirvana, which is chosen by the sages. (Dhs 2.39)
Thus ends the second chapter, the Section on the Teaching of the Dharma.
(3) The Section on Loathing the Body:
An Examination of the Body’s True Nature.
Even with honors, nourishments, meats, and even with beds, seats, and the like—
This body was never created by anyone for the purpose of being accepted as one's own.
The body is an enemy—ungrateful, unskillful, and always striking at one's vulnerabilities.
What wise person would commit a sin for the sake of such an enemy as the body? (Dhs 3.2)
The body is said to be a collection of impure limbs, as well as a vessel for many diseases and misfortunes. (Dhs 3.3)
Death and life are both imperceptible; death is present in every moment and remains imperceptible even to those who contemplate ultimate reality.
Life, once it has passed beyond a single moment, does not return, as is observed.
The body is something to be abandoned; having cast off this body— which is merely a manifestation for the sake of life and karma—
even though it has been pierced, it lies upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth.
Moment by moment this body decays and does not turn back;
yet, through the intoxication of youth, the foolish are deluded, their minds infatuated.
Intoxicated by the pride of wealth and grain, they act to their own detriment;
thus they surely meet with destruction and are consumed by their own evil deeds.
Those who do not take pleasure in the Dharma are not truly human; they are non-humans. They do not stand upon the path that leads to the city of Nirvana in reality. (Dhs 3.8)
How indeed can one obtain human birth, which is the means for crossing the ocean of existence and the great abode of all excellences?
For those who do not board the raft of knowledge do not cross over the ocean of existence.
The transience of life is like a flash of lightning or a whirling firebrand, resembling a city of the Gandharvas; the life of all embodied beings is always passing away with great speed. (Dhs 3.10)
One should never harbor pride regarding the body, which is momentary, fragile, transient, fickle, insubstantial, and terrified by old age and death. (Dhs 3.11)
For those who meditate, this body is indeed gone; it is a great abode of sorrows and is regarded as a field for both the auspicious and the inauspicious.

The body of that person whose limbs are adorned with knowledge, virtue, compassion, and generosity— the essence of which is solely the welfare of sentient beings— is considered to have fulfilled its purpose. (Dhs 3.13)

Liberation comes from the knowledge of the elements; this entire body is freed from death through the knowledge of the elements. This occurs directly from the analytical investigation of the bodily elements, and not otherwise. (Dhs 3.14)
He who, having abandoned the elements of the body, becomes attached to other elements,
is liberated from suffering only through the training in the nature of the elements.
Indeed, a deposit of gold does not lead to the pacification of suffering in the same way that one who knows the reality of the elements of the body is liberated from suffering. (Dhs 3.16)
From suffering arises further suffering; therefore, one who is skilled [in this] does not protect one who is afflicted by all the terrors of kings, thieves, and the like.
Therefore, that which is eternally useless should be avoided from afar;
by avoiding it a person is happy, but by associating with the wicked, he is miserable. (Dhs 3.18)
One who knows the reality of the bodily elements, who understands the true nature of the elements,
and who is devoted to meditation and study, burns away the mountains of afflictions.
Therefore, the wise person examines the elements born of the body;
by knowing their specific characteristics, liberation comes to embodied beings. (Dhs 3.20)
Thus ends the third chapter, the Section on Disgust for the Body.
(4) The Chapter on Turning Back:
For whom does time turn back?
For one who is not yet satiated by sensual desires, and for one who is parched with craving.
For one whose senses and mind are restless, this time passes away.
For that embodied being who is attached to pleasure and intoxicated by the sight of women, this time passes away while he contemplates what is impermanent.
For this foolish person, who is subject to birth and death, deluded by craving,
time revolves away.
For one bound by the prison of the realms of rebirth, overcome by agitation,
and deluded by the poison of negligence, this time continues to pass away.
For one who is addicted to restlessness and the like, who delights in the adornment of the body,
and whose mind is never satisfied with acquisitions, this time passes away.
For one bound by the five fetters, deluded by the six,
and bewildered regarding the way of the three worlds, this time revolves.
For those who do not understand the states of downfall, who are afflicted by discursive thoughts,
and whose minds are attached to worldly things, this time passes away.
While the mind is attached to sensual pleasures— which are delightful at that moment but harmful in their ultimate consequence— this time continues to pass away.
For one who is unacquainted with former suffering, who delights in divine happiness,
and who is unacquainted with separation, time revolves on.
For one bound by the net of karma, whose mind is thus agitated and who has strayed from the path of the righteous, time passes away.
For one who is ignorant of the faults of existence, whose mind is deluded by craving,
and who is submerged in the darkness of ignorance, this time passes away.
For the embodied being bound by the single noose of desire, lacking any support and deluded by the host of goddesses, this time revolves.
For one who has withdrawn from the senses, who is led astray from the true path,
and who knows the flavors of the three realms, this time revolves.
For one who knows restraint and non-restraint, yet is full of malice and has lost the path of the Perfectly Awakened One, this time revolves.
For one who has turned away from what is beneficial and harmful, who is dull regarding what ought and ought not to be done,
and who is like a child at play— time passes by.
As he is intent on sporting in the heights of rivers and waterfalls, and in the grounds of forests and groves, this time passes away for him.
As they delight in celestial palaces, upon mountain peaks, in forests that are mines of dharma,
and in the enjoyments of sensual pleasures, time passes by.
For the embodied being who is unattached to karma, dharmas, and their ripening,
yet attached solely to food, time passes away.
Even while residing within a body, they remain ignorant of the body; this triple world is perpetually exhausted by karma.
Fools wander like a wheel, incessantly, yet they do not realize it.

Those who are ignorant of the faults of the world, who ascend to the heights of existence which consist of downfall and rebirth, remain deluded and fail to apply their attention to those very faults. (Dhs 4.20)
For the wise one, the abandonment of sensual desires is the cause of happiness;
indeed, this is the supreme happiness: the abandonment of sensual desires by the wise one who is free from longing, whose sorrow has passed away, and who is free from fever.
The fruit of the sages' attainment of the final state is auspicious in its beginning, middle, and end; it is the supreme security which the weary sages,
having reached it, wander about free from fever.
Sensual desires are the causes of suffering;
the happiness born of desire may exist, but it leads to downfall.
Indeed, there is no particular excellence in desire that does not result in the ripening of suffering.
Therefore, a wise person should not be greedy for sensual pleasures in any way;
for they are extremely terrible and serve as the causes of the sufferings of saṃsāra.
Wandering through forests, groves, mountains, and lotus ponds, the foolish, driven by thirst, fall along with the deities.
An instruction on attachment to auspicious karma [is given] regarding the golden mountains and the peaks of lapis lazuli.
For even meritorious karma is exhausted; therefore, strive together with the gods.
As you wander among the delightful wish-fulfilling trees and by the rivers and springs, your merit will be exhausted; therefore, strive together with the deities.
In delightful regions and in forests rich with jewel-mines, you have never practiced what is auspicious; therefore, strive together with the deities.
With fivefold vigor that brings joy to the mind,
strive together with the deities to overcome the time already passed.
Due to their lack of knowledge regarding what is beneficial for the gods,
those whose minds are constantly attached and who are perpetually intent upon sense objects do not recognize that which would be a benefit to the gods, even if it were free from mantras.
This merit, diminished by the reviling of the gods, has reached its exhaustion;
the gods, who enjoy the fruits of their good deeds, must now depart elsewhere.
For those who are constantly attached to the auspicious, or who always perform auspicious deeds,
the cause for fools indeed turns out to be dissimilar.
Those who wait for death while continuing to enjoy [sensual pleasures] are people deluded by desire;
being of most excellent character yet ignorant, they are never established in the ultimate refuge.
Deluded by desire, those people who take pleasure in killing out of anger do not possess knowledge of the ripening of karma; they eat and wait for death. (Dhs 4.34)
Deluded by desire, those people eat and await death; surrounded by the fire of craving, they do not perceive that all things are equal.
Deluded by desire, those people eat and await death,
failing to perceive the terrible suffering born of separation.
Having feasted, those people, deluded by desire and with their hearts attached to women, await death; they do not perceive rebirth. (Dhs 4.37)
Deluded by desire, those people eat and wait for death;
they are not perturbed in any way by calamities, diseases, or sorrows.
Those people, deluded by desire, who cultivate association with evil friends and great anger, wait for death after having indulged [in worldly pleasures]. (Dhs 4.39)
Deluded by desire, those people eat and await death;
they have not cultivated their minds nor have they entered into reality.
Deluded by desire, those people eat and await death,
even though they are terrified of the fear of saṃsāra in all circumstances.
Having eaten, those people, deluded by desire, await death;
they are those who, regarding what ought and ought not to be done, never set their minds upon well-spoken words.
Deluded by desire, those people who do not possess the wisdom of reality and are not constantly devoted to the welfare of all beings eat and then await death. (Dhs 4.43)
Deluded by desire, those people who, being themselves deluded, destroy the Dharma for the sake of bodily pleasure, await death after having consumed [their lives]. (Dhs 4.44)
With a one-pointed mind, one should always diligently perform what is wholesome; and one should always avoid what is unwholesome— this is the characteristic of a wise person.
Having touched that ethical conduct which brings about the destruction of the means for falling into the lower realms,
one who has approached it will inevitably fall into ruin, deceived by negligence.
It is the nature of the subject to undergo change, but not that of the objects;
for the lords of gods go from all places— having gone, going, and yet to go—
and remain upon the delightful peak adorned with various jewels.
There are delightful peaks of lapis lazuli, as well as others adorned with forest garlands;
the sense objects are just like that, yet it is the person who undergoes change.
The regions of the earth, delightful with forests and groves, remain entirely unchanged in every respect; it is only the people who undergo transformation.
Those very lotus ponds, with stalks made of beryl and especially of gold, are what people revolve around.
The lakes and delightful rivers are filled with flocks of birds without interval;
likewise, these remain unimpaired, yet it is the people who undergo transformation.
The celestial palaces, chariots, and likewise the mansions remain intact; it is only the people who undergo change.
The world undergoes change, being deceived by sense objects; yet, even so, no agitation arises in the heart of the Noble One.
Through practice, the mind that wanders in saṃsāra becomes hardened;
because of this, I believe great suffering no longer dwells within the heart.
Just as animals bound by a spear in a household cage perish one by one, while the rest remain without agitation; so it is with those bound by the spear of karma.
This realm exists solely for those who desire pleasure;
thus have these foolish gods fallen from their state and been reborn.
Those who are intent upon sense objects are ignorant of death; beings are destroyed by negligence, for death bestows momentary suffering.
Like cattle devoid of alarm, they do not perceive death. (Dhs 4.57)
Afterwards, those of long-standing intentions, having fallen under the power of time,
will be consumed by the fire consisting of remorse, which leaves nothing remaining.
Knowing that death— which is terrible, unavoidable, and subject to the power of time— is certain for all embodied beings, one should practice the path according to the scriptures.
All unions end in separation;
in the sight of loved ones, there are always partings from those who are dear.
Union ends in separation—this is the eternal law of nature.
Whether in a moment, a lava, a muhūrta, by day or by night, or while on a journey, the wise person should contemplate death; there is no remedy for it.
Only those whose impurities have been removed attain peace;
they praise supreme mindfulness, for those whose impurities have been removed proceed toward the peace that is solely intent upon the highest good at the time of death.
Reflecting upon the nature of death, with whom is this fault attributed?
For when the mind is entirely free from fault, it becomes eternally tranquil.
The Tathāgatas have declared that supreme excellence is heedfulness;
this supreme excellence of heedfulness has been declared by the Tathāgatas:
namely, the constant mindfulness of death and the avoidance of unwholesome things.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Chapter on Turning Back.
(5) The Chapter on Impermanence: Pleasure ends in destruction;
for all pleasure indeed ends in destruction. No pleasure is found that is permanent.
Therefore, one should not associate with pleasure if one desires happiness for oneself.
Death drags away everyone—whether they are walking or standing still, laughing or even playing. Irresistible and of great velocity, the terrible death destroys all. (Dhs 5.2)
He does not abide here or in the hereafter wherever he may go;
nevertheless, being utterly deluded, he has fallen under its control.
Whether it be a child, a youth, or even an elder;
whether one is a householder or not a householder— when Death does not spare anyone.
Whether one is happy or suffering, virtuous or likewise so,
whether established in vows or not established in vows— when he does not draw them away [from the truth], [he is a true friend].
When he does not disparage one who is immoral or one who possesses morality, nor likewise a supreme donor, nor even a most excellent king; Dhs 5.6.
Whether it be a celestial being, a denizen of hell, or likewise an animal,
whether heedless or heedful, he does not drag that person down.
Whether one is born in the desire realm, established in the form realm,
or born in the formless realm, when that [craving] does not diminish, [suffering persists].
The noose of karma, the staff of old age, the staff of disease, and the great forest—this death, resembling a blood-drinker, comes taking away all sentient beings. (Dhs 5.9)
When such a terrifying and most dreadful death has arrived, the gods, deluded by desire, continue to act [heedlessly].
One should renounce all pleasure that ends in downfall— the suffering of a god falling from the celestial realm,
and the suffering born in hell, preceded by separation. (Dhs 5.11)
Just as even excellent food mixed with poison [is to be avoided], one should likewise renounce the happiness of the celestial realms, for it ends in a fall. (Dhs 5.12)
There is no comparison for the suffering of one whose merit is exhausted, who is wretched, who is abandoned by his own wife, and who is falling away from existence.
When the merit of a god is exhausted, like an elephant whose strength has faded and whose luster has vanished, his former happiness subsides and great suffering arises. (Dhs 5.14)
Even for a god, there is the fall from his station;
for one whose thirst increases through sense objects, whose mind is struck by grief,
and whose speech and bodily movements have become feeble, there is fear due to that fall.
The more one indulges in the taste of pleasure and sensual desires— the supreme deceivers— the greater indeed becomes their suffering. (Dhs 5.16)
The suffering that arises for one striving [for merit] from the worlds of the gods does not equal even a sixteenth part of the suffering in hell.
Having seen that the world of the gods ends in falling and that on earth it ends in death, suffering indeed prevails; therefore, set your mind upon what is truly beneficial.
Happiness ends in downfall;
there is no happiness in this world that does not end in downfall.
Having understood this, one should direct the mind toward the cause of all that is beneficial. (Dhs 5.19)
All suffering ends;
all accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; unions end in separation; for life indeed ends in death. (Dhs 5.20)
For one who is born, death is inevitable; there is no permanence for such a being.
This truth is not seen by those who have not awakened within the three realms.
Some perish in the womb, others likewise in the lying-in chamber;
some perish while crawling about, and in the same way, others are destined for destruction.
The rising and setting of the sun is seen to be certain;
likewise, for everyone who is born, death stands before them. (Dhs 5.23)
All pleasure ends in decay;
indeed, all pleasure ends in decay. He whose intellect is deluded does not perceive this, and when death arrives, he will experience suffering in his next birth. (Dhs 5.24)
The wise declare that performing wholesome deeds and being virtuous are always dear; indeed, they say that practicing the Dharma is happiness.
"All is impermanent and unstable; cyclic existence is always bitter in its transformation. It is said that this is the cause for the intellect to engage in the investigation of reality."
The happiness of those gods who are intoxicated by pleasure is impermanent;
for there is indeed suffering for a deity when falling away from the world of the gods.
There is indeed no comparison for it; for that is a hell within a hell. Do these people not realize that constant pleasure ends in a fall? (Dhs 5.28)
Deluded by pleasure, they perceive the world as free from old age and death;
yet that world is subject to the impurity of death and rebirth, and its number is beyond reckoning.
Nevertheless, men, deceived by craving, do not feel any trepidation.
Birth always approaches, and youth passes away swiftly; union and separation are seen to be innate. Yet those who are deluded, deceived by sense objects, do not perceive this. (Dhs 5.30)
Overpowered by craving, the gods fall;
the gods fall, rendered helpless and utterly deluded by craving. Such was that ground, those lotuses, and those various groves. (Dhs 5.31)
All things possess a superficial charm:
the peaks are delightful, vast, and filled with jewels;
there are lakes and various rivers adorned with precious stones. (Dhs 5.32)
Trees with variegated blossoms stand in diverse rows,
and there are delightful, vast palaces adorned with jewels.
Some wish-fulfilling trees are made of gold, some are pure lapis lazuli, some are silver, some are refined gold, and others are excellent trees composed of various combinations of these materials.
The lotus ponds shine, their beauty enhanced by the songs of bees;
and everywhere there are delightful ornaments worthy of the gods.
All this is momentary; it exists exactly thus, yet the person undergoes transformation,
appearing like an illusion, a bubble, or foam, and resembling a city of the Gandharvas.
For there is no happiness for any god who is deceived by craving; having destroyed all people and caused them to wander in the ocean of existence, [craving] prevails. (Dhs 5.37)
Craving alone is the root of suffering;
craving, which is like the fire of poison, remains here among the worlds.
Though unsatiated by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, it is tormented by the arising of [false] happiness.
Where have those hosts of gods gone, consumed by the fire of time?
In every way, this craving that spreads through the world has been fully understood.
Deluded by which, even the gods have fallen under the power of Time;
gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, and all mobile beings go to hell.
Bound by the noose of Time, all beings in this triple world go helplessly toward that noose of Time which is difficult to overcome; indeed,
this entire triple world is bound by the noose of Time.
Deluded by craving, they do not perceive death; and being helpless, deluded by the confusion of craving, they do not perceive it—
just as these gods [behave] by the hundreds and thousands.
Those who have perished, consumed by the fire of time and by sense objects born of wealth,
see the death of another, yet do not see their own.
Later, when misfortune has arrived, they experience their own suffering;
for their mind is always defiled by negligence and constantly delighted in sense objects.
Those who delight in negligence do not perceive the certainty of death, which dwells as a companion to all embodied beings, even though it is the ultimate end of happiness.
This army of Death approaches, crushing all like a potent poison;
neither mantras, nor medicinal herbs, nor rituals, nor even gods or asuras can withstand it.
For one bound by the noose of Time, there is no savior; those who are bound by the noose of Time find no protectors.
One whose face is covered with dust does not even recognize oneself. (Dhs 5.47)
The reason craving is to be abandoned is that this death, which results in the falling away from what has been attained,
will occur later for one who is always greedy and never satisfied by their efforts due to craving. (Dhs 5.48)
Death comes suddenly upon those who seek happiness without having seen it;
this great suffering sent by Death is your own obstinate attachment.
Immediately after this, a most terrible death will occur from this great mountain, which is adorned with forests and groves.
Bound by their own karma, wandering among sense objects and experiencing the fruits of their actions, they sport and dally for a time; yet there is no true happiness in craving anywhere.
Deluded by that very thirst of craving, they fall helplessly to the earth. (Dhs 5.51)
Just as fire invariably follows smoke,
so too does death stand at the heels of the signs of decay.
With every birth, death is certain; while health exists, disease persists.
Amidst prosperity, the arrival of misfortune is certain; with youth, innate old age is present. Separation from all beloved ones is certain; union does not remain constant. (Dhs 5.53)
The greatness of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā):
this nature of phenomena has been taught by the Perfectly Awakened One for the sake of constant light;
it brings about the exhaustion and destruction of both [extremes] for living beings. (Dhs 5.54)
For just as death is necessarily present once birth has occurred,
so too is merit-karma exhausted, for lifespans are indeed momentary.
Devote yourselves to restraint and so forth; O best of men, devote yourselves to the discipline of the Dharma.
All youth passes away, and life itself follows in its wake.
Everything is subject to destruction; all things perish at all times. Do not set your mind on negligence!
Heaven is not attained eternally, nor is the perfection of favorable moments ever permanent. (Dhs 5.57)
One should employ [the means] as quickly as possible before [the object] falls; for once it has fallen, its employment would be in vain. (Dhs 5.58)
This indeed is that Drumavana grove, adorned with various jewels,
covered by thickets of creeping vines, and graced with lotus ponds.
It is adorned with pure palaces made of Jāmbūnada gold, inlaid with jewels,
and beautified by various kinds of cascades and creepers.
Having pierced through the sky, Mount Meru, which stands high as a witness to these beings' karma,
will utterly cease to exist when the fire at the end of the eon subsides.
How much more so those gods there, who resemble bubbles on foam,
who are born and perish, deluded by negligence and intoxication?
Infinite pleasure and pain arise from the fruits of one's own desires;
just as gods fall from the celestial realms back into hell.
That supreme, bitter suffering exists everywhere amidst all physical and mental miseries;
yet that supreme, bitter suffering cannot befall one who is heedless.
The suffering of separation is recited as the foremost among the names of suffering; and that very suffering constantly prevails at the forefront in the celestial realm.
There will be separation from all that is dear and pleasing;
for you do not perceive, O gods, that life indeed ends in death.
But when the time of death has arrived, with the senses and mind agitated,
you shall know that supreme suffering which will inevitably come to pass.
Everything is momentary, like the wheel of a firebrand, resembling a city of Gandharvas;
all that arises within the three realms of existence is like a bubble on the surface of foam.
He who, deluded by a mass of foam, would construct a covering or a bed—
such a fool would seek a delusive taste in that which is conditioned.
Neither gods, nor humans, nor yakṣas, nor asuras, nor garuḍas can protect those tormented by their own karma at the time of death; such is the power of death.
As long as the most terrible King of Death has not yet arrived, so long must one perform virtuous deeds; do not suffer later.
The ordinary happiness born of desire for worldly objects, which arises from sensory experience, does not remain when the time of death has arrived; such is the view of the wise.
What will pleasures avail, what women, and what kinsmen,
to one being carried away by death from every side, even from the world of the gods?
All those stable grounds, adorned with forests and groves, remain as they are;
yet you, bound by the rope of death, are led away by Time.
Just as clouds in the sky, driven by the wind,
come together and then separate, so too do living beings in saṃsāra.
Just as flowers are seen by men when they have arrived in their proper season,
yet when the season has passed, they all depart just as they came.
Just as the gods rejoice in their meritorious deeds when the proper time has arisen, so too,
when that auspicious time has passed, they return whence they came.
Just as many leaves grow upon a tree season after season,
yet when that auspicious time has passed, they wither away on all sides.
Just as in the Parṇopama-sūtra it is said that this happiness is not free from fear;
happiness is constantly decaying, and no such thing as permanent unhappiness exists.
Just as rain during the monsoon season does not cease once it has fallen from the sky,
so too all this happiness departs and does not return.
Just as the cry of peacocks, when stirred up by the wind,
is heard for their own destruction, so too is this pleasure traditionally understood to be.
For just as that which is cast into a blazing fire is surely consumed in time,
so too is time known to be like a fire for those who move about like pieces of wood.
Some have come and some have gone by the hundreds and thousands;
yet, deluded by craving, they feel no sense of spiritual urgency.
To whatever extent one enjoys great happiness for oneself,
to that same extent there will certainly arise great suffering at the end, resulting from one's downfall.
Birth and so forth constitute a succession of sufferings:
birth is suffering, old age is suffering, and death is indeed suffering;
separation from those who are dear—this is the succession of suffering. (Dhs 5.85)
One does not fear death;
yet, seeing the fall of another, why is a person not shaken?
For this very same fall shall be mine as well, along with all my sins.
He who perceives danger from afar yet abides in right practice,
remains free from anguish and does not fear when the time of death has arrived.
When death is being experienced by one's own kinsmen and relatives with distress, the suffering at the time of death is impossible to describe. (Dhs 5.88)
For death ends in a fall, like a mountain collapsing; it overcomes powerful men without opposition, possessing great velocity and always striking down. (Dhs 5.89)
Knowing this, O best of gods, do not succumb to negligence;
for old age constantly brings about the dissolution of youth.
In life, death is always present; this state is ever-abiding.
Wherever its range extends, one must inevitably be consumed by the impermanent fire.
How much more so, then, the gods at the end of an eon, who are like foam or a plantain tree?
There is nothing whatsoever that is conditioned or unstable which could endure as knowledge.
That which is eternal or pleasant— such a state does not exist;
death should be understood as ever-present for all living beings.
Because no remedy for that can be found by any means whatsoever;
their physical form is momentary, and likewise, their youth is momentary as well.
Likewise, their happiness diminishes, yet those of little intelligence do not perceive it;
for all these various auspicious signs of theirs [are thus lost].
Just as it was destroyed by the wheel of time through the sequence of birth,
so too was this [world] lost in the past, with its hundreds and lakhs of various characteristics.
In the same way, the King of Death will snatch away even this birth of those whose minds are heedless and who always dwell in pleasure. (Dhs 5.97)
This noose of Time approaches for one's destruction, bringing about the ruin of happiness;
it causes the separation from happiness, health, strength, life, and beloved ones.
This powerful King of Death approaches;
for he has repeatedly drawn near to those who have been heedless.
The destruction of happiness is certain; life, together with its pleasures, will swiftly perish.
O gods, struck down by negligence, this long duration has been ruined.
Blinded by delusion, they do not realize it even when awakened by pleasure;
for when their radiance has faded, their faculties and minds become distraught.
They will fall into the realm of Yama; such is the fruit of knowledge.
Alas, this time is being lost, for happiness is but momentary. (Dhs 5.102)
Nevertheless, those whose minds are stained and who lack the eye of wisdom do not realize this;
though they dwell constantly in pleasure, they go from the pleasant to what is even more pleasant.
Just as these beings shall depart, so will the King of Death seize them;
yet the fool who does not despond in the face of old age, birth, and calamities [is rare].
Having attained that happiness among the gods which is esteemed for its virtues, he later, with a base mind, suffers at the time of death. (Dhs 5.105)
Life is fleeting and unstable, ending in destruction even after one has performed sacrifices;
for just as whatever ends in destruction is so, such too is the life of these beings.
Before long, this will undoubtedly come to pass:
as long as death has not arrived and the intellect remains unclouded. (Dhs 5.107)
A wise person should, by the power of the mind, maintain delight in the Dharma and sustain that devotion to the Dharma with mental strength,
even at the cost of losing their entire life and all happiness.
Separation from loved ones is certain,
and death, which brings about the separation from all that is dear, takes refuge in the body;
when that great meditation has arrived, death becomes most terrible.
There is no other refuge than the Dharma; therefore, one should delight in the Dharma.
For the joy that arises for a deity upon being reborn there—*Dharmasaṃgraha-sūtra* 5.110.
At the time when death occurs, no one experiences anything like that; it does not equal even a sixteenth part of the suffering of passing away. (Dhs 5.111)
All things do not go toward destruction even by taking a single step;
for from the very moment a person is born, they are destined for death.
But for one who is overwhelmed by various delusions, this fear does not exist when you have reached the supreme state that brings an end to the enjoyments of existence.
Then the foolish-minded person experiences that great fear born of death; for craving, deluded by poison, is bitten by the serpents of the sense-objects. (Dhs 5.114)
The gods do not always perceive the great fear at the end of their fall;
yet they fall, and thus they produce suffering for embodied beings.
Just as the birth and passing away of gods occur,
they are tossed about by the winds of karma and distressed by their own past actions.
Death leads away the man who is helpless and deprived of happiness; neither mothers, nor fathers, nor friends, nor kinsmen can save him. (Dhs 5.117)
This [death] comes to assist the person impelled by time;
for this person is without a companion, being by nature deceived.
The mind alone is the bond of fetters;
indeed, by the bonds of the mind’s fetters, people are bound.
In this world, neither a stranger nor one's own kin can be the savior of anyone.
One should practice the Dharma as if seized by the hair by Death;
for when the time of death has arrived, even one's own kin are like strangers.
As for this great abundance of happiness belonging to the gods that you behold—
The Great God, the King of Death, will forcibly seize that; this birth passes away swiftly, yet the fool does not perceive it. (Dhs 5.121)
But later, when misfortune has arrived, they realize it while suffering;
if there is fear of suffering, and if there is that fear of death which is so swift.
Apply your intellect to the Dharma; in this way you shall attain happiness.
Happiness that ends in destruction is always impermanent and unstable in every respect. (Dhs 5.123)
The state of divinity ends in a fall;
deluded beings do not find the happiness created by all the gods.
Having come into being, they inevitably pass away, for those who have arisen are necessarily fickle.
O gods, this law of nature is established for the sake of falling:
those gods who are intoxicated by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures and whose minds are fickle [shall fall].
The gods do not perceive that life ends in intense calamity;
for at the very moment a god is born, he is born for death.
One should direct one's mind toward the highest good,
for just as the day inevitably passes into night,
life is said to be like the day and death like the night. (Dhs 5.127)
Therefore, having understood both of these, direct your mind toward what is beneficial;
for this very purpose [is taught] for those men who remain under the sway of passion for women. (Dhs 5.128)
Thus, that which was desired has been forcibly crushed by the army of Death;
having deceived men and women who are deluded by notions of existence, non-existence, and the like.
At the time of death, those who experience the fruits of their own karma go to lotus groves, mountains, and the waterfalls of rivers.
Having played many times, beloved ones have come to the well;
death is inevitable, and separation is certain. (Dhs 5.131)
Nevertheless, men are always subject to the power of passion;
whether one is happy or suffering,
youth elsewhere has grown old.
The King of Death crushes one of low birth as well as one of noble birth; the King of Death crushes the handsome as well as the ugly, the powerful as well as the weak. (Dhs 5.133)
The King of Death crushes everyone—whether one has a protector or is without a protector;
likewise, death treats a king, a householder, or an ascetic all the same. (Dhs 5.134)
Whether cruel or mild, whether wealthy or poor, and likewise whether virtuous or devoid of virtue, the King of Death crushes them all.
The King of Death crushes both woman and man—whether one is a traveler or a householder, whether situated in water or on land. (Dhs 5.136)
Whether standing upon mountain peaks, or waking, or sleeping, or eating, or standing still—the King of Death crushes him down. (Dhs 5.137)
The King of Death, the subduer of all the world, crushes everyone—
whether they are on the ground, in a celestial mansion, in a foreign land, or at home.
This saw-like Wheel of Time, the King of Death, crushes the fortunate, the meritorious, the sword-wielder,
and even the righteous.
The King of Death crushes the sick man or the one with a healthy body,
the fierce one or the virtuous, as well as the miserly man or the wealthy.
Whether heedless or heedful, the King of Death crushes them all:
the denizen of hell, the hungry ghost, the animal, and likewise the human being. (Dhs 5.141)
The King of Death, his strength and zeal unabated,
crushes down those gods who dwell in the realm of desire and those who abide in the realm of form.
For the King of Death crushes all those who are powerful;
and even those gods in the formless realms who are established in meditative attainments—the King of Death crushes all those gods as well. (Dhs 5.143)
Whatever conditioned thing has arisen ends in destruction; indeed, every conditioned thing ends in destruction.
There is no conditioned thing whatsoever for which destruction does not exist.
Having understood this power of death and the fault of desire in its entirety, [one should act accordingly].
Cease also from being deceived by craving; desist from the ocean of existence, considering this calamity to be even more unstable than death itself.
Let the mind be thoroughly subdued;
let the mind be thoroughly subdued, for it is by this that the world is made to wander everywhere— from forests, groves, and mountains, and from celestial palaces.
All the gods, their minds clouded by negligence and deluded, having been struck down by the fire of time, shall be cooked again, their senses still craving the objects of desire.
Bound by the snare of craving, the gods will go to an evil rebirth;
indeed, the life and happiness of embodied beings pass away with great haste.
Yet the wise do not perceive it, like those blind from birth failing to see the true path;
for the life of all embodied beings is like a bubble upon the water.
Youth passes away as fleetingly as the waves of a river;
for even the Tuṣita gods, though they gaze with sidelong glances, are impermanent and subject to suffering.
Just as a wretched lamp inevitably goes out when its oil is exhausted, so too does passion, being abandoned, perish helplessly;
thus is the twelve-spoked wheel of great power brought to an end by the exhaustion of karma.
This wheel of Dharma is stable and should not be wavering;
it is delightful with its various objects and adorned with manifold pleasures.
All are swallowed by Time;
though they dwell in contentment, they fall helpless, having come under the power of Time.
Just as trees grow when they have fallen under the power of Time, so do all beings.
Furthermore, when their time has come, they become devoid of luster;
yet, having reached their proper time, the gods become happy once more.
Having returned once more to this cycle of existence, they indeed fall helplessly;
for when the time for karma arrives, this world revolves.
One who has fallen under the sway of time moves from happiness to suffering; whatever pure karma was performed previously, that too results in a great and evil outcome.
They enjoy this very heaven, and it perishes thereafter;
for everything that has a cause is momentary, especially so in this case.
This clinging to impermanence does not occur in every respect;
for all those conditioned phenomena that are considered permanent are entirely deceptive.
Deceiving people, he departs; this is the established nature of dharma:
just as rivers have swift currents, so too is the happiness of embodied beings.
Life is entirely momentary, yet fools do not realize this;
there is old age, disease, death, and misfortune when karma is exhausted.
These [conditions] belong to the gods who are eternal and move at will;
yet even for them, life is never certain, nor is there true happiness within the three realms.
Deluded by desire, the gods are rendered helpless and find no peace;
they are as unstable in every way as raindrops in the sky.
Likewise, all this happiness is always like a shower of rain;
it is like dust particles driven by the wind, colliding with one another.
Just as one who is helpless wanders in the sky, so too is the union of embodied beings;
though they may rejoice for a very long time, there is no permanence for those possessed of bodies.
Fools do not find this happiness in the inconceivable reality;
for that happiness which is stirred by the wind will end in destruction.
Those possessed by desire, deceived by their own minds, do not perceive that pleasure is mixed with suffering and is subject to destruction;
this pleasure, mixed with suffering, exists as if it were concealed. (Dhs 5.166)
Just as a jar adorned with a garland of lotuses may be filled with poison, so too is rice mixed with poison; it indeed ends in death. (Dhs 5.167)
Likewise, all this happiness should be avoided,
for it will lead to hell in the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the end.
Arising, duration, and dissolution—all things consist of arising, duration, and dissolution; all that is conditioned is so described.
And since all that is conditioned is suffering, is it not indeed the Blessed One himself who has said this?
Both worldly honor and pleasure,
as well as the momentary nature of expenditure,
happiness, and life itself— all these one should therefore completely avoid.
One whose mind is always fixed on what is truly beneficial in the beginning, middle, and end is well-restrained; such a person of pure consciousness does not falter at the time of death.
Death is inevitable;
death is certain, as is separation from those who are dear.
Yet, one does not reflect upon this while distracted by sense objects that deceive at the time of death.
That wheel of old age and death is unbearable and most terrible;
yet those beings who are like trees or gods, lacking vision, do not perceive it.
For every being born, there is falling away;
for a god who is thus falling away with impaired faculties and a distracted mind,
there is suffering that is easy to experience, for which no comparison exists here in this world.
Just as the great happiness of one whose mind is afflicted by craving increases,
so too does the great suffering of one who is falling away become unbearable.
Having performed conditioned karma without understanding the nature of its persistence,
one is consumed by remorse when the time of death has arrived.
One's own welfare must be established even before death;
as long as death has not arrived and as long as the perfection of favorable moments remains, so long should one establish one's own welfare—this is the path that brings happiness. (Dhs 5.177)
Having understood that there is falling from the worlds of the gods and death upon the lands of men, what man would place his trust in existence, which is fraught with calamity?
Just as the extinction of a lamp is certain when the oil and the wick are both destroyed, so too,
for whom could there not be a downfall from the abode of the gods through the exhaustion of their meritorious actions?
Just as the destruction of a wall is certain, the destruction of the mind is likewise established as inevitable.
Likewise, upon the destruction of karma, happiness necessarily perishes;
when their merit is exhausted, all the gods fall from the abode of the gods.
Impermanence is the downfall for all these beings;
death drinks up living creatures, and old age drinks up youth.
Disease drinks away health, yet the world does not realize it;
this has occurred very many times and has been observed in countless instances.
This [being] is born, it decays, it falls away, and it is reborn;
there is not a single moment, nor a brief instant, nor even a transition [in which this does not occur]. (Dhs 5.183)
In this world, death occurs with such delay that people do not perceive it;
yet those who have undergone it are numerous, and its occurrences are manifold.
There is no delay for death, nor does the world realize it;
all life is impermanent, and youth does not linger.
All beings are impermanent, yet the world does not realize this;
in the end, all things perish gradually, lingering for but a moment.
Bound by the thread of karma, the world does not realize this;
nor do the thousands of millions of gods who frequent forests and groves.
All things are closed by time, yet the world does not perceive it;
the gods, wandering in a state of impurity, are intoxicated by their craving for enjoyments.
All will go to dissolution, yet the world does not realize it;
happiness is like foam and bubbles, comparable to the objects of a dream.
It quickly goes to destruction, yet the world does not realize it;
for everyone, in every way, total ruin is inevitable. (Dhs 5.190)
And yet, the fool does not develop world-weariness toward cyclic existence;
even though he strives with every means and effort in every way, he does not become a savior when the most terrible time of death has arrived. (Dhs 5.191)
That which severs all happiness, that great mine of sufferings, and the separation from all bonds— this is designated as "death. (Dhs 5.192)
The bringer of fear to living beings, an ocean of sufferings, equal toward all, and the cause of delusion for the intellects—this is designated as death. (Dhs 5.193)
The one who cuts off the lives of beings and destroys their faculties,
who cannot be touched by any living creatures, is designated as Death.
Invincible to all beings and unconquerable by any actions, the destroyer of all living creatures is designated as Death. (Dhs 5.195)
The inevitable end of all principles for all embodied beings, this destruction of the group-homogeneity, is designated as "death. (Dhs 5.196)
Death is said to be the destroyer of the Kālacakra, along with the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
Lacking self-restraint and destructive, like fire to all embodied beings, cruel and irreversible—that is what is called death. (Dhs 5.198)
The destruction of the aggregates and sense-bases, as well as the mind of the formless realm,
and the great onset of the law of time— this is designated as death.
One should direct the mind toward what is beneficial, and not toward negligence; for that very negligence leads quickly to the downfall of embodied beings.
Exert yourself for the sake of the highest good; do not let your mind fall into negligence.
Life that has passed does not return,
just as the swift flight of birds or the wind.
In that same way, the life of all embodied beings passes away even more swiftly.
The wind returns, and birds return;
but for one whose life has been cut short, there is no returning again.
Karmas are swiftly exhausted, and the Ender approaches quickly;
yet even the gods do not perceive this inevitable separation.
Irrepressible and of great velocity, it destroys the four truths;
this inevitable and powerful death approaches.
The gods, heedless of the sacred revelation, have been easily deceived;
they do not perceive the great suffering that will inevitably come to pass.
For all that is conditioned, and especially for every convention,
there is destruction;
this is the nature of things in every state of existence.
Old age for the destruction of youth, the Ender (Death) for the destruction of life, and calamity for the destruction of beings— these indeed stand as the causes of destruction.
In such a great calamity and in this immense terror,
these gods are indeed heedless, even though they possess consciousness. (Dhs 5.208)
He who perceives future danger with the eye of wisdom should be known as a wise person; one who sees otherwise is a fool.
Upon the exhaustion of karma, happiness perishes;
all those of deluded mind are deceived by their own intellect.
Indeed, when karma is exhausted, they perish just as lamps go out due to the lack of oil. (Dhs 5.210)
Having enjoyed this unsurpassed happiness derived from manifold objects, the exhaustion of karma occurs, and a downfall will surely follow.
Because they do not comprehend impermanence, there is a delight in unrighteousness;
the life of embodied beings passes away as fickle as a wave upon the water, yet fools do not realize it is as essence-less as a bubble. (Dhs 5.212)
Indeed, by how many means could a mass of foam possibly endure for long?
But the gods do not endure for long; such is the nature of impermanent existence.
Under the very influence of greed, all this earth is seized by men who desire its fruits, while they remain indifferent toward death;
yet death is not perceived by those unwise ones who are attached to gain.
In beings deluded by ignorance, greed and desire increase moment by moment;
yet they do not perceive that the realms of saṃsāra are wasting away moment by moment.
He summarizes the three punishments:
"This punishment of old age approaches, bringing an end to the youth of men;
this punishment of disease has arrived to destroy health and vitality."
This triple staff is terrible, bringing about the destruction of both gods and asuras.
This fool does not understand; this ignorant person does not perceive the world, which is mutually enticed and fickle with affection for its own kin. (Dhs 5.217)

Bound by delusion, people do not perceive death and separation; one person follows after another who is closely attached, even those men who remain under the sway of sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. (Dhs 5.218)
The aggregate of karma brings about suffering; everyone will be affected by it, yet you are tormented by attachment.
It is an enemy that ends life, fearless and possessed of great power.
This death approaches without delay and with great speed;
it should be understood as a shifting and unstable process, as demonstrated by the aggregates of karma.
The destruction of the gods and others occurs;
[namely] the gods, nāgas,
gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
They were not able to cause his downfall; such was the power of that Tathāgata’s forbearance.
One who perceives reality does not fall into an evil state; one who perceives reality through action is known as one whose conduct is both steady and unsteady.
Being unstained by sinful qualities, he does not go to an evil state. (Dhs 5.222)
Thus ends the fifth chapter on Impermanence.
(6) The Chapter on Heedfulness: For one who delights in heedlessness, there is no liberation.
The sentient being who delights in negligence is not fit for liberation;
for one deluded by the poison of negligence, nirvāṇa is indeed far away.
One should not set the mind on negligence, nor should one be bound by negligent acts; negligence is the supreme enemy.
Even the gods, whose highest state is negligence, fall again into hell.
Having understood this intrinsic nature of phenomena—their arising and passing away—one should not set the mind upon negligence; for negligence is the supreme poison.
Negligence and vigilance are mutually opposed:
vigilance is the state of immortality, while negligence is the state of death.
Those who are vigilant do not perish, whereas those who are negligent are as good as dead forever.
Just as poison is, so is fire; likewise is negligence for living beings.
Sentient beings intoxicated by negligence go from suffering to further suffering.
Those who are ever heedful, immortal, and refined by every form of conduct,
attain supreme peace, where indeed there is no negligence.
For that living being who delights in negligence and does not perform auspicious deeds,
how can there be heaven for one who is thus deluded regarding the Dharma?
One should avoid negligence, for negligence is the supreme poison;
those who are heedful do not perish, while those who are negligent are as good as dead forever.
That mortal who, having attained good fortune, persists in negligence is not known as a wise man; he is the opposite, and not otherwise.
For there is no time for negligence, nor for joy in any way,
since it generates delusion in the mind at the time of death, which is of great power.
Under the guise of negligence, negligence itself is described:
"Joy is the smoke, and negligence is the fire that repeatedly consumes the gods;
deluded by sense objects, the foolish, being sightless, do not perceive it. (Dhs 6.11)
They see that the conditioned formations of embodied beings are uninterrupted;
for just as the deluded do not understand through sense objects, so too they do not perceive what is harmful.
Therefore, the wise declare that negligence is like poison;
happiness was never seen before by those of dull intellect who were negligent.
Just as those aided by negligence go again to hell, once the fruit [of their actions] has been reached, this negligence leads to remorse and suffering later on. (Dhs 6.14)
Heedlessness is seen by wise men to cause misfortune and to bring about every kind of ruin;
likewise, one who does not indulge in heedlessness generally attains what is wholesome.
He for whom suffering is desirable may indulge in negligence;
however, no one who is devoted to negligence will ever attain happiness.
For those free from negligence, there is the attainment of the imperishable state;
being devoid of negligence, they go to the unchanging state.
No one devoted to negligence can lead others to the sufferings of hell.
If the gods of dull intellect take pleasure in this [world] which is subject to destruction, then indeed no distinction exists between them and the animals. (Dhs 6.18)
Due to the power of negligence, the gods— who are devoted solely to heedlessness— fall from the world of the gods, each according to the diversity of their own karma;
they do not realize that their fall from the celestial realm is about to occur.
Constant suffering or a fall will surely follow for one who is near [to such states],
just as the gods superior to those in the world of the gods experience happiness for themselves.
Having reached the world of the gods, he who indulges in negligence awakens at the end of his fall, when his store of meritorious karma has been exhausted.
Do not become intent on negligence; negligence is not fitting for the gods.
Those whose [minds] are struck down by faults through negligence fall from the abode of the thirty-three.
A person under the sway of negligence goes to ruin;
every person deluded by negligence is consumed.
Later, when that [negligence] has departed, he is protected by the [teacher’s] instruction. (Dhs 6.23)
Fools, deluded by the honors shown to them, constantly roam this ground born of defects, where the grass of heedlessness grows lush.
The causes of desire are fickle, treacherous, and intense forms of negligence;
a hero should not trust them, for they are indeed like dreams.
Desire is the cause of hell;
sleep is not the cause of hell, but desires are the causes of sleep.
Therefore, having abandoned this desire, one should always practice good conduct.
Through heedfulness, one is able to attain everything— that state which has not been fully attained by the gods who are deluded by sensual desires.
That state is reached by heroes, by men devoted to heedfulness.
Saṃsāra has heedlessness as its root; likewise, the abode of the gods has heedlessness as its root.
Those who are intoxicated by the poisons of heedlessness are submerged in the perils of existence.
Darkness has heedlessness as its root, and ignorance is a harmful horse;
for those who are deluded by darkness, the eye of wisdom does not exist. (Dhs 6.29)
Heedlessness consists of delusion;
for it is not described as being like fire with its roots and flames.
Likewise, heedlessness is proclaimed to be the foremost among all forms of delusion. (Dhs 6.30)
With a mind scorched by the fire of negligence, one acts in such a way that those fools become deluded and go once again to hell. (Dhs 6.31)
Intoxicated by negligence, those gods who are of a fickle nature experience only pleasure; forgetting the suffering of separation, they long for the joy of union. (Dhs 6.32)
Life ends only in falling;
for when great suffering has arrived, life indeed ends in a fall. Afterwards, one experiences a bitter taste; happiness is fleeting and ends in a fall.
Union ends in separation; happiness always ends in falling; youth ends in old age; and for all embodied beings, every action ends in its conclusion. (Dhs 6.34)
Saṃsāra is bound up with the drama of karma;
for all embodied beings are indeed fettered by their wholesome and unwholesome actions.
Like actors, they perform their roles individually in various states of existence.
Bound by the drama of karma, saṃsāra revolves forever;
the wise person should not place trust in it, for the course of karmic actions is impermanent.
Heedlessness is the supreme fault; heedlessness is like all poisons—let it be utterly abandoned. Those who are liberated from heedlessness, however, [are truly free].
They have crossed over the ocean of existence.
A transgressor who has fallen into a precipice may perhaps survive;
but one who has fallen into negligence shall never be happy.
Negligence is the supreme fault in all actions; for one who is negligent, there is never any auspiciousness, whether by night or by day. (Dhs 6.39)
Whatever happiness there is, whether mundane or considered supramundane, that is destroyed by negligence; therefore, one should avoid it.
Heedfulness is the state of immortality;
heedfulness is the state of immortality, while heedlessness is the path of death.
Through heedfulness, those gods attained preeminence among the gods.
Samsara has heedlessness as its root, while heedfulness is the true goal;
therefore, one who abstains from heedlessness is happy at all times.
If one fears suffering, one should abandon negligence;
for he who desires eternal happiness and fears suffering must indeed desist from negligence, for negligence is like poison to human beings. (Dhs 6.43)
Stricken by the sleep of negligence and deluded by the poison of heedlessness,
even those people who have purified their selves fall into a precipice.
Heedfulness is the highest good;
heedfulness is the supreme good, never negligence. Through heedfulness one is happy; through negligence [one suffers].
They are suffering.
Those deluded by negligence go to hell;
for men deluded by negligence are further stupefied by liquor.
Fie upon those who are utterly bewildered by negligence! They wander again toward hell.
Bound by the snare of negligence and dwelling in the ocean of sense objects,
the god, fettered by craving for sensory pleasures, sports in manifold ways.
At the very moment a god is born, that happiness perishes;
yet, being helpless and their minds shrouded by negligence, they do not perceive it.
Under the sway of negligence and subject to the power of desire, one remains forever unsatisfied;
those whose minds are deluded by negligence are constantly intent upon sense objects,
yet they are truly happy with happiness while remaining insatiable in their enjoyment of desires.
Burnt by the fire of desire and deluded by negligence,
they do not perceive that all strength ends in destruction, for life indeed terminates in ruin.
Many thousands and millions of gods, scorched by the fire of desire and deluded by negligence, [perish].
Those possessed by negligence fall;
every person is carried away, deluded by negligence.
Only later, when misfortune has arrived, does he realize that this is its fruit.
Carelessness is seen by the perceivers of reality as life-taking as poison;
it constantly burns like fire and cuts like a weapon. (Dhs 6.53)
At first he appears like a friend, but later he becomes like an enemy;
thus, heedlessness prevails among all the gods.
For gods, asuras, humans, and especially for nāgas, heedlessness is seen to be the cause; it brings about all manner of misfortunes.
He who is constantly overcome by negligence does not deserve excellence;
a person devoid of excellence drags himself down to the hells.
Various kinds of actions are performed by those animals who are deceived by negligence;
their intellect is always intent upon sexual intercourse and eating.
When well-performed deeds have become the lot of the celestial dwellers,
where then will those who are heedless go?
Struck by the winds of karma and overcome by the waters of negligence,
the gods fall like trees, each in their respective realms of rebirth.
Even among the gods, a sorrow born of spiritual urgency arises hundreds of times; yet though they are born as denizens of heaven,
such sorrow born of urgency does not arise within their hearts.
Having drunk from delusion this intoxicant defiled by negligence, the denizens of heaven fall into a fierce hell surrounded by fire.
Human birth is extremely difficult to obtain; its success or failure depends on whether those who have attained it remain heedful.
Having secured this human birth, those who perform virtuous deeds become destined for the world of the gods.
Having obtained this human state, so difficult to attain, those who are heedless wander about due to that heedlessness and fall into hell.
At the time of death, the heedless being who delights in negligence indeed suffers; he who previously turned away from compassion later torments his own mind at the time of death.
The burning power of negligence is such that fire does not burn it in that way, nor does a weapon cut it;
yet negligence arising from the five senses is burned in such a manner.
Likewise, pleasure takes the form of suffering, and likewise, an enemy takes the form of a friend;
for those who are heedless, that [duality] is constant. Therefore, one should avoid such [heedlessness].
Lust, mingled with the thirst for negligence, increases that very passion; these three fierce enemies destroy the happiness of human beings. (Dhs 6.67)
Those wise ones who are constantly devoted to negligence and not to the Dharma,
when the time of death arrives, are overpowered by the messengers of Yama.

Considering negligence to be like poison, those wise ones who abandon it are blessed; indeed, those who guard against negligence as they would poison will become partakers of happiness when the time of death arrives.
Heedlessness is the supreme death; heedfulness is the supreme happiness.
Therefore, those who desire happiness should never set their minds upon heedlessness.
Delusion regarding the elements and sense-bases is an obstacle to the higher goods;
this delusion regarding the elements and sense-bases acts as a hindrance to the higher goods.
It gives rise to negligence, which leads to the abandonment of all virtuous actions.
For one who is caught in the machinery of the defects, heedlessness—the messenger of the gateway of illusion, the leader of delusion, and the sinful—proceeds forth. (Dhs 6.72)
Those who delight in negligence go toward the mouth of death;
those fools who delight in negligence have come into the grasp of death.
But all those who serve negligence have gone to their destruction.
Even the gods, if they are negligent, find their merit exhausted;
through negligence, the merit of the gods is destroyed. Confused by pleasure, they fall; at that time, where is there any protection for them? (Dhs 6.74)
The practice of the true Dharma is indeed compassion for living beings;
likewise, the sole dharma that leads to welfare is the vast self-restraint born of mercy.
Patience is also always appropriate, as is constant compassion toward all creatures.
At the time of death, when great fear prevails, these [virtues] become one's strength;
therefore, they should be cultivated with effort by those free from negligence.
Peace arises only for that living being who knows the method of knowledge;
it is better to avoid ignorance than to always guard knowledge.
That being who knows the method of knowledge—
His heedlessness is pacified;
for in this matter, the abandonment of heedlessness is certain to achieve the goal of man.
Only for one who delights in heedfulness is the accomplishment of the goals of human life attained;
only for one who delights in heedfulness is the goal of man esteemed by the wise.
Heedlessness is generally bondage, while liberation results from its absence.
Bondage results from indulging in negligence;
this is the definition of liberation and bondage according to the view of the wise.
Having understood this, the Lord who always protects through vigilance [is truly a god].
Later, at the time of death, he will know the fruit of that.
Contentment alone is the means to nirvāṇa;
for in whatever measure contentment is constantly cultivated by ascetics, to that same extent does nirvāṇa proceed before them. (Dhs 6.80)
May dispassion toward all desires and toward nirvāṇa arise;
that which is never within the domain of Māra shall prevail.
See how for human beings, the abandonment of suffering occurs through knowledge alone; observe the constant activity of the mind.
He who possesses perpetual exertion and constant wisdom—how could he ever encounter suffering?
Who is one liberated from bondage?
He who has transcended past fears, who is wise regarding the present,
and who knows the methods for the future— he is liberated from the bonds of the afflictions.
Always delighting in heedfulness, wary of mistrust,
cultivating right perception, and pure, he stands near to Nirvana.
Great happiness is destroyed by negligence;
even the gods, having attained great happiness, are destroyed by negligence.
How much more so for those fools who serve under the power of negligence?
That man is as good as dead who indulges in heedless conduct;
he is dead while still alive who is constantly negligent in maintaining knowledge.
The difference between negligence and diligence is recognized as this very distinction between negligence and diligence:
one should avoid death, fault, and negligence, which is the root of suffering. (Dhs 6.87)
