The gods are eternally joyful, and we are eternally joyful;
no distinction is perceived between the birds and the gods.
If the practice of Dharma is not seen and that practice for liberation does not proceed,
then those [beings] among the gods have become equal to birds.
Those who are free from negligence and who always delight in the Dharma are gods on the path of truth in this world; they do not dwell in negligence.
If the gods are always devoted to play and their conduct is characterized by heedlessness,
then no distinction whatsoever can be found between the gods and the birds.
One who has fallen from the Dharma does not shine by birth,
especially since birth is distinguished by one's actions;
no one who has fallen from the Dharma becomes excellent by virtue of their birth.
Those who revile this saṃsāra, which is by nature subject to total decay, are like those intoxicated by liquor; they are always [reviled] by birds and by those of deluded intellect.
Those whose intellect remains established and undeluded within the domain of the Dharma are truly gods in this world; they do not wander in heedlessness.
Those who understand that suffering arises from the cause of birth are truly fortunate;
they are the gods, and not those who are attached to even beneficial sensual pleasures.
Those who are not distressed in this cycle of existence when repeatedly separated from servants, kinsmen, and relatives, are like birds; they are gods.
Excessive intoxication from drinking liquor is seen as the greatest negligence by those who perceive reality:
for while the drinking of liquor may wear away, negligence never wears away. (Dhs 6.97)
Intoxicated by negligence, the world wanders through the five realms of existence; struck down by negligence, it roams the five realms of existence.
Therefore, one who is intoxicated by negligence is surpassed by all means.
Negligence is even more base than liquor;
while liquor intoxicates embodied beings for at most a single day,
negligence does not wear away even after wandering for ten million eons.
Those who are free from heedlessness have gone to the imperishable state;
but those who fall under the power of heedlessness become birds among men.
Indeed, a person seeking their own welfare must certainly avoid negligence,
for the Buddha has taught that the afflictions are under the sway of negligence.
Even for the sake of the gods, negligence must certainly be abandoned;
if birds of small mind act out of negligence,
why then would the gods [indulge in] negligence?
They do not abandon them, especially.
But that evil-minded person who, due to negligence, does not perceive danger from afar,
will certainly be consumed by remorse when calamity has arrived.
They protect you from the terrible fall from the world of the gods by means of their gifts;
reflecting on this, you must never indulge in negligence.
Those who are constantly devoted to negligence do not partake of happiness;
for negligence is the root of suffering, the one most dreadful root.
Thousands of millions, hundreds of thousands, and billions of lotuses,
as well as innumerable [beings] among the gods, have been scattered by negligence.
Heedfulness is the supreme friend, and heedlessness is the enemy;
heedfulness is the supreme friend that is always beneficial to human beings.
But negligence is the supreme enemy; one should instead have another as one's friend.

This [heedlessness] brings an end to all that is auspicious; it is as extremely terrible as poison, the supreme path to the miserable states of existence—this is what is called "heedlessness. (Dhs 6.108)
Those men who are heedless due to negligence and who are likewise enamored by sense objects are deluded in mind and are constant consumers of suffering.
Those who are devoid of knowledge, disregarding fear and suffering, become equal to beasts; for them there is neither fear nor suffering, nor is there the vision of wisdom.
Possessed by those beasts, they were not seekers of happiness in the past.
The delight in food and sexual intercourse resides in the hearts of animals;
if that same delight belongs to the gods, then they are equal to animals.
Heedlessness is indeed a synonym for death;
for these [senses] sport excessively, standing before that which is to be reached by death.
When the time of death arrives, they will yield a terrible fruit.
Like poison, this must be avoided by all, for it is most difficult to endure; negligence is but another name for death within the hearts of embodied beings. (Dhs 6.113)
Death crushes those who were previously destroyed by negligence;
it is said that this constitutes a single portion of the happiness of a life lived according to the Dharma.
Heedfulness alone is the path to heaven;
it is renowned as heedfulness, the guide to the path of heaven. Profit and loss are both equal [in its regard], and likewise is liberation. (Dhs 6.115)
Heedfulness is a virtue and heedlessness is indeed a fault;
yet heedfulness and heedlessness are both equally present as virtue and fault.
Only those embodied beings with deluded minds perceive them in such a way. (Dhs 6.116)
They guard against the enemy and avoid [evil] through knowledge;
the three branches of the poisonous tree of negligence are firmly established.
Old age, disease, and death are ever present above him;
yet old age and the other afflictions do not oppress a person who is endowed with virtuous conduct.
The wise person who delights always in heedfulness remains happy in saṃsāra, being forever free from fear;
yet faults constantly cut him down—therefore, one should never embrace heedlessness. (Dhs 6.119)
One who is always free from fear attains unsurpassed happiness;
yet that happiness which arises from negligence is indeed eternal fear.
That which is liberated from that [suffering] is happiness, certain and imperishable;
yet hundreds of men here are utterly deluded by negligence.
Nevertheless, they remain under its control, established in negligence;
for the four perversions reside upon negligence.
Through the abandonment of negligence, even those enemies of the world perish—
that which consists of manifold conceptual constructions and manifold perils and fears.
Devoid of negligence, the gods, being virtuous, enjoy imperishable happiness;
that the world wanders in suffering is the result of negligence.
By abandoning negligence alone, one attains imperishable happiness. (Dhs 6.124)
All dharmas that have destroyed the outflows perish through negligence;
and this negligence of the gods increases further and further.
"How shall the gods, deluded by negligence, attain liberation?
Having reflected upon this with a tranquil mind, one should deliberate thus. (Dhs 6.126)
I should establish my welfare in such a way that it brings about happiness— whatever that may be—
beholding whatever deities there are and whatever happiness they possess, even if it be the slightest.
Only through the conditioned does the attainment of the state of permanence occur; for having gone to all that is permanent, this is the source of the conditioned.
Those conditioned phenomena that are unstable will inevitably perish.
Even the gods become partakers of suffering through the power of negligence;
those gods who are devoted to negligence are constant partakers of suffering.
The mind of those people who have been struck down by negligence acts in such a manner.
When separation occurs, one is tormented by suffering regarding sense objects that are full of desire and enveloped by craving.
By that, those gods who are subject to negligence have been deceived;
for the cultivation of negligence is the root of all misfortunes.
The avoidance of negligence brings security; its avoidance is auspicious, great, and the source of all well-being.
Yet sentient beings do not attain happiness, but are instead beset by sufferings.
One should exercise such discernment as fish do in water;
for those gods have fallen under the sway of negligence and are subject to women in heaven.
Those who are negligent become partakers of suffering; consumed by the fire of women, they are constant partakers of misery.
Therefore, with diligent effort, one should avoid women, as ordained by the gods.

One whose mind is agitated by desire should cultivate fortitude through the thought that it must be done, as well as regarding what ought and ought not to be done, and likewise concerning dharma and adharma. (Dhs 6.135)
For a person whose self is destroyed, that nirvana is indeed far away;
yet one who knows the reality of the absence of heaviness is skillful within the domain of the Dharma.
Only those who possess virtue attain happiness;
one who desires dharma and desires its fruit obtains such happiness.
Those who constantly follow dharma have washed away the stains of their sins.
Only those who are deluded by negligence experience suffering; those who dwell without negligence are always seen to be happy.
One who was previously struck down by negligence and deluded by negligence [suffers].
Even a god falls into negligence through intoxication;
whether a god or a human, such a person is not near to happiness.
That person who is intoxicated by liquor is eternally dead. (Dhs 6.139)
All men who are held by the faults of intoxication fall into hell;
the fault that arises from lack of restraint is designated as "intoxicant."
The gods, constantly deluded by intoxicants, go to hell;
they protect those who have not yet arisen, but never those who have already arisen.
Due to intoxication, the gods are defiled by their own forms and utterly deluded by sensual desires;
the gods are deluded by desire, and likewise by liquor as well.
The heedless person does not perceive reality;
they do not see the truth here, just as those blind from birth cannot see the path of the virtuous.
A mind agitated by heedlessness does not discern reality.
Therefore, heedlessness should be avoided on all sides like fire;
through heedlessness, the wholesome qualities that are the source of dharma are destroyed.
The indulgence in the poison of negligence leads only to destruction;
one who indulges in the poison of negligence does not see the path at all. Ten qualities perish for those who indulge in the poison of negligence.
The four meditative absorptions perish for one who is heedless;
the Buddhas, who are free from desire, praise heedfulness.
Those who are heedful become free from old age, while they loathe heedlessness—the cage of old age and death.
The heedful are liberated from old age; the heedless are consumers of suffering.
Heedlessness alone is bondage; this heedlessness is the bond that afflicts those of dull intellect. Through heedfulness, the virtuous have gone to the assembly of the gods. (Dhs 6.148)
Therefore, those who indulge in negligence fall even further;
a negligent person is never liberated from the entire cycle of existence.

For by the snare of the noose of heedlessness, embodied beings are bound such that they always perform what should not be done as if it were their duty, and perform their duty as if it were something improper.
Those who are heedful attain a succession of excellences;
through heedfulness, a person perceives everything as it truly is—not only in worldly affairs, but how much more so in those pertaining to the higher realms! Dhs 6.151.
The wise who have reached the further shore of intelligence do not praise negligence,
for it will cause the merit of the celestial beings to be utterly exhausted.
Then they will realize that the fruit of negligence is indeed bitter, for it brings about ruin;
this is the case for those whose minds are attached to sensual pleasures and who indulge in them until their end.
Therefore, there will be great suffering arising from downfall for those who constantly desire sense objects and whose minds are fixed on hope.
For those who are utterly intoxicated by the sight of women, there will be a downfall;
they constantly indulge in sensual pleasures, devoted to negligence and passion.
At the time of death, all those women will be abandoned;
when a god passes away, no one at all follows him.
Those who desire liberation abandon evil deeds through their actions; everything that goes before follows after them,
and this is indeed appropriate.
One should always cultivate what is beneficial and avoid all that is evil.
One should abandon negligence and intoxication; one should be free from negligence.
This negligence is the root of existence; indeed, negligence does not lead to peace.
Having reflected upon heedlessness and heedfulness, the wise person prospers in happiness.
This specific characteristic of heedlessness and heedfulness has been declared;
having reflected upon that, the wise person should always practice good conduct for the sake of happiness. (Dhs 6.159)
One who practices the Dharma never encounters suffering; a person who does not practice the Dharma never attains happiness.
Thus, living beings wander through cyclic existence according to their own karma.
Heedlessness leads to downfall;
for what purpose is this world destroyed by heedlessness?
Heedlessness is the destruction of the highest goods; heedlessness is the ultimate bondage.
Heedlessness leads to downfall, and heedlessness leads to hell;
heedlessness alone is proclaimed to be the sole cause of suffering.
One who delights in heedfulness attains nirvāṇa; therefore, a person seeking happiness should completely abandon heedlessness.
Those by whom heedlessness has been relinquished have attained the immutable state.
For he who delights in heedfulness is indeed close to nirvāṇa;
this state of heedfulness is the foremost step toward nirvāṇa.
One who is heedless is always miserable;
heedlessness is proclaimed to be the cause of downfall.
Every heedless person appears as if possessed by madness. (Dhs 6.165)
Such a person becomes insignificant in this world and is cooked in calamities;
the heedless man, though capable, behaves in a contrary manner.
Regarding causes, the ripening of karma, as well as death and rebirth—
the fierce fire of negligence drags one toward the hells;
therefore, for the sake of liberation from hell, one should utterly abandon negligence.
Those men who, having completely conquered negligence, are constantly devoted to knowledge,
cut through the bonds of the afflictions and attain the state where happiness arises.
Bound by the threads of karma and mounted upon the swing of the mind, sentient beings wander through worldly prosperity; do not indulge in negligence.
The happy one becomes miserable, and the miserable one indeed becomes happy; even the husband becomes satisfied. Do not indulge in negligence! Dhs 6.170.
One becomes a mother, a father, or a wife, and likewise a mother again; there is a great transformation among these—do not indulge in negligence.
From negligence arises passion; from passion, hatred is produced.
Having entered the path of vice, he runs headlong toward the hells.
Established in wisdom and free from negligence, one attains the auspicious path;
ascend the palace of wisdom and reach the unsurpassed security of yoga. This is the auspicious and supreme path: that which is devoid of negligence.
By that path, the wise constantly proceed toward Nirvana.
Contradiction regarding the perfection of the path, which corrupts the continuum of the mind, and the severing of the bridges of Dharma—this is proclaimed to be negligence. (Dhs 6.174)

Stricken by negligence, people go to destruction; negligence is seen as that which corrupts mindfulness and destroys right conduct. It leads to the ultimate state of miserable rebirths; thus does negligence prevail. (Dhs 6.175)
A man who is reviled by many does not find his own welfare;
like one who is as if dead, he finds nothing that should not be said nor any purpose among his duties.
These beings, who bear the forms of gods, are equal to animals;
struck by negligence and deluded, they dance and laugh.
Those who have arisen from the path and do not fall away, yet destroy their receptivity (kṣānti),
are like those caught in the ocean of human existence, running after heedlessness.
He is the progenitor of all faults, the bondage for those of evil deeds, the thief of all dharmas; thus does the enemy that is heedlessness proceed.
For all auspicious actions, negligence is indeed the enemy—not internal actions, nor external ones in any way.
A living being struck by negligence does not perceive his lost position. (Dhs 6.180)
With minds distracted by play and longing for dance and music,
those dwelling in the abodes of the gods will perish, even though they are not yet satiated with divine sense objects.
Deluded by negligence, these beings laugh even in the face of danger; they do not distinguish between the path and what is not the path, being equal to those born blind. (Dhs 6.182)
Only within the realm of desire do the heedless wander; wandering in the realm of desire like a wheel, they move through the five destinies.
Indeed, falling from the meditative absorptions is the very work of negligence.
Action performed through negligence leads to a downfall;
having attained the fourth station among the formless realms through worldly [attainment], they wander upon the swing of delusion—that is the activity of negligence. (Dhs 6.184)
Bound by the fetters of negligence and constrained by the snares of craving,
these mindless beings do not perceive this entire triple world.
That those who abide in the Dharma, having perceived the fear of craving,
proceed [to liberation] and no longer experience exhaustion— that is the activity of heedfulness.

Under the influence of negligence, a person encounters only suffering; the Tathāgatas declare that the suffering born of separation from what is dear arises in the hearts of men precisely through the practice of negligence. (Dhs 6.187)
For there are three misfortunes in the world by which this world is destroyed:
disease, old age, and death, which arise from negligence and laziness.
Just as all medicinal herbs, grasses, and other plants sprout from the earth,
so do the various afflictions of the heedless arise.
The sprout of the poison of negligence consists of attachment to women, the drinking of intoxicants, and sporting with the objects of the senses;
restlessness and indolence are the sprouts of the poison of negligence.
The definition of heedlessness and heedfulness:
"Heedlessness is supreme suffering; heedfulness is supreme happiness.
In brief, this is declared to be the definition of heedlessness and heedfulness.
Therefore, negligence should not be indulged;
for that reason, negligence must not be pursued by a person,
as it is the very foremost of all miserable states.
Having abandoned that source of thousands of sufferings,
the Buddhas proceed to the further shore of existence.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Chapter on Heedfulness.
(7) The Chapter on Loathing Desire:
Regarding the fact that desire is the cause of hell:
One should not take delight in desires; desires are the ultimate deceivers.
The bonds of cyclic existence are terrible; they are all causes for rebirth in hell.
For one who guards themselves amidst sensual desires, there is endless suffering;
for one bitten by the serpent of desire, there is no happiness whatsoever.
It would be better for one under the sway of passion and the like to cut out one's own tongue with a sharp-edged razor than to utter words driven by desire. (Dhs 7.3)
Deceived by passion, tormented by hatred, and fallen under the power of delusion, sentient beings utter unpleasant words. (Dhs 7.4)
One who is under the sway of passion always experiences the most intense suffering; even one who has suppressed minor passion may commit many evil deeds.
That fool, governed by passion, shall obtain misery after misery. (Dhs 7.5)
He speaks of the transformation of sensual desires:
"There is no satiety from these desires; they are neither pleasant nor eternal.
Because their transformation is extremely intense, one should therefore avoid them. (Dhs 7.6)
Men overcome by passion dwell in the abode of hell;
but for those who do not fall under the power of passion, there is no fear of hell.
The poison of sensual desire must be abandoned;
for desires arise from fierce and violent states and are fierce in their ultimate transformation.
Desires are like the fire of poison and should be avoided with great effort.
For one who has abandoned sensual desires and is constantly devoted to liberation,
unwholesome states perish just as darkness does at the rising of the sun.
The fire of desire casts one into hell;
having deluded the various sense-faculties that know the objects of the senses, these desires, which captivate the minds of the foolish, cause them to fall into hell. (Dhs 7.10)
Such is the magnitude of the fire of passion for one who is attached to the five sense objects through the five senses:
even for a moment, the fire of passion is never satiated by those sense objects. (Dhs 7.11)
Fire is born from conjunction; it is not born from disjunction.
Yet, through the very same conjunction, the fire of passion in men is extinguished by disjunction.
Fire does not burn from afar, for it has no object [at a distance];
yet the terrible fire of passion, which burns intensely, is equally fierce whether near or far.
Born from the wood of conceptualization, possessing the crooked force of longing,
and fueled by the ghee of craving— this fire of passion is also a burner.
For once this body has been burned, the fire is extinguished;
yet the fire of passion, being liberated from name and form, is never extinguished at all.
Fire, being an extreme burner, causes agitation among living beings;
yet even the exceedingly sharp fire of passion does not cause such agitation in men.
Arisen from the five sense-faculties and enveloped by the five objects of sense,
this fire of passion burns living beings through the force of the wind of craving.
Born from the friction-stick of discursive thought and nourished by sense objects, it burns like wood; yet it is not visible to people.
For just as the great fire of passion burns with increasing intensity,
so too do those blinded by passion indulge in their own pleasure.
Fire is a source of illumination, yet the fire of passion is shrouded by darkness;
therefore, the wise person should avoid the fire of passion as one would avoid the cold.
He speaks of the transformation of sense objects:
"A living being who is attached to sense objects can never be happy; sense objects, once bitten by sense objects, are terrible in their consequence. (Dhs 7.21)
Neither at the beginning, nor at the end, nor in the middle; neither in this world nor in the next, do sensual objects ever provide happiness in any way whatsoever. (Dhs 7.22)
For every fool is never satiated by sense objects, which arise from the play of craving, just as fire is not satiated by fuel. (Dhs 7.23)
Unsatisfied with sense objects, all these people are utterly deceived;
intent on their habitual pursuits, they are consumed by these very defects until death.

He describes the state of those blinded by the delusion of desire, who act according to their whims: "This indeed is the activity of delusion; if the gods were equal to the birds [in the sky], they would truly be gods. (Dhs 7.25)
At the end of the eons, the Lord of Rivers is praised for being scorched;
yet the eye is not satiated by forms, even in hundreds of millions of eons.
The ocean may reach satiety through its waters, such as those in its depths;
however, there is no satisfaction for the ocean's vision through objects of form, for it truly has none.
What pleasure can be conceived for one who is insatiable regarding sensual desires,
compared to the satisfaction that belongs to the embodied being who is free from craving and whose sorrow has passed away?
Blinded by great delusion, they become intoxicated, and these fools do not realize it,
just as the trees that serve as fuel for the Malaya fire are consumed in an instant by a mild flame.
Sensual desires are essence-less and deceptive; they have the nature of being stolen away in a dream and are like cities of the Gandharvas.
Sensual desires are empty, vain, and without substance; they are supremely deceptive.
Are desires equal to delusion, or are they comparable to a ripening fruit?
Desires that bring benefit to the world are proclaimed to be like fire. (Dhs 7.31)
Having understood the danger of desire— that by which embodied beings are deluded regarding its fruit— those who show it to others are pleased with one who is free from longing.
Even when conceived of otherwise, they return to their inherent nature; thus, for those who commit evil in every way, sensual desires are like poison in this world. (Dhs 7.33)
Their minds unsatiated by sensual desires, those gods fall once again; deluded and deceived by desire, they plunge into hell. (Dhs 7.34)
He censures women:
"Women are as fickle as the waves of a river and like streaks of lightning;
they possess the power of whirlpools and fish, and are the abode of the poison of the world of desire."
Desires increase when they are contemplated; once increased, they are like fire.
Desires are thus at their height both at the beginning and at the end; therefore, one should abandon desires.
Regarding the fruit of indulging in sensual desires:
for just as they are pursued, so do they increase;
yet sensual desires, when touched by the flames of fire, result in bitter ripening.
Regarding the fruit of abandoning sensual desires, it is said:
"Thus, always knowing this fault, the wise person should avoid sensual desires; for one who has turned away from sensual desires, there is ultimate happiness. (Dhs 7.38)
The fire of desire causes even the gods to fall;
countless thousands and millions of gods fall into the hell of the burning of desire, which is as terrifying as fire. (Dhs 7.39)
Just as those who seek happiness avoid fire, poison, and weapons,
so too should sensual desires always be avoided, for they are the causes of hell.
No man has ever been seen or heard of who, while under the sway of desire, was not deceived by desires nor afflicted by suffering. (Dhs 7.41)
Therefore, enough, enough with sensual desires; do not set your mind upon them.
In all circumstances, all sensual desires are like fire and poison.
In this beginningless cycle of existence, enemies arise from the mind;
yet, because of the sense of "I," there may be joy, which can never be found through sensual desires.
Delight born of desire is tainted, yields bitter fruit, and arises from suffering;
however, that delight which is free from desire is declared to be true delight.
The supreme goal of yogis is that which yogis attain by taking refuge in it; however,
pleasure produced by desire does not lead one to the immutable state.
One censures the decay born of desire; though sweet and delightful at first, it is like fire in its ripening.
Pleasure born from the fire of desire leads to hell.
Delightful at first sight, sweet, and always charming in its middle,
it is peaceful and pure in the end, leading one to the immutable state.
How can the foolish abandon that which is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end, ever as beautiful as a mother, and instead pursue the pleasure born of desire?
Sensual pleasure produced by desire burns constantly at its beginning, middle, and end; it is painful and perpetually enveloped by faults and other evils.
How can it be pursued by the foolish, when it is not seen to bring any true happiness? (Dhs 7.49)
Like a beautiful poisonous cluster of blossoms that burns upon touch, so too is pleasure produced by desire; it is like poison in its ultimate consequence.
Just as fire, when offered oblations, is extinguished by its own burning,
and as a sprout grows through the act of being scorched, so too is the pleasure produced by desire.
For a moth sees the fire but does not see the harm of its burning;
likewise, those of unrefined intellect perceive only the pleasure produced by desire.
The burning caused by passion that is constantly experienced by those full of desire—
such a burning, like that of a moth in a flame, they do not perceive at all.
Falling due to negligence regarding sensual desires is certain;
therefore, O gods, abandon the poison of desire and live forever.
May there not be a fall through the negligence of a birth lived in vain.
Those whose wholesome karma is exhausted and who are constantly deluded by sensual desires,
being deceived by the delusion of desire, abandon that [state] and go to hell.

Deluded by desire, he drinks the flower of the poisonous tree; just as a bee is made to drink the flower of a poisonous tree, so too does the deluded one enjoy this pleasure which is inherently poisonous. (Dhs 7.56)
Some unfortunate commoners might even survive after drinking poison;
yet for one who has drunk the poison of desire, life is not so difficult to regain.
Just as fire blazes in hell for the non-discerning,
so does the fire consisting of desire burn the inhabitants of heaven here.
For the fire of desire is indeed injurious;
this fire consisting of the bonds of the Vedas burns the hungry ghosts excessively.
For the fire that burns is injurious to men, being of the nature of constant seeking.
Thus, having avoided [the fires] on all sides as if they were equal to fire,
the entire world, deluded by desire, is burned without exception.
The mind attached to sense objects causes one to fall into calamity;
it is ever-fickle, great, and runs toward sense objects with a virtuous heart.
O fool, do not abandon that which you perceive as being in the future during times of calamity. (Dhs 7.61)
Guard your mind against sensual pleasures; it awakens only through calamity.
When a flood of misfortune has arisen, one suffers remorse thereafter.
Deluded by desire, they do not perceive even great danger; intoxicated by the vain intoxicants of desire, these gods are inherently weak.
Whirled about by desires, they wander on and do not see the great peril.
For those gods who place their trust in desires that bring about harm,
being devoid of wisdom, they awaken only later to their separation [from those very things].
Sensual desires are supreme deceivers; yet those who are not wise do not perceive this, being utterly deceived by their own minds.
Sensual pleasures, which are supremely deceptive, have become momentary and sweet.

One should not place trust in sensual desires, whether they have been obtained hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, or even billions of times; for once acquired, those desires are lost again, and a man should not trust in them.
Deluded by sensual desires, one is like a moth being consumed by the fire of hell;
from sense-objects comes intense bondage, and all such things are causes for hell.
Therefore, having abandoned them completely, let the mind be directed toward the highest good.
First stained by passion, then repelled by hatred,
and deluded by ignorance, they act contrary to what they have heard.
The fool, deluded by sensual desires, pursues them again and again;
like a moth, that deluded one is consumed by the fire of hell.
Those under the sway of desire fall even from the world of the gods; the fall from the celestial realm is inevitable in every respect.
Knowing this, one should never here become subject to desire.
Beings deceived by desire and deluded by desire,
dragged away by the snares of desire, fall perpetually into hell.
Having abandoned desire, one should apply the mind to one's own welfare; O beings, let this very calamity [of distraction] be turned toward your own welfare.
By means of a mind that is self-restrained, embodied beings do not suffer remorse.
Those men who are always bitten by the poison of the mind through the force of desire— those fools, struck by the fire of passion, fall under the power of death.
There is no satisfaction in desires, even when they are pursued with thirst for what is beneficial;
for even thirst does not produce satisfaction, and the mind is never truly satiated.
Through the lamp of knowledge, the senses attain satisfaction from their objects;
never will there be satisfaction for the senses through sense-objects themselves,
unless those people extinguish them with the lamp of knowledge.
Destruction through the pursuit of women is certain; for when a woman is served, she produces hundreds of discursive thoughts, just as a fire fanned by the wind increases in intensity. (Dhs 7.76)
Inflamed by the fire of desire, they never attain peace;
perceiving that, the wise one who contemplates the reality of Buddhahood constantly extinguishes desires, which are perpetually ignited by the fire of passion with impetuous force.
All those wise ones who always have deluded minds and are constantly intent upon sense objects— whatever they delight in is entirely the activity of delusion.
For when served by the wise, the fire of the sense-objects increases;
bound by this snare, it is like a fire fanned by the wind.

Even the immortals, when overcome by passion and constantly intent upon sense objects, fall from their immortal state; these beings, deceived by the passion of delusion, fall from the world of the gods.
With their minds absorbed in them, these beings delight in sense objects there,
and they do not perceive the suffering that will arise from separation.
This pleasure at first, which is divine and endowed with the five qualities, is indeed painful and brings only suffering born of separation;
it does not equal even a sixteenth part of the sorrow arising from that separation.
For the obstruction of sensual desires is brought about by people themselves;
likewise, for one who possesses craving, satisfaction never arises from those very desires.
For one who pursues sensual desires with a mind that is never free from longing, suffering never attains peace; for one who constantly indulges in desires,
the suffering that persists as a latent tendency throughout the long night is never extinguished.
The fool is protected [from evil] only briefly; he awakens only through calamity.
But when calamity has arrived, he finally understands that this is its fruit.
For these sensual pleasures, though appearing sweet and auspicious, are extremely terrible;
they are the messengers of hell, wandering about as doers of harm.
Those who are consumed by the fire of sense objects go to hell; that mortal among them who places his trust [in such objects] is one whose eye of knowledge has been disparaged.
That man, for whom the fire of sense objects is like a mere cloud, goes to hell.
Sensual pleasures offer little taste and little substance; they constantly deceive men.
Like a city of the Gandharvas, these pleasures appear auspicious only in their fleeting flavor.
Even gods, deluded by sense objects, go to a miserable state,
just as the light of a lamp is repeatedly covered by ashes.
And the gods, deluded by sense objects, do not bestow [favor] upon one who is lacking in mental composure.
Constantly following the dictates of desire and impetuously attached to sense objects,
they do not perceive the great suffering that is inevitably to come.
He whose mind regards sensual pleasures as delightful will later, when calamity has arrived, lament like a fool.
For one blinded by intoxication with desire and deluded by sense objects,
there is no constant happiness— that which is the unsurpassed among all pleasures.
In comparison with internal happiness, sensual pleasure is most inferior;
whatever sensual pleasure exists in the world and whatever pleasure arises from craving, this does not equal even a sixteenth part of that single internal happiness. (Dhs 7.93)
The lustful person never enjoys happiness; as long as desire remains in one's heart, one does not abide in bliss.
Worthy of experiencing all suffering, such a person runs headlong into the hells.
There is no satisfaction for humans even with hundreds of sensual enjoyments;
where there is pleasure, there is no satisfaction for those who indulge in sense objects.
When indulged in constantly, sensual desires increase again and again;
once increased, they become like poison and lead to one's downfall.
Skilled in misfortune, terrible, and always causes for falling,
the festivals of the sense-objects do not abandon them.
For that ocean of vision, there is no satiety with forms;
likewise, there is no satiety with tastes, even with those that are pleasant and delightful to the mind.
The nose is never satisfied even by perfumes;
tactile sensations, when experienced through direct contact, are indulged in yet one is never satiated.
Even with lovely and very sweet sounds, the ear finds no satisfaction;
nor does the mind, though confident in its gratification, find contentment as it continues to grow.
The six sense-faculties, when uncontrolled and restless in their attachment to pleasure, cause one to fall into the realms of desire; thus,
being constantly robbed of their stability, they wander repeatedly through those various spheres of sensual enjoyment.
There is no satisfaction for the gods, just as there is none for elephants with grass; this is the very nature of fire: it knows no satiety.
These six fierce fires, fanned by the wind of discursive thought,
constantly wander, robbed of their senses, through the various realms of desire.
Those whose senses are consumed go to hell;
by them this world is burned, yet the unintelligent person does not perceive it.
These things, appearing auspicious through their taste, are indeed the causes of hell.
One who is deluded by desire is deceived by pleasure; desires are cravings for sense objects, like licking serpents.
This excellent-eyed horse, however, is not deluded by desires.
A man under the sway of desire is like one deprived of sight; being utterly deluded and pursuing pleasure, desire drives him toward the hells.
One who is deprived of sight is not cast into hell, provided he is endowed with virtuous conduct.
Therefore, it is better for a man to be sightless than to be under the sway of desire;
fools are incapable of being deceived by desires that bring about harm.
For those who act according to their desires, knowledge and the like are difficult to obtain; deluded by their own minds, they do not feel weary of sensual pleasures.
Neither knowledge nor discernment exists for those who act according to their desires. (Dhs 7.108)
Desire leads one to the abode of death;
having struck down the suffering born of desire, those who again fall under the sway of desire— desires that appear in the form of friends but are like the fruit of the *kimpāka* tree— are destroyed.
They lead them to the abode of death and to the miserable states again and again.
Just as the waters of many rivers cannot be turned back,
so too the happiness attained by men never turns back in any way.
That man who is not satisfied with sensual pleasures, despite having repeatedly attained the enjoyments of forests and groves that bring happiness, goes to the lowest state.
A living being overcome by negligence, intent upon the relish of sensual pleasures,
is constantly guarded by [the senses] regarding forms, yet it is subject to transformation.
How indeed, O gods, will those beings whose nature consists of dense shadows and who are mixed with karma be able to move within the realm of desire?
Sensual pleasures should never be indulged in;
for even if they were eternal, those pleasures would still be like poison.
Although craving for sensual pleasure causes suffering, that craving for sensual pleasure is not of a different nature from birth;
it is even more so in that it is eternally for the sake of suffering, empty, and merely the self.
How can those of unawakened intellect protect themselves amidst those ripenings of suffering?
Foolish and dull-witted people are protected by the flavors of sensual desire;
they do not perceive the danger, which is like the fruit of the *kimpāka* tree.
Bound by forms, sounds, and the like, and afflicted by craving, these people, deluded by the fruits of their evil deeds, burn incessantly and without autonomy. (Dhs 7.117)
Having tasted sensual pleasures, which are like poisonous fruits,
men whose minds are not satisfied by craving fall again into hell.
Just as rivers swell when rain falls upon them,
so too does the fire of the gods increase through the downpour of sensual desires.
There is no end to the pleasure of sensual desire;
even a fish born of the water is seen to be afflicted by thirst.
In this same way, a deity, though their happiness has increased, is not satiated.
Just as there is no end to space, nor even any doubt of such an end,
so too there is no end to sensual desires for those possessed by desire, nor is there any exhaustion of them.
The ocean, garlanded with waves, may find no satisfaction through waters and the like;
yet for one who is unsatiated by desires, there is no satisfaction whatsoever.
Foolish gods are not satiated by objects they have not yet attained;
devoted to their constant craving for pleasure, they are never satisfied by sense objects.
Desire leads to torment,
not to peace,
even when intense calamity has arrived and one is falling repeatedly.
Therefore, one is tormented by that object; desire for what is beyond it cannot be overcome.
Having observed these men who betray trust out of lust, people abandon them when they fall into calamity; for such men indeed perish.
There is no happiness for one who is insatiable, nor can one be satisfied by sense objects; having understood those things which appear to bring satisfaction, one should abandon them. (Dhs 7.126)
Having abandoned sense objects, peace—which is the root of happiness—should always be cultivated; for sense objects are considered to be unhappiness.
Therefore, O gods, having avoided the serpents that are sense objects, you should abide in the bliss of peace.
Great fear arises from sense objects such as killing, imprisonment, and disease; it is through these very sense objects that delusion is born here in this saṃsāra. (Dhs 7.128)
Unions end in separation by the hundreds and thousands;
this has always been seen in birth after birth by the followers of the Sugata, who perceive reality.
The cycle of existence consisting of manifold pleasures is indeed of the nature of sense objects;
for manifold pleasure is found within sense objects, and through sense objects one is born again and again in every birth. (Dhs 7.130)
Those things which cannot be avoided even through hardships by one whose mind is undeluded—those very same things those blinded by delusion and lacking in wisdom pursue once again. (Dhs 7.131)
Those who indulge in the enemies that are the sense-objects are fools;
for a man always avoids them out of fear of being deceived by those enemies.
Indeed, the sense-objects are like enemies; they can never be brought under control.
Bound by desire, they are always foolish through delusion;
how is it that these fools, deluded by their own karma, do not renounce [it]? (Dhs 7.133)
Just as someone out of fear of fire might yet resort to that very fire, so too does one who is deluded by sense objects indulge in those very sense objects. (Dhs 7.134)
Just as a noose bound together with sinews may appear beautiful to the eye,
so too this noose of sensual objects, though most cruel, appears delightful.

Sensual pleasure leads to destruction, just like the taste of the *kiṃpāka* fruit, which is sweet at first and appears highly beneficial; likewise, such pleasure for human beings results in ruin later on. (Dhs 7.136)
Just as a moth, deluded by infatuation, falls upon the flame of a lamp and is consumed by it, so too is this [worldly] pleasure sought. (Dhs 7.137)
For just as fools, not knowing this, touch fire out of a desire for the pleasure of a beautiful body, thinking "this will be happiness," so it is with this [pleasure]. (Dhs 7.138)
The mere cessation of thirst alone gives rise to happiness, just as a beautiful wild deer, afflicted by thirst, runs toward water;
yet for that [deer], there is no actual cessation of thirst—this is what is intended by "happiness. (Dhs 7.139)
The gods are never satiated, they do not become satiated, nor will there ever be satisfaction through sense objects; therefore, desire does not lead to peace.
Intoxicated by sense objects, they experience suffering;
sensual pleasures, though providing happiness in the present, do not bring about welfare in the end.
Delighted by sense objects, the gods are always distracted in mind.
For one who is intoxicated by various pleasures and deceived by sensory objects,
no peace exists when the time of death has arrived.
Death approaches in due course, and it is certain to come even for the gods who are captivated by sense objects and whose intellects are distracted by desire.
Sensual desires are harmful; may the gods recognize today for me the suffering born of separation from them.
One should not dwell upon sensual pleasures even for a moment. (Dhs 7.144)
Burning with the fire of passion and utterly deluded, beings are born with a fear of their own impermanent bodies; yet sensual desires are eternally harmful.
Time, in turn, pursues those who are thus deluded. (Dhs 7.145)
The gods, being utterly deluded, are constantly consumed by the fire of passion;
yet, even while burning, they praise the ultimate reality again and again.
Constantly wandering like the wheel of a chariot, deluded by sense objects, they remain attached to those very objects and are not protected; thus, suffering remains as their lot.
This entire triple world revolves like the wheel of a chariot.
Sensual desires are like a city of Gandharvas;
beings, deluded by ignorance, are eternal consumers of suffering.
Sensual desires are proclaimed to be equal to lightning and the circle of a whirling firebrand.
In a dream, they are like a city of Gandharvas—deceptive and illusory.
The mind that clings to the five aggregates dwells in suffering; a wise person should not form the notion of a self regarding what is impermanent, suffering, and empty.
The five aggregates have been declared by the Asuras to be devoid of any inherent nature, even when appearing auspicious.
Otherwise, even a wise man is forcibly overcome by sensual desires as if by poison;
yet that sage has reached the further shore, is peaceful, and is compassionate toward all beings.
Turning his face toward nirvāṇa, he attains peace by casting off the snare consisting of the afflictions, standing in the very presence of nirvāṇa.
For one who is distracted by sensual desires, talk of peace is in vain; and for one who delights in the practice of passion, no discourse on faults will take root.
How can there be peace for that person whose mind is thus distracted?
Let one observe how the bewildered mind runs toward sense objects;
having strayed from the path of the true Dharma, it is reborn in the hells.
What is the use of desires that are unstable, fleeting, and perishable— desires comparable to lightning,
resembling the *kiṃpāka* fruit, poison, weapons, or fire, and which are the causes of suffering?
The fire of desire increases the more one indulges in sense objects;
for as they are cultivated, they grow accordingly.
Indeed, these things bring no satisfaction and are the causes of the burning of fire.
Only by abandoning sensual desires do people attain happiness; those gods who, though desiring happiness, are bewildered by the defect of burning passion—
by abandoning inauspicious desires, they will thereafter find true well-being.
Sensual desires are as fleeting as a flash of lightning;
they deceive the deluded person, acting like a snare that ensnares them.
Their appearance is as unstable as a flickering eye; sensual desires are indeed comparable to a flash of lightning.
Those who, driven by thirst for sensual pleasure, pursue desires higher and higher, are consumed by the fire of passion; from one burning, they shall pass to another.
For those gods who are deluded by desire are indeed most utterly foolish; or rather, so are those who do not go toward that supreme happiness which is happiness itself. (Dhs 7.159)
For one who goes toward nirvāṇa, there is no happiness without liberation;
therefore, one should not indulge in sensual desires, for the pursuit of desire is painful.
The sense faculties of one who indulges in passion are never satiated by their objects; and when there is no satisfaction, how can happiness ever truly enter? (Dhs 7.161)
He knows its end on both sides— from the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra—
and he abandons the evil desires that dwell within the realm of craving.
The arising and passing away of desire should be properly observed:
"These mountain peaks are beautiful with various trees;
by resorting to them, one contemplates the arising and passing away of desires. (Dhs 7.163)
One should accomplish what is desired through ethical conduct and faith, not through the fetters of desire; for that which is born of desire leads to destruction.
One does not obtain through ethical conduct and faith that which is the cause of misfortune.
For this death born of desire leads one into the wilderness of saṃsāra.
Having abandoned evils, one should follow the path of peace that brings happiness,
wherein the forest is called a bond only when it is disconnected from desire;
therein one shines forth from evil, and therein peace is the bringer of happiness.
That alone is called great knowledge; it is wealth that is indestructible.

Those who are liberated from the thirst for sensual pleasures, who are not attached to desires and not enticed by craving, have reached the auspicious state; they do not enter the fire of desire. (Dhs 7.166)
Unsatisfied men surely perish;
there is never satiety with sensual desires. Desires are not known to lead to peace; joined with their companion, craving, they blaze like fire. (Dhs 7.167)
Men, gods, and likewise serpents perish when they remain unsatiated;
indeed, they are utterly destroyed, becoming merely fuel for the fires of hell.
For one deluded by craving, who is struck down by discursive thoughts and deceived by sense objects, this King Death will become the sovereign over him who is bewildered by craving. (Dhs 7.169)
Those addicted to sensual desires do not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful; for those who are deeply attached to the enjoyment of desires, there is no such distinction.
All people are utterly deluded by all the objects of the senses known as "desires."
Those gods who follow the sway of desire are bound by sense objects themselves and are dragged away by sense objects themselves, for they are deluded in mind;
but those who are endowed with the qualities of the Buddha do not follow the sway of desire.
Regarding the definition of "the steadfast":
he who is not deluded by pleasures—especially those sensual desires present now that are full of faults—is called "steadfast. (Dhs 7.172)
He describes the state of the gods who have fallen into sensual desires:
"The gods have fallen into sensual desires that are as diverse as dream-bodies, like garlands of flames, and equal to the cities of the Gandharvas. (Dhs 7.173)
The gods have fallen into vast wildernesses—the sense-pleasures—which give rise to craving and bring about destruction at their end. (Dhs 7.174)
The gods have fallen into these desires, which are trivial, possessed of three holes, comparable to the current of a river, flickering, and exceedingly difficult to traverse. (Dhs 7.175)
The gods have fallen into desires that are as unstable as the moon reflected in water with waves stirred by the wind, and as fleeting as worlds within a whirling wheel.
The gods have fallen into sensual pleasures that are equal to a circle of lightning flashes, comparable to a mirage, and as essence-less as foam.
The gods have fallen into desires that are like the core of a plantain tree and comparable to the flapping ears of an elephant, as fleeting as the force of a river's waves. (Dhs 7.178)
The gods have fallen into these sensual pleasures, which are like the fruit of the *kiṃpāka* tree, whose nature is like fire, and which resemble rays of illusion. (Dhs 7.179)
Desire is to be avoided by means of the goad of knowledge;
for those who perceive reality ward off sense objects with the goad of knowledge—
those objects which are considered unliberated, fickle, intense, and the cause of all misfortune.
Sense objects alone are the cause for falling into hell; and the hope for sense objects belongs to the deluded whose minds have been stolen by their own conceptual constructions.
This very thirst for life approaches as the noose of death.
A bond.
Sensual desires cook the living being of feeble mind in hell;
yet those fools, deceived by delusion, do not perceive this.
All sense objects are fickle, like a city of Gandharvas;
for they bring about suffering and are the five causes of hell.
Passion born of conceptualization causes one to fall into hell;
from conceptualization passion arises, and from passion anger proceeds.
A person overcome by anger experiences the hells. (Dhs 7.184)
Therefore, one should strive to attain nirvāṇa preceded by the renunciation of sensual desires; having abandoned desire, expelled anger,
and likewise abandoned delusion, the wise person should be oriented toward nirvāṇa.
For those traveling the path to Nirvāṇa, desire must be avoided like an enemy; sense objects should be known as enemies, and Nirvāṇa alone as a friend.
A person whose attachment to sense objects has come to rest attains Nirvāṇa.
Unstained by the impurities of desire, one attains stainless radiance;
free from greed and unstained by the impurities of desire, with faults abandoned, the thirst for arrows destroyed,
and with defilements utterly exhausted, that person of stainless radiance proceeds to peace, enjoying his own fruit.
One who seeks happiness attains peace only by abandoning desire; he who has pulled himself out from the mire of desire is free from fault and always seeks the welfare of all sentient beings.
Stainless, with a mind that is neither agitated nor bound,
he forcibly attains the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Chapter on Loathing Desire.
(8) The Chapter on Craving:
The fire of craving itself is hell.
The fire of craving, which blazes for the sake of continued existence, is said to be cool;
yet it is the fire of hell for those in hell, and the fire of craving throughout the three realms.
For this fire that arises in hell is like the fire at the end of an eon;
it is a fire filled with many flames, produced from the cause of craving.
Through the exhaustion of karma, evildoers are liberated from hell;
yet men who follow the sway of craving are burned within the three realms.
In beginningless saṃsāra, the fire of craving is the supreme binder;
the fire of craving leads to hell, therefore the fire that produces hell does not originate from external fire.

The fire of craving burns both the body and the mind; even the infernal fire of hell could not cause such extreme burning of the limbs. It is the fire of craving that produces physical and mental torment for human beings. (Dhs 8.5)
The fire of craving is distinguished by its commonality with ordinary fire;
therefore, the fire arising from the cause of craving is even more distinguished.
The fire of craving belonging to those in hell is considered to be truly incomparable.
This fire arises from the three times, resides in the three places, has three causes, and illuminates the three types of action.
It should be known as arising from the three times, and likewise as being beyond the fire of craving.
The fire of craving is always and everywhere a burner:
the fire of passion burns in heaven, the fire of hatred likewise in the animal realm, and the fire of delusion burns in evil states; yet the fire of craving remains present at all times.
The fire of craving has pride as its smoke and envy as its flame; it originates from the wealth of conceptualization.
This fire of greed consumes the world, not the fire born of sensual desire. (Dhs 8.9)
The fire of craving increases precisely through the indulgence of sense objects;
for those who are bitten by the venomous serpent of greed, no peace exists.
When greed is served and cultivated, it increases all the more.
There is no enemy on earth equal to greed; just as fire increases manifold upon obtaining fuel, it is possible to restrain [fire], but not so greed.
The fire of delusion cannot [be extinguished]. // Dhs 8.11 //
Deceived by greed, the world revolves like a wheel;
in this world without beginning or end, there is no enemy equal to greed.
Deceived by greed, they enter the waters of the ocean,
and they also enter into battle, which is dense with a multitude of weapons.
For it is out of greed that kings destroy one another;
pierced by the terrifying points of spears and swords, they fight out of thirst for wealth.
Those who are liberated from the poison of craving, who have discarded the embers of greed,
and for whom a clod of earth and gold are equal, are indeed close to Nirvana.
The fire of greed is more dangerous than all others;
one is consumed by the greed for wealth that is utterly improper. Fire is not dangerous in that place where the fire of greed prevails. (Dhs 8.16)

Without the pacification of greed, talk of nirvāṇa is in vain; a wise person should swiftly strike down those [defilements] through the effort of supporting themselves against greed. For one whose greed is unextinguished, nirvāṇa remains far away. (Dhs 8.17)
Those men who renounce the happiness of existence and do not rejoice in the joy born of desire for existence do not encounter the suffering born of existence even in their dreams.
Death drags away people bound by craving, just as a *śambūka* snail drags along fish caught in a net;
likewise, death draws forth sentient beings who are bound by craving. (Dhs 8.19)
Just as a deer pierced by poisoned arrows does not release the poison anywhere it runs toward, so too does the poison of craving spread wherever men go. (Dhs 8.20)
Just as a fire consumes dry fuel, so does the movement of the river flowing with its current, which pursues one's own course, burn the foolish. (Dhs 8.21)
Sense objects are pleasant at first sight but resemble a blazing fire in their maturation; therefore, craving must be abandoned if true happiness is desired. (Dhs 8.22)
Just as fish caught on a hook are subject to death, so too do those tormented by sense objects run about in misery. (Dhs 8.23)
The fire of craving is greater even than hell;
both hell and its inhabitants are established upon great craving.
Mortals who live off the wives of others fall into destruction.
Even a sage who is impelled by craving experiences suffering;
a sage is not one who is impelled by the craving for improper actions and thoughts.
Arising from the six sense faculties, it burns with the fuel of sensory objects. (Dhs 8.25)
The fire of craving indeed burns even the gods;
the fire of craving burns the god, whereas the bodily fire does not burn him in any way.
Enveloped by pleasure, delighting in pleasure, [they are consumed] by pleasure.
They have been deceived.
Deceived by craving, one does not even perceive the fall;
deceived by craving, they do not perceive the fall.
The entire cycle of existence is enveloped in craving and filled with garlands of flames.
People who have fallen under the power of the fire of craving go to an evil rebirth;
the world of the gods is likewise surrounded on all sides by the fires of craving.
The fire of craving increases constantly; the one who is impassioned, helpless, and brought under the sway of sensual enjoyments is consumed.
Just as a flame grows ever stronger upon obtaining fuel, so does it increase. (Dhs 8.29)
In whatever way humans obtain pleasure, the fire of craving increases;
it consumes men just as a wood-fire, though illuminating by its burning, consumes the fuel.
The fire of craving burns the world and cannot be avoided;
yet those who have crossed the vast river made terrifying by conceptual constructions [are liberated].
Those who are empty of the snare of craving attain supreme peace;
for those whom craving does not afflict have indeed reached supreme peace—
those who are liberated from the snare of craving and are devoid of the fault of attachment.
For those wise ones are freed from the stain of evil and are devoid of sorrow;
whereas men have been deceived by craving for thousands of millions of eons.
Deceived by craving, the world worships craving itself; fallen under the power of illusion and delusion, they do not renounce sense objects.
Deceived by craving, the world pursues craving itself.
Just as a thirsty man drinks salt water, a living being is not satisfied by it, yet he becomes parched again and again. (Dhs 8.35)
One should not indulge in craving, which causes suffering;
for an inferior person, afflicted by craving, exerts himself only toward sense objects.
Therefore, one should not indulge in craving, for that craving is difficult to overcome. (Dhs 8.36)
One under the sway of craving is never liberated;
for a person under the sway of craving is not released from saṃsāra.
Even after experiencing unsurpassed pleasures among the gods, living beings [return].
Dragged away by the noose of craving, they fall into hell;
dragged away by the noose of craving, they fall into hell once again—a place devoid of self-mastery, lacking even the slightest goodness, and consisting eternally of bitter suffering. (Dhs 8.38)
Satisfaction never arises from craving;
by being liberated through the abandonment of craving, one attains the true path.
For one who possesses craving, how could there be satisfaction regarding sense objects?
That is true contentment which belongs to the embodied being who is free from craving and devoid of sorrow;
yet such people are deprived of it by their own discursive thoughts and led astray by negligence.
Through craving, even gods go to hell;
through craving, gods who were satisfied fall back into hell. That gods have gone to hell is the ultimate mockery.
Having become supreme players, living beings, deluded in mind, have fallen under the sway of desire and do not tremble at the cycle of existence.
Through craving, one attains a state of extreme suffering;
deceived by craving, they go from sorrow to even greater sorrow.
Just as the attainment of pleasure increases, so too does that ensnaring craving grow.
For one who is scorched by the fire of the net and possessed of craving, there is no end to the number of discursive thoughts that drag one toward the hells. (Dhs 8.44)
Those who pursue sense objects enter the very mouth of death through craving;
however, the King of Death drags away those who are free from discursive thought.
Those who are under the sway of discursive thoughts and desires go toward the realm of craving.
Those who are heedless regarding the taste of sensual pleasures and are attached to sense objects remain in suffering;
seeing one who enjoys true happiness, the wise do not desire such a state for beings who are heedless regarding the taste of sensual pleasures and who crave sense objects. (Dhs 8.46)
Embodied beings are scorched by craving; like a net, it constantly afflicts them as it binds them.
This very fivefold object-base is not scorched at all by craving.
Those who are liberated from craving become stainless;
being stainless through liberation from craving, they do not go to the city of evil.
The defects of conceptualization are crooked, arising from the dust of the threefold afflictions.
Driven by craving, people wander in the ocean of saṃsāra; they fall into the deep waters of negligence, serving the passion for women.
They are fickle due to the sounds of singing and musical instruments, and because of the rapid consumption of liquor.
With all their sense-objects covered and their minds tossed by turbulent waves,
they flow along the treacherous rivers of craving, never finding a secure course.
And those gods, utterly deluded and deceived by passion, plunge [into this state],
having been produced from the wood of the three defects by the force of the wind of negligence.
The fire of craving burns the hosts of gods, yet they do not realize it—
not for even a single moment, nor a lava, nor a muhūrta, in any way whatsoever.
This ground of craving, filled with the water of discursive thought, is not enjoyed by gods who have fallen under the power of craving; it is the ultimate limit. (Dhs 8.53)

Burning with the serpent of craving and brought under the power of time, beings become helpless in that place where the gods, following the dictates of desire, sport; [a place] governed by the fierce mind and other faculties, wherein the poison of craving spreads. (Dhs 8.54)
Why do you lament in vain, having been bitten by the five-headed serpent?
This river of craving is vast, originating from five sources.
Constantly scattered by the Indra’s net of craving and delusion,
the gods are thus ensnared in conceptual proliferation that they do not partake in what is auspicious.
Sprinkled with the clarified butter of the objects of craving, desire certainly increases; for the senses are never satiated by pleasures in any way.
Just as fire grows when sprinkled with clarified butter, so too does craving increase.

Driven by craving, people wander through various states of existence with manifold pleasures; this craving is a net that destroys the world, constantly causing men to roam among the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals. (Dhs 8.58)
Free from craving and released from bondage, one attains the supreme goal;
while fools cling to the swing of death and rebirth,
those of virtuous conduct who are free from craving have gone to that supreme goal.
The wise, who have cast off their bonds, are free from sorrow and free from distress;
they who do not follow the sway of craving always attain happiness.
Those sages are not pierced by the snares consisting of the suffering of birth.
The relinquishing of craving impels toward knowledge those whose minds are directed toward wisdom in all circumstances;
those whose minds are released into the signless and who have cast off craving.
Having cleared the wilderness of defilements, they have reached the shore where happiness arises.
Those who are intoxicated by craving and delusion wander from existence to existence; likewise, those hosts of gods who are deluded by pleasure and happiness will wander from existence to existence.
Day and night, craving torments those who engage in fraudulent dealings that steal the hearts of others,
or those who are full of ignorance and constantly long for burning affliction.
Neither by night nor by day does their heart become serene.
Those who are overcome by greed become like straw fire; one should not place trust in them by nature, for their minds are dominated by greed as they covet the property of others. (Dhs 8.64)
Fear of the serpent that is the fuel of sense objects is indeed appropriate;
for every man fears the fuel of sense objects as he would a serpent. Those men are utterly overwhelmed by greed for sense objects alone. (Dhs 8.65)
Under the sway of craving, they take birth in various wombs;
upon death, they go to hell and likewise to the realm of hungry ghosts.
Even when liberated from that, they emerge from the fires of hell.
Those who constantly desire [sensual pleasures] become partakers of suffering; for five hundred births they remain thus full of longing.
Pale and dejected of countenance, they are perpetually subject to misery.
All human beings have their minds afflicted by greed.
Those who are endowed with discernment, who have abandoned greed, and who always long for knowledge—
those wise and virtuous ones have attained the supreme goal.
Those men whose hearts are set on nirvāṇa are forever free from greed and delusion.
For one attracted by greed there is downfall;
for one bitten by the venomous serpent of greed, downfall is certain.
As it is being practiced, the world certainly increases again and again.
Just as fire increases when it takes up dry fuel,
so too do sentient beings who delight in the thirst for wealth become intent upon the acquisition of wealth.
When the time of death has arrived, people abandon their wealth helplessly;
however, whatever is produced through yoga does not perish at all.
One whose nature is greed goes to a terrible hell;
by that wealth, the greedy person is led deeply into hell.
Others enjoy that wealth, while he alone is defiled by the sin.
They go to a terrible hell and are consumed by remorse;
for misfortune appears in the form of gain, and suffering in the form of pleasure.
A wise person should practice the renunciation of greed;
this greed dwells in the heart even while appearing in the form of a friend.
A wise person should not rely upon greed, for the fire of greed burns constantly. (Dhs 8.74)
Burnt by greed, sentient beings become destined for hell; scorched by that [greed], they subsequently go to hell.
For these worldly possessions are common to all and devoid of true happiness.
Liberation from the fear of craving alone is what brings them true welfare; why then do those of dull intellect commit evil for their sake?
For one who is liberated from the fear of craving and is free from all hope, [there is no further bondage].
For the wise one who has transcended doubt, the state of being is eternally established;
while the world rushes after prosperity, it does not perceive adversity.
Prosperity ends in decay; indeed, prosperity ends in calamity, just as the day ends in its passing.
Just as prosperity remains for a time, so too does misfortune remain, even that which is evil.
Even gods fall into hell because of sensual enjoyments; one who is not satisfied with desires is consumed by craving for them.
This is true even for one whose desired prosperities are constant and who always seeks what is agreeable. (Dhs 8.79)
If one does not destroy them, their craving remains; though craving destroyed brings happiness, those gods who are thus absorbed in sensual enjoyments go to hell.
The Tathāgatas declare that all such ignoble conduct leads men to fall into hell by the hundreds. (Dhs 8.81)

The deluded do not understand the life of an ascetic; the wise know it to be the activity of a vast woman. Those who are infatuated do not perceive that their own life is short and fleeting. (Dhs 8.82)
Through craving, good deeds are destroyed;
though good deeds perish, craving itself does not perish.
Sentient beings, passing from existence to existence, do not perceive what is auspicious or inauspicious.
The desired fruit of the auspicious is that which the gods enjoy;
likewise, the inauspicious is seen as the unhappiness born of falling into the lower realms.
Those who have abandoned both the auspicious and the inauspicious become free from old age and death;
those who have abandoned the auspicious and the inauspicious are devoid of the fault of attachment.
They have gone to the supreme state, which is free from old age and death.
Enveloped by the river of craving, people do not understand that wheel of existence with its five spokes, which is preceded by craving as its hub;
surrounded by the river of passion, the world does not perceive it.
This vast river of craving should be known as having turbulent whirlpools of faults and being infested with crocodiles of volitional constructions; yet the world does not realize this.
Craving deceives throughout the three times;
craving is a deceiver in the three times and constantly produces ignorance. A wise person should not place trust in it, for it is indeed the bond of saṃsāra. (Dhs 8.88)
Craving, which is the cause of bondage for the world, appears like a friend at times, yet it cuts one down like an enemy;
a wise person should not place trust in it, for it is indeed the fetter of the world.
For it is possible to cut through a bond made of iron or likewise of wood;
but it is not possible for those who constantly seek sensual pleasures to cut through the bond of craving.
He for whom this severance of bonds is desired, and for whom imperishable happiness is desired—
such a person shall be liberated from craving and become one who creates wealth through wisdom.
Through knowledge, the cutting down of the tree of craving must be accomplished;
the light of knowledge is the light of happiness, while suffering is known as the darkness of craving.
Therefore, by relying upon the light, the wise man dispels the darkness.
With the sharp sword of wisdom, one cuts down the tree of craving;
having cut down that tree, that person attains unsurpassed happiness. (Dhs 8.93)
For this river is indeed full of defects and turbulent with its sources;
a wise person does not abandon existence without first casting off these defects.
Relying on the boat of wisdom, one crosses to the far shore of the river of craving— the river that flows through the three worlds and is difficult to cross due to its whirlpools of negligence.
By fully relying on the boat of wisdom, they go to the shore that is free from affliction.
Great desire is a vast canopy under which the foolish come;
therefore, you must bind this great desire with the eye of wisdom.
Great desire itself is a wound of the heart;
for that greedy person in whose heart such a severe wound of great desire arises, there is no happiness, neither by night nor by day. (Dhs 8.97)
But when it has arisen from conceptualization and is fanned by the wind of craving, the fire consisting of great desire burns the hearts of men. (Dhs 8.98)
Through greed, people do what is harmful to themselves;
with minds enveloped by greed and small-minded, men abandon even their essential lives out of thirst for wealth. (Dhs 8.99)
For wise men declare that all the evil deeds which people commit on this earth are performed for the sake of acquiring wealth.
Those who do not commit acts of violence and even those who enter into blazing fire—
all this they do through the fault of greed, bringing harm upon themselves.
Various sufferings, such as weapons and the wind, enter [them] from all sides; indeed,
deluded men [experience this], for greed is the cause therein.
The fire of desire resides eternally in the hearts of men who constantly crave much; however,
for one who has attained contentment through fewness of desires, there is peace of heart.
Just as fire attains extinction only through fuel,
so too for men who desire fire, an increase is produced by means of wealth.
Contentment with few desires alone is happiness, O King;
for kings who were insatiable for wealth have gone to their death by the millions, and others likewise shall go to their death. Therefore, contentment with few desires is happiness.
Only one who is free from craving attains happiness;
for humans, the characteristic of suffering is the desire for pleasure. (This [craving] should be abandoned with every effort.)
This has been stated by the investigators:
"This is the auspicious and supreme path by which craving is brought under control. (Dhs 8.106)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Section on Craving.
(9) The Chapter on Disgust for Women:
Women alone are the root of misfortune;
women are indeed the root.
For those who are not devoted in any way to their own welfare—sin and the loss of wealth being certain—how could happiness ever arise for them? (Dhs 9.1)
Women, who delight in harmful actions and abound in deceit and envy, exist for the destruction of men in both worlds. (Dhs 9.2)
Those who are virtuous yet full of passion always speak one thing, while others always say something else; moreover, they speak one thing in their hearts and quite another in their speech.
Sweet at first encounter yet subtle in their ripening, those of diamond-like minds do not expect honor for their assistance; those of light-mindedness do not remember the help they have rendered.
Women possess hearts with the nature of lightning and are exceedingly fickle;
having destroyed hundreds of dear things, they remember but a single unpleasant act.
Women, whose hearts have the nature of lightning, are the very ground of sin.
Demonstrating that women are the cause of destruction:
Men of crooked minds desire the destruction of their own welfare for the sake of women;
the destruction of a woman is, in this world and the next, the immediate destruction of oneself. (Dhs 9.6)
The sight of a woman burns like fire;
indeed, among all sense objects, the sight of a woman is born as the sole cause here.
Having overwhelmed all other sense objects, the blazing fire of women is great.
Preceded by the revelation of the faults of women, one should contemplate the loathsomeness of females:
"Even from union, there is separation; even from remembrance or conversation, this fire arising from the burning of women laughs within. (Dhs 9.8)
Women are always born together with passion, just as fires are born together with the act of offering oblations in this world. (Dhs 9.9)
The burning that arises from fire would not be like the intoxication caused by women, which arises within the hearts of embodied beings.
"Women have been declared by the great seers to be the causes for the destruction of the entire world, for the ruin of all dharmas, and for rebirth in hell. (Dhs 9.11)
Sweet in speech yet intolerant, like poison in their hearts, and unstable in their affection—no man is truly dear to them. (Dhs 9.12)
In one moment they are dear to them, and in another moment likewise they are not dear;
their affection is unstable, fickle, and comparable to a mere flash.
Skilled in the causes of deception, they are constantly devoted to their own affairs;
their minds are always intent on association, and they are perpetually dedicated to pride.
Neither gods, nor humans, nor piśācas, uragas, or rākṣasas are such bondsmen as women are— who are like the poison of Time.
These women do not remember a kindness received, nor virtue, nor even valor; their minds are unstable, equal to the force of the wind.
Where women are protected, there prosperity exists;
but those who are indifferent in times of calamity will surely abandon a man.
Wherever men go, women follow them there;
yet these women very quickly abandon a man who remains stationary.
Just as a female bee always abandons a withered flower,
so too does a beloved woman abandon a man who is destitute of wealth.
With hearts as cruel as swords, fierce, fickle, and shrouded in darkness, women have been created by some cause for the destruction of men. (Dhs 9.20)
That which is called the bondage of the gods is considered to be like the bondage of women;
those bound by the fetter of women fall again into hell.
For this is the foremost of all passions: the passion that arises from women.
After one's mind has been consumed by the passion for women, the fire [of hell] burns it later.
Even when actions are directly before him, a man whose heart is deluded and who is overcome by passions does not perceive them, being utterly infatuated by lust for women. (Dhs 9.23)
Having gained the trust of a man in matters of interest by repeatedly doing what is pleasing,
they abandon him through the loss of his wealth, just as serpents cast off their skin.
Women, who embody all means of seduction, have been protected in every way;
yet these most cruel women cannot be brought under one's own control.
A man with a steady mind should never place his trust in these women, who possess all manner of deceptive natures and fickle hearts. (Dhs 9.26)
Those mortals who are subject to women and are constantly seeking after sensual desires will have their final sight of the world of the gods.
Enticed on all sides by the fivefold music,
they encounter the suffering of calamity, which is certain to come to pass.
These are those fickle women for whom you have conceived passion;
having abandoned you, they have gone from there to another.
For the nature of those women who accompany [a man] is twofold:
