they frequently pursue a man in times of misfortune, yet they abandon him in times of prosperity.
Like deer, these women delude a man who is infatuated by passion;
yet when misfortune arrives, those of light mind abandon him.
When a severe calamity has arrived, women do not remember past favors, nor hospitality, nor endearments, nor even their own kin. (Dhs 9.32)
Just as a bee abandons a withered flower and flies elsewhere,
so indeed do women abandon a man when misfortune has befallen him.
Disregarding affection, fickle, and fond of strife,
all women are like honey mixed with poison.
They delude men with sensual desires and especially with their words;
a wise person of steady mind should not place trust in them. (Dhs 9.35)
Are men deluded by these [sensual pleasures], or are they naturally enamored of them,
that they do not act upon beneficial advice, just as one heading toward Muṣṭika does not?
Women, who are composed of magical illusions, especially deceive gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas. (Dhs 9.37)
And this is the foremost of all bonds, namely that which consists of women and is so firm;
bound by this, men wander in the prison of worldly existence.
There is no bond more binding than this bond of the heart—the bond of women;
men bound by the fetters of the heart's bond are deluded by suffering. (Dhs 9.39)
The noose consisting of women burns and cuts; yet it does not burn [the body].
It follows one who goes among the denizens of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Just as a physical body is bound by a great cord,
so too this formless mind is bound by the cord of women.
No other snare is seen by which women bind;
one should recognize that this great bondage consisting of women is immeasurable. (Dhs 9.42)
Bound forever by this noose of liberation from suffering— which is actually repulsive— men are not released from the ocean of existence.
The great snare consisting of women binds all six sense-faculties;
however, some other snare binds only the body alone, or perhaps not at all.
This bond is indeed not firm; it is made of six metals, yet it is difficult to release for a man of dull intellect who is attached to the enjoyments of a passionate mind.
In these vast fields of action bound by the machinery of sinews,
I have come here equipped with the sharp sword of blood for the purpose of death.
The wickedness of women consists especially in their deceit, fraud, and guile; they are impetuous, fickle, and possess wandering minds, being like enemies who deceive at every moment. (Dhs 9.47)
Confused by the sounds of ornaments and by their own delusive speech, women who are skilled in deception quickly captivate a man. (Dhs 9.48)
Just as a six-legged bee moves among various kinds of flowers,
so do these fickle women move among various kinds of mortals.
Just as the *madhurikā* flower, having been drunk upon, goes elsewhere,
so too do women depart impetuously after having drunk from a man.
Skilled in seizing wealth, ever wrathful and difficult to approach,
they quickly deceive a man and depart for another place.
Women are weapons of illusion that are being forged; comparable to the kālakūṭa poison, they are skilled in the arts of destroying men. (Dhs 9.52)
Just as wind, space, and fire cannot be bound by men,
so too women cannot be guarded by men through hundreds of means.
Women are the supreme cause of misfortune, disease, and death, as well as of evil deeds and the destruction of the practice for liberation.
The reason why people in this world fall among various kinds of deceitful evildoers is other men's wives.
The innate fickleness of women is not pacified by childhood alone, nor by youth, nor even by old age; it is like the radiance of the sun.
The friendship of those [women] is impermanent, like sparks from blazing flames;
yet their enmity is eternal, like that of stones with the wounds they inflict. (Dhs 9.57)
Women lose interest in one who is destitute and become attached to one who possesses wealth; as long as there is wealth, so long are there women—how could there be women for one devoid of wealth?
Neither by service, nor by gifts, nor by various kinds of favors can women whose minds are like blazing fire be brought under one's control.
Just as a man is compliant and acts according to their will,
so too do women, who are supremely skilled in deception, ensnare him.
Just as a snake is concealed by a flower-parasol, or as fire is concealed by ashes,
so too is the mind of these women concealed by their physical beauty.
Just as the flower of a poisonous tree is pleasing to the sight but not for one's peace, so too should noble women,
who are like poisonous trees, be avoided from all sides.
A man who longs for the sight of women and is intent upon sensual objects finds no enjoyment of happiness in this world, nor in the next. (Dhs 9.63)
Neither by fire, nor by weapon, nor by force, nor by living beings can this bond consisting of women— which is difficult to overcome— be escaped.
This web of faults,
consisting of women, wanders upon the earth;
the wise man who is free from women is honored in this world.
Just as men do not initiate their own actions through their true nature,
so too women protect [their husbands] and yet abandon them for the sake of an improper object.
Having beheld the god whose wealth of purpose has vanished and who is deprived of his own power by his own karma, fickle women possess no influence at all.
The pleasure of women is momentary; this happiness that has been attained is likewise fleeting.
Men always experience these four types of suffering.
A woman is like poison and fire;
therefore, those things which are like poison and fire should be avoided. For any living being who is fickle and always prone to the arising of faults [is likewise to be shunned].
Therefore, women are completely devoted to those who show them affection;
for the sun is not the cause of darkness, nor is fire the cause of cold.
Affection does not remain even slightly in the hearts of women,
just as this earth is stable or as the wind is always in motion.
Women remember only faults;
likewise, there is nothing done by women that is not faulty; they are always remembered as being full of defects.
Even when men have exerted themselves for a long time and enticed them many times, women [remain thus].
When misfortune arrives, people abandon one just as swift birds leave a dried-up lake;
upward-flowing rivers are not seen to turn back, nor is movement downward desired for stones.
Mountains have no movement, and women possess no true friendship; likewise, they always cut away the bodies of men, as well as their virtue, wealth, and fame.
The source of the web of misfortune and the arising of faults would be as hard as adamant yet soft; one should abandon it, just as one leaves the sun at night.
A woman should not abandon those who are incurable, especially considering their past lives;
she should not cease her ministrations through acts of service, gifts, pleasant speech, or by deceiving them.
Women whose minds are like blazing fire cannot be won over;
they remain indifferent in times of pleasure and abandon one in times of calamity.
Having enjoyed happiness many times in forests, groves, and mountains, they forget their benefactors and remember only a single fault.
Women are the bondage of the world;
indeed, when intense calamity has arrived, people treat women with contempt.
Women are the bondage of the world, increasing their deceptive forms. (Dhs 9.79)
The base are the abode of many downfalls and faults;
through craving, they bring about the destruction of the entire world.
Just as this great bondage of women is difficult to endure,
so too is this great bondage in the world consisting of sensual passion.
Abstaining from women alone is conducive to the highest good;
thus it is understood through investigation by means of other efforts that they bring [men] under their control.
By the many arrows of desire.
Having been defeated by even the slightest [faults], women fall under the power of desire;
they are the ground of passion, envy, and deceit, their minds as flickering as lightning.
Those whose origin is greed and egoism are by no means to be trusted;
they are as sharp as weapons and fire, and their souls are enslaved by the snares of desire.
[They fall] into the unevenness of a precipitous abyss for those whose minds are equanimous toward the profound,
while their own minds are occupied with the deceptive magic of hostility toward others.
For those whose very selves are like untimely death, vajra-fire, and kālakūṭa poison, who repeatedly delight in a multitude of manifold faults; Dhs 9.86.
If even a fragment of virtue dwells in the minds of women,
fire, though touched and fanned by the wind, burns them only after a long time.
Fire burns only upon contact with the sight of a woman;
therefore, women should be avoided by one who desires the highest happiness.
For one who desires their own welfare, the constant avoidance of women—the cause of the snare of desire—is the supreme thing in this world. (Dhs 9.89)
But that man who desires liberation should avoid women;
for one who is attached to pleasure is likewise intent on wealth, lazy, fickle, and deceitful.
A man who pursues evil and eats delicacies does not see what is auspicious;
but one who is diligent, energetic, steadfast, and righteous should avoid women.
A man who is skillful and has faith in cause and effect shall possess excellence.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Section on Contempt for Women.
(10) The Section on Aversion to Alcohol; Demonstrating the Means for Describing the Abandonment of Drinking Alcohol:
One should not indulge in drinking alcohol, for alcohol is indeed the ultimate poison.
Wholesome qualities perish through the habitual indulgence in drinking intoxicants.
The intellect of one who constantly consumes intoxicants is unstable;
there is neither strength, nor wisdom, nor dharma for such a person. Therefore, one should avoid intoxicants.
Wise men have declared that among all forms of destruction, intoxication is the worst;
therefore, one should not indulge in intoxicants, for they destroy a person. (Dhs 10.3)
Unwanted and evil states arise from the habitual indulgence in drinking intoxicants;
therefore, one should avoid the drinking of intoxicants as one would poison. (Dhs 10.4)
The faults inherent in the consumption of intoxicants cause the depletion of wealth, produce evil, and are the ultimate cause of indolence; therefore, one should avoid them entirely.
Wine is an inflamer of passion and likewise of anger;
it further inflames delusion; therefore, one should avoid wine.
Alcohol is the root of misfortune, of laughter [at one's own ruin], and of hell;
it is indeed useless, being the cause of the destruction of all the sense faculties.
For that [mind] is indeed the locus of excessive joy and its expression, of grief and fear, of the fault of speech, of extreme lack of self-control, and of harshness. (Dhs 10.8)
Men whose minds are deranged by liquor are equal to beasts; they do not discern what ought to be done from what ought not to be done. Therefore, one should avoid liquor. (Dhs 10.9)
For a man intoxicated by liquor is considered dead even while living;
he who desires life and happiness should always avoid liquor. (Dhs 10.10)
Intoxicants are the abode of all defects;
intoxicants are the abode of all defects. They always cause every misfortune, serve as a staircase to all evils, and are a great dwelling place for darkness. (Dhs 10.11)

Through intoxicants, there is a fall into the world of hungry ghosts or into hell; through intoxicants, men go to hell and likewise to the world of hungry ghosts; deceived by the fault of intoxicants, they go among the animals. (Dhs 10.12)
Wise men have declared that liquor is poison even more virulent than poison, a hell even more terrible than hell, and a disease more grievous than any other disease. (Dhs 10.13)
The demonstration of the harm caused by liquor is for the sake of destroying the faculties of the intellect and for the exhaustion of the jewel of Dharma; moreover,
excessive liquor leads to the destruction of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Even kings who possess the eye of the scriptures fall into a state of light-mindedness through liquor;
how much more so common mortals, who are already hindered by their addiction to drinking?
Alcohol is the destroyer of all virtues; it is the supreme destroyer of shame.
When consumed by mortals, alcohol leads to ruin. (Dhs 10.16)
Through liquor, the distinction between knowledge and ignorance is shown to be void:
"A person whose mind is stolen by liquor perceives nothing at all—neither knowledge nor discernment, neither effects nor actions. (Dhs 10.17)
The means for the torment resulting from the consumption of intoxicants:
a living being suffers suddenly, is tormented suddenly,
and becomes a sinner suddenly.
He who indulges in intoxicants.
Alcohol causes the delusion of the intellect;
it is that which deludes the intellect and destroys both worlds.
It is established as the sole fire for the extinction of the qualities leading to liberation. (Dharmasaṃgraha 10.19)
In its practice, liquor is like the *kimpāka* fruit; it is sweet when consumed but extremely bitter in its final digestion.
Investigators have declared that liquor is even more of a *kimpāka* than the *kimpāka* fruit itself.
Alcohol is the means for attaining hell;
a wise man should not place his trust in alcohol, thinking, "It will speak to me like a human being. Alcohol has a cold touch but a hot ripening; it leads one to hell. (Dhs 10.21)
In prosperity, intoxication is a calamity, especially for the gods;
for in whatever measure there is joy in pleasure, in that same measure there is calamity upon its loss. (Dhs 10.22)
Beings intoxicated by the madness of drinking liquor, following the power of delusion,
drink that beverage consisting of the delusion of testimony out of thirst for its flavor.
Having drunk the intoxicating beverage consisting of delusion, impelled by time, they fall from heaven into a manifest hell; therefore, one should not touch liquor.
From seeing and from drinking, the consumption of intoxicants generates delusion.
Through seeing, touching, and drinking, intoxicant maddens a person;
therefore, one should avoid the drinking of intoxicants from afar. (Dhs 10.25)
From seeing arises greed; from touching, the emergence of scent;
from scent, the longing for taste; and from tasting, the basest of thoughts. (Dhs 10.26)
The wise declare that from the consumption of liquor one falls into all manner of most base states; the wise say that liquor, when consumed, serves to negate both name and form. (Dhs 10.27)

The indication of the fruits of drinking liquor causes the speech to falter, the brain to reel, and the eyes to wander; one who is thus confused, deluded, and possessed of false perceptions understands nothing at all. (Dhs 10.28)
Even women mock the drinker of liquor;
even women mock this man fallen upon the ground—motionless, like a piece of wood, and still as he lies prostrate on the earth. (Dhs 10.29)
The drinking of intoxicants is more degrading than even death;
for one of high repute, death is proclaimed to be preferable to the drinking of intoxicants. It is worse than the hālāhala poison and greater than imprisonment. (Dhs 10.30)
Abstaining from the drinking of intoxicants is conducive to welfare, for thirty-six disadvantages reside in the consumption of intoxicants.
Therefore, one should recognize these disadvantages and always avoid them. (Dhs 10.31)
The drinking of intoxicants leads even a wise person to defilement;
for one who is highly born and learned, such defilement is a great calamity.
It renders a living being as light as a *kāśa* flower, making him of feeble character. (Dhs 10.32)

Burning with the fire of sensory objects, one becomes devoid of discrimination between what should and should not be done; for those submerged in negligence, they are further captivated by sense-objects through the drinking of intoxicants, which causes great delusion of the mind.

What more need be said of the drinking of intoxicants, which burns one with the fire of sensory objects, causes one to be ignorant of what should and should not be done, and leads one to seek out forests and groves?
The drinking of intoxicants leads to delusion and evil;
wine may be pleasant in its flavor, yet it is terrible in its ultimate transformation.
One who experiences the fruit of that evil transformation is reborn in the hells. (Dhs 10.35)
Drinking [liquor] produces delusion; from delusion, one is drawn toward evil deeds.
With a heart impassioned by desire, the fool rushes headlong into the hells.
The drinking of liquor, which establishes one's baseness, first produces an excellence [of intoxication], but in its ultimate ripening it brings about supreme wretchedness;
it effects the cessation of thirst, yet afterwards it causes a most terrible burning.
It first destroys one's intelligence and afterwards destroys one's happiness;
therefore, that man is wise who does not indulge in intoxicants. (Dhs 10.38)
Those who indulge in liquor become like birds; men who consume intoxicants go to a state similar to that of birds.
Liquor, which produces equal delusion, is the great poison of infatuation. (Dhs 10.39)
Those who are deluded reach an evil destiny;
but by those for whom liquor is viewed as poison, the supreme state has been seen.
By those, however, who have drunk that bitter [liquor], copper-colored blood has been drunk.
He who, deluded and possessed by the drinking of intoxicants, performs actions that cannot be remedied, goes to an evil rebirth in the end.
For those who indulge in the drinking of intoxicants, destruction occurs;
for in one place, all evils are [contained] in the consumption of intoxicants,
since it causes ruin.
And restraint has the mind as its root.

One who drinks intoxicants loses their virtue, for there is no one-pointedness of mind and no discernment of the teachings. A monk who is devoted to evil through the indulgence of intoxicants [falls from his state]. (Dhs 10.43)
For a being whose mind is deranged by liquor and who destroys his own virtue, there is neither this world nor the next. (Dhs 10.44)
He does not know the proper modes of conduct, nor the right time, nor the appropriate place; being opposed to the true Dharma, he speaks whatever is trivial. (Dhs 10.45)
First, he himself does not know what it is that I am saying;
how then will he recognize the ugliness of harsh speech toward another? (Dhs 10.46)
One incurs the contempt of the world and falls away from dharma;
death is seen by men resulting from the consumption of liquor and fire. (Dhs 10.47)
The drinking of intoxicants brings about contempt;
for it leads to the destruction of friends in the past and present, and in the future, intoxicants cause the ruin of those who are base—thus, liquor is the destroyer of the three times. (Dhs 10.48)
Intoxicants are indeed corrupters of the Dharma;
they lead to the destruction of name-and-form and the destruction of the mind for embodied beings.
Intoxicants, which generate arisen faults, are corrupters of the Dharma.
Abstaining from intoxicants is for the sake of the Dharma; drinking [intoxicants] does not lead to death.
Men who are composed, virtuous in Dharma, and abstainers from intoxicants go to the supreme state where death is not found. (Dhs 10.50)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the Section on Contempt for Alcohol.
Now follows the second inspired utterance:
"The mind, speech, and likewise action—these are the fetters of evil; know that there are ten: hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal realm, hunger, and the five types of indolence."
(11) The Chapter on the Mind:
The mind proceeds like a king—
fathomless, treacherous, intense, pervasive among all beings, and great.
The mind of the entire world proceeds like a king.
Those who hold their minds and know that [truth] attain the supreme goal;
those who hold their minds and know that [truth] have gone to the supreme goal—[whereas] those unsteady in hellish karma experience present fear that is invisible. // Dhs 11.2 //
This leads to rising from [meditative absorption], and this leads to an evil rebirth;
yet that very same thing, when stainless from beginning to end, attains Nirvana.
All phenomena are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are made of the mind;
with a well-purified mind, one speaks or acts. (Dhs 11.4)
The mind runs after him who is under the power of the mind;
but for him who is not under the power of the mind, his mind always reaches its end. He utterly destroys the afflictions, just as the rising sun dispels the darkness. (Dhs 11.5)
Those consumed by the mind go to destruction;
the mind is the supreme enemy, for no other is considered an enemy.
Beings who are consumed by the mind are always like dull-witted ones consumed by time. (Dhs 11.6)
For that fool, deluded and with senses unsubdued, who has fallen under the sway of the mind,
there is no equal to his suffering, and for him, nirvāṇa is far away.

A man who is under the sway of his own mind goes to hell; no other enemy is so easily won over as the mind, for it does not hide itself. This very mind binds a person to the command of King Yama. (Dhs 11.8)
One who is constantly devoted to sense objects never possesses true dharma;
being utterly deluded regarding the path of the true dharma, such a person leads one to the great hell.
The mind is the supreme wild horse; fire is its best tamer.
If not subdued, it swiftly leads one certainly to hell. (Dhs 11.10)
Those who have fallen under the sway of the mind have long since gone to hell;
but those by whom it is swiftly restrained do not follow after suffering.
Happiness and suffering arise in accordance with the mind; in whatever way the minds of men undergo transformation, so too do their experiences.
For one who performs virtuous deeds and for one who performs evil deeds, [the results] endure for kalpas.
Action depends upon the mind, and the mind depends upon action;
it is proclaimed that saṃsāra arises from the conjunction of mind and action.
Whatever action a man performs here with a wicked mind,
he is cooked in hell because of it, tormented by the Jālinī [hell].
The cycle of existence is indeed the activity of the mind;
evil depends upon the mind, for it is proclaimed that cyclic existence arises from the mind as its condition, born of causes and conditions. (Dhs 11.15)
Deceived by their own minds, sentient beings fall under the power of evil;
due to that sin, they go to hell, which is a place of supreme and great terror.
One should not be subject to the mind, but rather be subject to the Dharma;
one should not fall under the power of the mind, but always abide under the power of the Dharma.
One who practices the Dharma is eternally happy, while one who practices evil possesses no peace.
All fruit is dependent on the mind;
all action is dependent on the mind; fruit is known to be dependent on the mind.
For the mind is the fruit, and likewise the fruit is understood to be the mind. (Dhs 11.18)
Everything is conceived by the mind, and the world follows the nature of the mind;
for there is no place to be found that does not follow the power of the mind.
The auspicious is considered the supreme means for achieving nirvāṇa, the root and causal basis for both liberation and bondage;
by the auspicious a living being is liberated, and by the inauspicious one is swiftly bound. (Dhs 11.20)
Those who have fallen under the power of the mind never attain nirvāṇa;
deluded by the snare and come under the sway of the mind, sentient beings do not reach nirvāṇa, just as those blind from birth cannot find the right path. (Dhs 11.21)
Having conquered the five senses, he never experiences evil;
likewise, with a single-pointed mind, he performs his actions throughout various states of existence. (Dhs 11.22)
Just as the mind, radiant with five colors, is praised according to what is perceived,
so too does karma manifest in existence, variegated by the five sense faculties.
The creator of the mind becomes manifold;
for the person, as the creator of the mind, appears as manifold through objects of perception.
The mind that creates the mind is empty and is not perceived at all in any way.
The mind performs both beautiful and ugly actions;
it creates a diverse array of beautiful and ugly things, just as a wall serves as the ground for a painting.
Indeed, the mind performs both beautiful and ugly deeds in that very same way.
Action follows the mind;
just as the mind remains fixed throughout day and night, so too does action continue to follow it day and night. (Dhs 11.26)
Having failed to perform virtuous deeds, men who follow the fluctuations of their own minds fall helplessly into evil, deceived by the enemy that is the mind.
For this mind is the performer of action; wherever it is directed, by means of its great movement, it performs that very act. (Dhs 11.28)
By means of a particular transformation, wherever they are directed by the mind, those who wander through the three realms of existence are sent there. (Dhs 11.29)
The taming of the mind brings happiness;
all actions of embodied beings depend upon the mind.
Therefore, a mind that is always subdued leads one to the state that is beyond falling away.
Wherever the mind—which is difficult to withstand and falls swiftly—may be directed, its subduing is excellent; a subdued mind brings happiness. (Dhs 11.31)
By him whose mind is always subdued, faults are always conquered;
for the wise one who has conquered his faults, suffering never arises.
The very light movement of the mind is itself suffering;
whatever suffering one may have for oneself and whatever suffering exists in another—all that is the unbearable, light movement of the mind. (Dhs 11.33)
Mind alone is the lord of all—of gods, asuras, and nāgas, as well as piśācas, uragas, and rakṣasas; mind is the one supreme sovereign. For the king is indeed the mind.
That belongs to the three realms of existence.
The mind experiences the suffering born of delusion;
the mind leads one to the realms of the gods and to the human worlds;
and the mind leads one to the states of woe.
The mind causes living beings to wander in delusion.
For one who is deluded by the mind, ruined, infatuated by sense objects, and consumed by craving, unsurpassed suffering persists. (Dhs 11.36)

From the taming of the mind, the experience of happiness arises; [otherwise,] it wanders alone, is ever-deluded, difficult to restrain, and possesses great power; it is ever-tormenting, ever-visible, fickle, and swift-moving. (Dhs 11.37)
For those wise ones who thus subdue such a mind have transcended the bonds of Māra and have reached the further shore where happiness arises. (Dhs 11.38)
The fickle mind is fashioned for hell; for it is crooked through its intentions, intense, bottomless, and indeed restless.
Even a bright mind, when resting in darkness, is fashioned for hell.

Freed from defects, one attains that very state which is unfallen; thus, being freed from defects and no longer following the power of the senses and their objects, and unstained by evil dharmas, one leads oneself to the unfallen state. (Dhs 11.40)
A pure mind engages in pure action; born of causes and conditions, that mind carries yoga and is supreme.
By the power of transformation, it proceeds swiftly in that manner. (Dhs 11.41)
When not under the control of the mind, karma becomes fickle;
it performs one action and then various actions, being ever-shifting.
It is both single and manifold, moving, subtle, and does not remain for even a moment beyond its arising. (Dhs 11.42)
The demonstration that saṃsāra is like an illusion:
It is always difficult to discern that which is bodiless at all times;
who is it that leads one to the end of the world, and by what means does one go? (Dhs 11.43)
And having gone, where does it abide? That which performs the actions of the body—its actions are visible, yet no accumulation [of them] is seen.
The subduing of that [passion] for which no remedy exists is difficult;
it pervades all beings, is terrible, acts swiftly, and is visible to the eye.
That which is seen as more evil than evil is this world that is like an illusion;
that which is seen as more meritorious than merit is that which is firmly established upon the true path.
The proof of its being like an illusion is that its destination is not known and its movement is never seen;
yet it carries away everyone who is wounded, and these [fallacies] are equal to "quibbles" (jātyuttara).
This is not cut by a weapon, nor is it burned by fire;
yet all people, being sightless, are indeed cut and burned.
That which is a firm rope of karma binds a person in suffering,
leading them through thousands of other births, yet it is not seen.
A tamed mind alone brings happiness;
in a moment it becomes virtuous, and in a moment it becomes non-virtuous—
the mind is fashioned by virtue and non-virtue.
The tamed brings happiness.
The mind, excessively greedy for the objects produced through the six gates, leads one to the end of the world, yet it does not perceive its own calamity.
For one whose mind is serene, there arises the unsurpassed happiness that brings about the highest good;
just as water is clear and just as the sky is clear, so too the serene mind is led to supreme bliss. (Dhs 11.52)
People are seen to be subject to excess because they arise from the objects of discursive thought;
O King of the Mind, those subjects become your companions.
The restless mind causes one to wander through saṃsāra;
wherever the mind runs, there the ignorant run after it,
led by their mutual force.
They wander in the ocean of the three realms of existence.
Through a distinguished mind, an excellent rebirth occurs; the distinction among beings arises from the clarity of the mind and likewise from their actions.
No distinction is perceived for one who is devoid of the qualities of action.
Praise for one whose mind is well-composed:
One whose mind is well-composed constantly observes the nature of phenomena;
he does not fall under the power of faults, just as the divine sun dispels the darkness.
If a householder possesses right view, he attains nirvāṇa;
and he in whose mind supreme right view resides—
even though he is a householder, he should be known by me as one liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra.
The wise go to the divine realm which is auspicious and stainless; therefore, one is not afflicted by fault.
The wise man does not incur impurity and is born in the divine realm.

Those whose minds are disciplined proceed toward happiness; for those by whom this mind— which is as fickle as the gateway to sense-objects and as winding as a river’s course— has been disciplined, they are gods who partake in auspiciousness.
The path of unrighteousness does not lead to what is auspicious; relying on the way of unrighteousness, people, driven by the power of evil,
wander for a long time in saṃsāra, their minds utterly exhausted.
The mind changes from moment to moment;
this mind transforms manifoldly in every instant.
Light by nature and fickle, it is like an illusion or a celestial city of the Gandharvas.
One whose mind is fickle becomes bound;
that very bondage is considered by the wise to be the attainment of knowledge and discernment.
Moving far away with great speed, it runs about in many ways.
One who sustains the mind through fortitude enjoys happiness;
for the mind, when being carried away by the objects of the senses, is always difficult to restrain.
He who holds it steady through fortitude is wise and one who goes to the further shore.
The wise man who sustains fortitude, wisdom, and freedom from delusion, and whose mind is not distracted by sense objects— he is the learned man in this world.
A virtuous mind is that which restrains sensual desires;
in whatever way one directs the mind, in that way one perceives sensual desires. Through virtue, there is the pacification of desire; through non-virtue, its increase. (Dhs 11.65)
One whose mind is unpacified encounters suffering,
while one whose heart and mind are peaceful casts off desires in this world like poison or weapons.
One of unpacified intellect perceives those [desires] as if they were a jewel on a serpent's head.
One who is under the sway of the mind does not attain a fortunate rebirth;
these sense faculties and their objects are dependent upon the mind.
Through the process of mental attachment, transformation proceeds.
The praise of the wise refers to that very same person after an interval; the wise one awakens.
How can transformation, which is perceived through the commonality of form, be considered separate?
An investigation into the true nature of the mind:
Just as with form, so all objects are causes of the mind;
the mind, when subdued, is ever peaceful, whereas it is censured when mixed with faults. (Dhs 11.69)
Just as each individual grain of rice, though diverse in its fragrance and form,
attains a state of union, so too does the mind proceed in manifold ways.
For one performs action wherever the mind runs;
this world proceeds according to that speech which follows the lead of the mind.
The mind that has wandered toward sense objects possesses extreme speed and great power; [it is difficult to calm].
A hand that is self-controlled brings auspiciousness to embodied beings.
Through a tamed mind, there arises the vision of reality;
but by one who is untamed, impulsive, and dwelling in all manner of evil,
the entire triple world is wandered through, and he does not perceive reality.
Agitated by the friction of the wind, the world wanders in saṃsāra, just as the ocean, agitated by the friction of the wind, revolves;
joined with the Lord of the Mind, this world is constantly whirled about. (Dhs 11.74)
The virtuous mind flourishes in happiness;
for the mind brought forth by virtue is directed toward virtuous things alone.
Likewise, one experiences the results of virtuous conduct and runs toward those [states].
The mind that carries yoga attains a state conducive to yoga; the human mind that carries yoga is indeed equal to wind and water,
and it flows in whatever direction the state conducive to yoga is attained.
The mind runs and revolves; the mind runs swiftly and revolves swiftly.
It leads [the soul] swiftly, O Lord of the Gods, within the world.
In the lands of inheritance.
The mind is characterized as the agent of all phenomena, the sustainer of all actions, and the leader of all deeds; this is what is meant by "mind-ness. (Dhs 11.78)
One should not trust the mind; indeed,
one should never place trust in the mind, for it constantly strikes at one's vulnerabilities— especially since it is difficult to master, fickle, and particularly volatile.
The movement of the mind is described:
in one moment it goes toward the auspicious, and likewise in another moment it goes toward the inauspicious;
it quickly becomes indeterminate, for its course is not fixed.
Its future destination is not known, nor is its departure ever found;
it arises from what has not existed before, and having come into being, it passes away.
The mind is devoid of form; no aspect of it exists, nor does its accumulation exist.
There is no apprehension whatsoever of that which is entirely bodiless.
The description of the accomplishment of conditions:
that which is obtained through the totality of causes and conditions arises again; for the condition consisting of the gem and the moon—
Fire is known through its effect.
The mind runs toward the sense organs, forms, and so forth; likewise, the arising of consciousness occurs in relation to the sense organs, forms, and so forth.
The mind of a single [individual] is not known; it is observed only as a composite.
The mind is difficult to restrain;
having thus understood that it is difficult to ward off from all objects,
one should fix the intellect upon the true Dharma and never at all upon sensual desires.
The mind is fickle, fierce, exceedingly restless, intense, unbearable, and possesses great power;
the mind performs actions that the foolish do not perceive. (Dhs 11.86)
The mind is the initiator of suffering; the mind is the cause of every action in birth after birth.
It is that which initiates suffering, by which the fool runs hither and thither.
The defect of the mind is indeed the great defect;
wind and the other humors are not defects. Passion and the like are considered the defects.
Through wind and the others, a person is not reborn in the states of woe.
The defect of the mind is a great defect that constantly reveals evil; therefore, one should not rely upon them, nor upon things such as wind and so forth in this world. (Dhs 11.89)
A mind following passion becomes corrupted;
yet, when the body perishes, the bodily afflictions such as wind and the like vanish for embodied beings.
For one who has [overcome] passion and the rest, they shall not recur even in hundreds of future births.
Therefore, one should never be subject to the power of passion;
for the supreme inner welfare is attained by transcending passion.
The mind itself becomes the physician;
he who is a doctor of the mind is a true healer, not merely a physician of the body.
One should know the mind as the healer; the worldly physician is not considered such.
Burnt by the karma of one's own mind, one falls into hell;
karma is inconceivable and equal, yet it cannot be grasped by the mind.
Burnt by the karma of one's own mind, one runs toward the hells.
The mind becomes pure through meditation alone;
that which is the welfare of one with an even mind does not arise anywhere else.
The fool pursues the heart that has already departed, though it must be protected. (Dhs 11.94)
The man who has taken refuge in the forest but remains under the sway of the mind suffers due to the deceptive trap of meditation and its objects;
yet that foolish one, having abandoned that [true] mastery over the mind, exults in this [false] mastery.
Those fools who wander through the activities of the mind, bound by the snares of the mind,
are led helplessly to a terrible hell, deluded by their own karma.
An Examination of the Diversity of Mind:
Even that which is considered a good mind is not regarded as true mind by the wise;
it is merely the mind of karma, the great mind, variegated by the states of the three realms.
Indeed, by means of various methods, sentient beings wander through the five realms of existence;
all of that is the work of the painter Karma, who has painted it in its manifold variety.
Bound by the power of the mind, this entire collection of karma has been variegated by the painter that is the mind; by this, the whole world is bound and wanders, deluded. (Dhs 11.99)
The mind of kings is destroyed by rain, heat, dust, and smoke;
yet it is a marvel that the mind does not perish even after a thousand million eons.
Even the earth goes to destruction and the ocean dries up;
yet the wondrous variety created by the mind persists as long as its experience endures.
When the mind is heedless, there is no fixed destiny; beings, governed by various destinies, enveloped by various destinies, and pursued by various karmas,
wander through the five realms of existence under the power of their diverse minds.
The mind of foolish men runs toward sense objects;
it does not accumulate unwholesome karma by which they would run to an evil rebirth.
The mind is always restless and ever-unstable;
therefore, the mind must be constantly guarded— restless, unstable, harsh,
perpetually attached to sense objects, and enveloped by the poison of craving.
A mind attached to sense objects causes one to fall into calamity; it runs toward the object and does not perceive that this very pursuit is a calamity.
Only later, when calamity has arrived, does one experience the fruit of one's actions.
One whose mind is concentrated experiences happiness;
for one who fears the lower realms, the mind becomes concentrated.
With a concentrated mind, one attains happiness after happiness.
One who has conquered the mind attains happiness;

for those steadfast ones by whom the mind has been conquered, they are considered happy in this world—[the mind] which is treacherous, fickle, intense, unbearable, and possessed of great power. (Dhs 11.107)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Section on the Mind.
(12) The Section on Speech: One who desires nirvāṇa should avoid harsh speech;
the wise person should avoid harsh speech and be one whose speech is correct and free from fear.
Delighting in sweetness, he stands near the nirvāṇa of the ancient one.
Observing speech, one should always speak [truthfully] and avoid that which is defiled;
those men who are overcome by verbal misconduct go to hell.
For an embodied being who has transgressed this single dharma of truthfulness,
and who has crossed over the world of the living, there is no evil deed here that he cannot commit.
One should not employ false speech;
one should not utter any lie that causes others to lose trust. For by such speech, one is bound in saṃsāra and never beholds a happy rebirth.
Deceptive speech, which causes hatred toward all virtuous people, is a wilderness for all wholesome qualities; thus false speech proceeds. (Dhs 12.5)
As soon as a mortal is born, a dagger is born in his mouth;
later, by speaking ill-considered words, he cuts himself. (Dhs 12.6)
That speech which one utters falsely is the banner of all failure, the progenitor of all evil, and the sole source of darkness. (Dhs 12.7)
Deprived of truth and abandoned by all that is virtuous, such men go like blades of grass in this world, suffering in states of misfortune.
A wise person should not speak falsehood, for speaking untruth is painful;
such a person becomes foul-smelling, lacks happiness, and is tormented by remorse.
Truth is great in its majesty,
and for one who does not abandon truth, there is no lack of dharma;
yet for one whose dharma has been set aside, the suffering born of manifold causes remains.
Truth is the lamp for all phenomena; it is the light for all things. To the virtuous, truth is as dear as a jewel.
Truth has been declared by those free from fever to be the supreme path to heaven.
Truth is indeed that for which liberation does not go to heaven for one who speaks untruth;
for persons devoid of truth are proclaimed to be equal to beasts. (Dhs 12.12)
Those for whom truth does not exist are the lowest of the low; truth is the staircase to dharma and the great source of all lights. (Dhs 12.13)
Truth has been declared by the wise to be the path of those whose dharma is liberation, the supreme wealth among all riches, and the protection against evildoers. (Dhs 12.14)
Truth adorned with speech is the ornament even of ornaments;
it is the supreme light among lights, and the eye even for those who possess sight.
Without wealth, truth alone is the ornament even of ornaments.
Those persons who possess truth go to the supreme goal— the incomparable treasure, the unassailable truth that accomplishes everything. (Dhs 12.16)
A king adorned with various ornaments does not shine in that way;
rather, the wise man adorned with truth shines like a god.
Neither mother, nor father, nor friends, nor kinsmen are a refuge in this way as hearing [the Dharma] is; therefore, one should be devoted to truth.
Falsehood is proclaimed to be the greatest of fires, the supreme poison among poisons,
and the staircase to the miserable realms. (Dhs 12.19)
O Lord, a person should avoid falsehood, for its touch is equal to poison or fire;
indeed, he who is consumed by falsehood is said to be "burned."
Since truth and falsehood are mutually contradictory, a person should not speak untruth with all their might.
All suffering, beginning with fear, is declared by the wise to be untruth.
The supreme fire among fires could even consume the ocean;
how much more so one who speaks falsehoods, who is like a mere log or a clod of earth?
That man who abandons truth and resorts to falsehood is a sinful soul who, having cast away a jewel, takes up a stone. (Dhs 12.23)
He who does not hate himself, or for whom hell is dear,
that person of no intelligence practices false speech, which is like fire to one's own body.
This truthful speech is the ornament of all embodied beings;
why do those of wicked intellect abandon truth and resort to falsehood?
Truth is indeed the foremost of virtues, while falsehood is remembered as the foremost of faults.
Having abandoned virtues, how can a fool run headlong toward faults?
Falsehood is proclaimed to be the seed of all suffering, while truth is likewise the very source of happiness; therefore, one should not be a speaker of untruth.
For a man who speaks the truth is dear to every embodied being; a speaker of falsehood is like one with a defect in his eyes. Therefore, one should not be a liar. (Dhs 12.28)
Men who are like gods are always drawn toward virtue and are speakers of truth; whereas those who belong to hell are deluded people whose minds are devoted to falsehood.
Truth is the supreme among virtues, and likewise, falsehood is the foremost among faults;
a man who avoids faults and detests vices is the best of men.
That which arises from happiness, results in happiness, and ripens in happiness,
leads one to attain the truth that goes toward Nirvāṇa with ease.
Falsehood arises from suffering, yields bitter fruit, and ripens along with suffering; what man would not utterly abandon it, for it is the end of all happiness?
Truth does not come from another land, nor is it sought from another;
truth is the supreme of all sacred fords, yet it is not encompassed by the waters of a ford.
The Buddha has taught that truth is the supreme lamp among lamps;
it is the supreme medicine, which eternally destroys suffering.
Both nectar and poison reside within the tether of the human tongue;
nectar is said to be truth, while poison is said to be falsehood. (Dhs 12.35)
For one for whom falsehood is intended, truth remains firmly established;
yet for one for whom poison is desired, false speech would be what is sought.
Destruction by poison is certain; destruction by false speech is certain.
That man who speaks with falsehood exists as one who is dead. (Dhs 12.37)
For that which is beneficial and wholesome for oneself is by no means so for another;
since it later leads to the suffering of others, how can it be practiced by men?
In every land, I have witnessed thousands of births and deaths; a single false word may cause more than a thousand to be born or destroyed. (Dharmasaṃgraha 12.39)
The extraction of the noble-born and the ornament of the twice-born, as well as the vision of the path to liberation—this is designated as truth. (Dhs 12.40)
For those beings who have slain the horse of craving by means of truthful actions,
truth— as previously described— is said to be the supreme teacher, the Sugata.
In this world without beginning or end, those who have crossed to the further shore of craving know that there is no refuge here; thus do the knowers of the Dharma understand the truth.
The noose of covetousness should not be pursued;
those who speak the truth are always invulnerable to afflictions, just as mountains are invulnerable to thunderbolts.
Those men should be known as slain who [have severed it].
They are deceived by covetousness.
This [mind], which is equal to the minds of others, is deceived by forms and other sense objects;
it is a snare of covetousness that is not frequented by the wise.
The self is consumed without being transformed, like a fire by the light of its oil;
for one whose mind is burnt by covetousness, no cause [for liberation] is found.
Malice indeed deludes sentient beings; therefore, it must always be avoided, for it gives rise to the poison of bitter expectations.
Sentient beings, deluded by malice, have their minds constantly absorbed in it.
Those men who are cruel by nature and intent on malice do not attain peace, like serpents dwelling in their holes. (Dhs 12.47)
For them there exists no happiness, just as darkness does not exist by the sun;
they have neither dharma nor a collection of wealth, neither religious duties nor kinsmen.
Those whose minds are struck by ill-will harm all people;
indeed, this ill-will is said here to be a mine of darkness.
Malice is proclaimed as that which causes harm to one's father;
non-malice is the supreme good, and malice is never so under any circumstances.
But those who are devoted to non-malice go to the immutable state;
he who speaks otherwise than what is certain is an unrighteous speaker of dharma, not one who is righteous.
That man who speaks of the Dharma and practices the Dharma itself is not considered a thief by the world at large; he is not regarded as an ordinary thief. (Dhs 12.52)
He goes to the eternal state, having gone to which one does not grieve;
yet the person who is slain by false speech is proclaimed as merely worldly.
It is only sometimes after hundreds of supramundane eons that [such a thing] is spoken;
therefore, a supramundane statement is in no way like a mundane one.
The bondage of saṃsāra is seen as worldly speech like poison;
it is well-established that one who delights in craving is always liberated from merit.
The wise declare that person to be transcendentally fortunate who,
though deluded, does not fail to accept the beneficial truth and the words of the guru.
The speaker of truth is always honored by the deities;
yet when misfortune later befalls him, he suffers within his own mind.
The speaker of truth is always self-controlled and is honored by the deities. (Dhs 12.57)
He becomes beloved by the world and later rejoices among the gods;
he becomes beloved by the world and later prospers within his own heart.
Furthermore, a beautiful face is born for him in the worlds of the gods.
A person who speaks what is untrue commits an offense against all sentient beings;
resembling a mass of darkness, he is equal to one who is dead even while living.
Why did his tongue not fall out—that organ which utters words of praise—when he spoke false speech that destroys one's truly existing virtues? (Dhs 12.60)
A serpent is present in his mouth, and a fruitless thorn is present in his mouth;
fire blazes within his mouth for him who speaks falsehood with his speech. (Dhs 12.61)
False speech proceeds as a tongue bound by entangled snares that are the primary causes for hell, and it acts as a cutter of the causes of the Dharma.
For one who is evil-minded and fallen, speaking falsehoods, there is neither mother nor father, nor is there a Buddha, nor even the vow of restraint. (Dhs 12.63)
One who speaks false speech suddenly becomes light and undergoes six transformations; he is even abandoned by the deities. (Dhs 12.64)
For one whose speech is unrefined, who acts without reflection, who is prone to anger,
fickle, and of little merit, suffering remains endless.
Even upon seeing the suffering of another, a being who commits offenses against other beings,
knowing that [suffering] to be like a calamity to himself, is one destined for hell.
Those mortals who always speak one way but do not act accordingly, (fall into hell).
Truth alone is the staircase to heaven and to nirvāṇa; truth is the ladder to heaven and the very door to nirvāṇa.
Therefore, one should always be devoted to truth and always maintain mindfulness directed toward the Dharma.
One should not speak untruth;
the Supreme Person attains the state that is free from sorrow and free from decay.
The wise man should avoid falsehood, which is censured by those who perceive the truth.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the Section on Speech.
(13) The Section on Karma: The experience of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome actions;
the certainty of the results of both wholesome and unwholesome deeds.
All well-performed deeds are experienced [in their results], for embodied beings are indeed bound by their karma.
When an action is undertaken, it is experienced by its doers—a mind that is deluded, intoxicated with pride, and a dweller in the city of craving. (Dhs 13.2)
One enjoys the fruit alone,
yet one performs evil deeds together with many companions;
alone, in birth after birth, one experiences the fruit of that action.
There is no separation from one's actions; in this world, whether good or evil, they follow one who departs for the next life along with all of one's kinsmen and relatives.
Wherever merits go, there the fragrance follows;
likewise, auspicious and inauspicious karma follows one who departs.
Bound by their own karma, living beings are heirs to the fruits of their actions.
By means of good deeds they go to the world of the gods, and by means of good deeds they remain in the worlds of the gods; yet likewise, by means of evil deeds, they go below.
Whatever suffering born of the fruit of karma arises, its outcome is bitter.
Its counterpart is the asura, which is born within the three realms;
born from the three humors and arising from the three types of mind, it ripens within the three realms.
The maturation of that karma is observed within the three realms;
it arises from the totality of causes and conditions, just like a measurement.
One person does not experience the fruit of an action performed by another;
for the evil committed by one is not ripened by another.
Indeed, every living being is the heir to the fruits of their own good deeds.
The ripening of this threefold karma—of the three types previously mentioned—occurs only for oneself; it does not ripen for anyone else.
The conduct resulting from the ripening of these forty [actions] becomes terrible.
Regarding the description of the fruit of karma:
one person performs the actions, and another alone experiences the fruit; one crosses over the difficulties, while the other becomes a mere companion. (Dhs 13.11)
A person who, out of dependence on water, commits an evil deed,
does not indeed consume the food of even hundreds of other people at any time.
For an action performed by one does not transfer to another;
I believe that in this world there is nothing without beginning or end, nor is anything created by others.
One who has committed evil deeds while experiencing the taste of suffering born of pleasure wanders in saṃsāra, driven by the wind of karma.
Whose dharma increases?
For one who disregards reality and whose mind is distracted,
all dharma increases.
He captivates the mind by being veiled by the Dharma.
Who go to hell?
Beings deceived by the mind and deluded by the mind— those evildoers, having no other refuge, go to hell, from darkness to deeper darkness.
For in this saṃsāra shrouded in darkness, the teaching of the Buddha is difficult to find;
those to whom the Dharma is not pleasing go from suffering to even greater suffering. (Dhs 13.17)
In beginningless saṃsāra, living beings, shrouded by the net of karma,
are born and likewise die due to the cause of the fruits of their own actions.
Gods are born in hell, as are those of the nature of hell-beings; likewise, humans go to the realm of hungry ghosts or indeed to hell. (Dhs 13.19)
It is observed that happiness arises from virtuous action alone, and likewise, suffering or even happiness arises mutually; furthermore,
when afflictions and dharmas arise in a birth, they are produced by causes extending back to previous lives.
Beings in saṃsāra have always performed incalculable karma;
therein it is possible for the wise to proceed, with the exception of the Tathāgatas.
The fruit of unrighteousness is not good; it does not ripen as something contrary [to its cause].
Indeed, the correspondence between cause and effect is observed in various kinds of water.
The cause and fruit of similarity are never indeed reversed;
for conditioned forms, their cause arises from conditions.
Every fruit of action has a cause;
no fruit is seen to be without a cause, especially in hell.
Bound to a collection of causes, it ripens within the hells.
For those who have committed grave and deep transgressions and are destined for evil,
the connection between action and its fruit ripens in the hells.
Regarding actions that are performed at specific times and places, those who show the path of reality have observed that their desired fruit is not seen. (Dhs 13.26)
Having first presented an illustration, [it is shown that] the fruit is indeed dependent upon karma:
"Just as light is dependent upon a lamp, so too is the fruit dependent upon karma;
for everything conditioned arises from the mutual production of fruits. (Dhs 13.27)
The establishment of dependent origination is as follows:
indeed, things are seen by those who perceive reality to be mutually causal and existing under mutual influence, appearing so through the continuity of similarity.
The connection between cause and effect is not maintained by those who posit a creator god (Īśvara) and so forth;
rather, conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharmāḥ) have been taught by those who see reality.
In this beginningless saṃsāra, where causes and conditions arise, similarity is observed through karma; it is not to be conceived as something contrary.
The true nature of the Buddha is such that living beings dwelling therein are subject to karma and born from the cause of karma;
he is the Buddha who knows the reality of the fruits of karma.
Thus it is called. (Dhs 13.31)
For whom does peace not exist?
For those fools who oppose the path and what is not the path within the teaching of the Buddha, there is no peace, just as there is no darkness for the sun. (Dhs 13.32)
Happiness depends on karma;
happiness is seen to depend on karma, and likewise the mind depends on happiness. Thus, one should understand the mind.
Those phenomena which are investigated through analytical discernment.
The fruit of well-performed action is that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, resembling bubbles upon the water;
therefore, O mortal, one should perform good deeds both in this world and in the next.
The fruit of action is seen in this world; indeed, its diversity is directly perceived.
For that man who is devoted to negligence, his own self is certainly not dear to him.
Bound by the extremely firm rope of karma, which is very difficult to loosen and tightly fastened,
the foolish do not go to the supreme city of Nirvana.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the Section on Karma.
(14) The Chapter on Fetters: The attainment of Nirvana through knowledge, by means of the weapon of knowledge.
Having severed that [bond], they are liberated and free from fever;
the fortunate ones proceed to the state of cessation where only the wise exist.
For the wise declare that the fruit is indeed similar to its cause;
for embodied beings, a fruit dissimilar to its cause never ripens.
Embodied beings who are bound in saṃsāra by the conditions of causes and the conjunction of the conditions for birth are liberated [only] when they are released from them. (Dhs 14.3)
The means to supreme peace is to sever that [bond] which is tightly bound, firm, and difficult to endure;
by doing so, they go to the supreme peace where suffering is not found. (Dhs 14.4)
A living being is constrained by karma and is ripened by karma; indeed,
no happiness is found that is easy to attain within saṃsāra.
For those beings whose minds are deluded and who are bound by suffering within suffering, there is no guide to the true path who might liberate them from this misery. (Dhs 14.6)
For those who are not constantly devoted to the Dharma, who are not always devoted to truth,
and who are perpetually addicted to sexual union, their suffering does not diminish.
Dharma brings happiness both in this world and the next; it is always like a mother, like a father, and indeed like a friend and a kinsman.
Indeed, the Dharma has been taught by the Buddhas in this world and in the world beyond.
Sentient beings abide within the three states of existence, fallen under the power of the three defects;
these people constantly move through the three realms and have descended into the triple world.
Those who are under the sway of the three types of actions and are devoted to women, drink, and the like, do not attain the state of liberation; they wander upon this earth.
For whom does suffering not exist?
For those who do not neglect the Three Jewels and who have come under the influence of the three types of awakening.
But for those who avoid the three views, suffering does not exist.

Established in the continuity of the three times, free from feverish distress, perceivers of reality, content with the practice of the three divisions, they have transcended sorrow and proceed toward cessation.
Those who are established in the three groups [of qualities], who engage in the three types of action,
and who are free from defects and have transcended feverish distress, shall no longer dwell in saṃsāra.
Those who know the methods of the path and the non-path, who contemplate existence and non-existence,
and who are detached from the cultivation of mere loving-kindness— they go to the supreme goal.
What should a person resort to?
With an untroubled mind and a serene heart.
A person should always honor wise brahmins who remain under the control of the Dharma.
Those who have truly taken refuge in truth through mindfulness, having abandoned the impurity of the mind and desisted from the longing for worldly existence, are indeed liberated beyond doubt.
Constantly bound by suffering and pleasure, and repeatedly deceived,
living beings who are cheated by delusion go to their destruction.

By which evil qualities is heaven not attained? Lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, laziness, and association with evil friends—these are not seeds for the celestial realm; therefore, a wise person should not take delight in them.
The man who constantly follows evil, devoid of shame and lacking remorse, falls from a precipice; he awakens only afterwards.
Those seized by anger, envy, and fear do not go to heaven;
for those whose minds are possessed by anger, envy, sloth, torpor, lack of faith, delusion, grief, and fear, they are not capable of reaching heaven. (Dhs 14.20)
The drinking of intoxicants, the consumption of nectar [as a pretext], false views, greed,
the commission of violent acts, and cruel deeds are the causes for performing such actions.
The fruit of wrong view is the supreme failure to see; wrong view is never a good thing.
Men who are utterly deluded by false views go to hell. (Dhs 14.22)
Failing to perceive the cause as causeless, people regard the impermanent as permanent;
deceived by false speech, they go to a fierce hell. (Dhs 14.23)
Through their painful splendor, those who are intent on false views and arrogant in their own wisdom delude other people.
Indeed, those people who act as the cause for this world, which is by nature suffering, fall right into the dense darkness of delusion as if into a great ocean. (Dhs 14.25)
The wise describe the tormenting discharge of arrows as that state of mind which, at the end, pierces one from all sides like a mountain of afflictions.
Liberation from the serpent of the afflictions, which is preceded by wisdom,
is attained by those men who perceive reality and are free from conceptual constructions.
Deceived by one another's opinions, this entire world does not attain supreme peace, wherein nothing false is spoken.
Restlessness, association with evil, laziness, and greed—these are the causes of hell; indeed, they are the abandonment of ethical discipline. (Dhs 14.29)
The drinking of intoxicants, constant violence, gazing upon the wives of others, greed, and a cruel mind—these are the causes of hell. (Dhs 14.30)
Slander, association with the wicked, false views, lack of restraint, and even fickleness of mind— these are the causes of ruin that constantly destroy a person. (Dhs 14.31)
Accompanied by ignorance, harshness, false speech, and arrogance—
these do not lead to happiness in this world, nor in the next.
Who are those to be avoided?
If this world is generally deluded, why are others not [avoided] as well? And if the world were undeluded, who would be submerged in suffering? (Dhs 14.33)
The Tathāgatas declare that such behavior belongs to ignorance;
false pride and excessive pride should be avoided in every way.
Indeed, these must always be shunned, for they are the causes of the tree of suffering.

The wise ones, most noble, who are constantly devoted to destroying the afflictions, having severed all those bonds, go to the immutable state; it is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end, both in this world and in others. (Dhs 14.35)
Through the indulgence in the defilements, their destruction occurs;
yet the indulgence in those very defilements is seen to be the cause that sets ignorance in motion.
Therefore, the afflictions must always be avoided, and unsurpassed wisdom must be cultivated.
Liberation comes through knowledge;
liberation comes through knowledge, and it is not said here to come through afflictions.
For by the fire of knowledge, the wood of the afflictions is consumed without remainder.
Knowledge consisting of desire generates afflictions;
for what purpose is it obstructed by those afflictions? It is ensnaring, delighting in sense objects, and once more, knowledge consisting of desire is a cataract that afflicts the eye. (Dhs 14.38)
Through the medicinal food of the words of the Perfectly Awakened One, passion is extinguished;
by the General of the True Dharma, the army of passion has been censured. (Dhs 14.39)
One should employ auspicious speech;
once uttered, auspicious speech must be carefully scrutinized.
For the four perversions shine forth like bubbles.
Likewise, the eight worldly dharmas destroy the entire world.
The raft of knowledge is capable of carrying one across; the rivers arising from the net of craving are difficult to cross due to their hundreds of discursive thoughts.
Having boarded the raft of knowledge, the auspicious sages cross over.
For whom does liberation not exist?
For those deluded men whose minds are fixed on the elements and who indulge in desire;
for them, liberation is never found through the five states.
The fire that is ignited by improper mental attention is extinguished by the rains of proper mental attention.

How can the blindness born of ignorance be removed? This blindness in men, produced by ignorance and having arisen over a long period of time, cannot be dispelled by a lamp lit for only a short while. (Dhs 14.44)
By the light of knowledge, the three defects are destroyed;
those deluded by passion and of dull intellect ripen in hell. But the wise are not destroyed, for they proceed toward nirvāṇa.
The three defects of embodied beings are destroyed by the light of knowledge.
Therefore, one should delight in complete knowledge, ethical discipline, and patience;
for those who are undeluded, the three defects of embodied beings perish.
Dimmed by the fire of knowledge, the great fuel of their afflictions is consumed;
their bodies submerged in disease, they move within the confines of their beds.
Wherein one goes to that supreme Veda which has the fruit of deluding the mind;
there, many various sufferings are experienced throughout the various states of existence.
This is always the activity of delusion regarding these five types of beings;
for those by whom the three faults that burn this world have been conquered.
Happiness arises through the yoga of knowledge;
having extinguished that fire by means of the yoga of knowledge, one becomes happy.
Therefore, one should constantly consume the mountain of afflictions with the fire of knowledge.
For one who has burned away the mountain of afflictions, the state of bliss is firmly established.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the Chapter on the Fetters.
(15) The Chapter on Evil: One who is ignorant of the fruit of evil suffers remorse;
it should be understood that the fruit of an evil deed being committed is bitter.
The deluded person who does not understand suffers later.
A person reaps the fruit of every sinful deed;
therefore, one should not practice evil if one desires happiness for oneself. (Dhs 15.2)
Even for the sake of liberation from even a small yet most terrible hell, those of sinful mind,
having fallen under the sway of delusion, commit further sins.
One should not trust even a small amount of evil that leads to hell; for by a small fire, all the trees on a mountain are consumed. (Dhs 15.4)
There is no enemy equal to evil;
through evil one goes to hell, and by evil one is consumed with burning heat.
Through evil one does not attain nirvāṇa; there is no foe equal to evil.
For a person of evil conduct does not prosper in happiness anywhere;
therefore, one should not practice evil if one desires one's own happiness. (Dhs 15.6)
Giving their approval to the virtuous while finding it difficult to follow the path of evil,
sinful beings of feeble mind take delight in their wicked deeds.
The ripening of which is bitter and brings remorse later for those of small mind—how can the fruit of such accumulated karma not be seen? (Dhs 15.8)
Therefore, one should not commit evil; the experience of evil is painful.
Evil and its maturation ripen with certainty for those who are wicked.
For evil does not [harm] evil; therefore, one should avoid evil.
For one who has completely abandoned evil, there is indeed no fear of evil.
One's own committed evil brings suffering; it is not experienced without being examined.
The fruit of merit is excellent, while the wickedness of evil ripens as torment.
But for a person who, having committed evil, does not subsequently practice what is auspicious, there would be no such suffering as that from falling upon weapons or into fire. (Dhs 15.12)
Just as false evil is imputed to those among the wicked who have practiced it,
so too [is merit] for one who has forever turned away from evil and possesses a virtuous mind.
For a peaceful monk, nirvāṇa is not far off;
for one whose face is serene, nirvāṇa is not distant.
Men who perform evil deeds go from misery to even greater misery.
Men who perform virtuous deeds proceed from happiness to even greater happiness;
for indeed, the fruit of intense evil is never attained as happiness.
Or rather, the fruit of happiness is intense; it never ripens as something contrary.
In this beginningless saṃsāra, the fruit of well-performed deeds is happiness. (Dhs 15.16)
It is taught that well-performed actions likewise have a painful fruit;
evil is seen to follow from evil, and similarly, good follows from what is auspicious. (Dhs 15.17)
The evildoer is reborn in the hells;
one of sinful conduct who hates what is auspicious is reborn in the hells. But for one who has abandoned evil and whose mind is ever virtuous, [there is no such rebirth].
Nirvāṇa, which is beyond perception, is reached by grasping with the hand; it is stainless, and these dharmas, auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end, always give rise to happiness.
Therefore, one should avoid evil, for the fruit of sinful action is bitter in its beginning, middle, and end;
therefore, evil should always be avoided and goodness should always be embraced. (Dhs 15.20)
For one who has abandoned evil, happiness is eternally established;
yet in this beginningless saṃsāra, why do people—burned by their own sins and following the power of delusion—fail to feel weary, O fools? (Dhs 15.21)
Evil is sweet at first, but in its result it is like fire;
yet the man who commits evil is censured by the whole world, while the doer of good is always peaceful. Therefore, one should avoid evil. (Dhs 15.22)
The wise who demonstrate reality have seen that evil is undesirable and harmful, resulting in bitter sensation at the time of its ripening;
therefore, a person of intelligence should avoid both evil and the ripening of evil.
Sin certainly exists in the sinner; there is no sin that lacks its consequence.
Evil conduct leads to destruction, whereas compassion leads the mind toward the auspicious.
"Evil always rests upon evil, and likewise, dharma rests upon dharma;
this has indeed been declared by the wise who demonstrate the truth. (Dhs 15.25)
Those who are devoid of evil attain supreme happiness; certainly, fools are unconscious of it when misdeeds are dear to them.
But those who have turned away from evil go to the supreme destination.
Having attained this human state so difficult to find, for one who finds great pleasure in evil, there is a most terrible deception that inevitably leads to sin. (Dhs 15.27)
There is a difference in the ripening of the fruits of the auspicious and the inauspicious:
he who becomes detached from evil and is exceedingly attached to the auspicious attains happiness after happiness, or indeed proceeds to liberation. (Dhs 15.28)
This person becomes fortunate who cultivates auspicious deeds;
but he is the most unfortunate in the world who cultivates evil.
Sin, which is censured by the virtuous from beginning to middle and to its end,
and which follows after evil, is seen to lead to rebirth in hell.
One who performs virtuous deeds attains happiness and goes to the world of the gods;
one who performs virtuous deeds and has conquered the senses shines exceedingly in the world.
Upon the dissolution of the body, such a person is constantly reborn in the world of the gods.
The ripening of evil is most terrible;
for it is said that the fruit of a misdeed follows upon the misdeed itself.
Likewise, the fruit of a good deed is seen to arise from a pleasant ripening.
The transformation of even a small *vibhītaka* seed is extremely terrible.
A sign similar to the fruit of evil karma has been seen:
a living being is dragged toward a miserable rebirth by evil, as if by fish-hooks.
A fish is released from a hook, but one is not released from evil by means of evil;
even the suffering of a single day caused by evil brings misery in every way.
Just as the odor of impurity is indeed repulsive to embodied beings,
so too is the fragrance of virtue delightful when it has not perished in an evil rebirth.
Just as a fragrance remains in a flower even when it has perished,
so this evildoer, constantly following the dictates of desire, continues to move.
Who are those who act virtuously?
One who is constantly lazy and untruthful does not deserve prosperity.
For those [who are thus], the night is endless.
The mind is established in evil.
Dawn breaks for those whose minds are fixed on evil;
but for men who are free from envy, full of goodness, and who act virtuously, it is already day.

Those who have committed little evil attain happiness; those beings who are not of an evil nature are always moving in the sky. Just as a boat with a light load floats and does not sink, so it is for them. (Dhs 15.39)
Suffering arises from an evil friend;
likewise, a person of slight sin floats and does not sink.
A person cannot be happy through association with an evil friend.
Having encountered a wicked friend, one becomes intent on all forms of fire;
yet he who knows the rules for undertaking actions always perceives the subtle meaning.
Such a person is not smeared by evil, just as the sky is not smeared by mud;
by listening to what he has not heard before, and by reinforcing what he has already heard, he becomes firm.
The wise person should avoid evil, which is the mark of a fool; by avoiding it, he is reborn among the gods after death.
This thorough knowledge of virtues and faults is the characteristic of a wise person.
The characteristic of the deluded is the failure to discern virtues and faults; this is the mark of a fool:
the transference of virtues onto faults, and likewise the transference of faults onto virtues. (Dhs 15.44)
The characteristic of the deluded and the undeluded:
one who knows the truth of faults and virtues always becomes a partaker of sorrow; whereas the doer of evil...
A person stands toward himself like an enemy.
Likewise, for a person who performs virtuous deeds, he behaves like a friend;
yet for one who has not died, he enters the grounds of the dark hells.
The intellect of one who is devoted to evil, constantly intent upon sense objects, fickle in its delight in sense objects, and always following after passion—[is lost]. (Dhs 15.47)
That man who shares in suffering has no discernment regarding the dharmas,
nor does he understand the cause from which great suffering arises— like a fire that has been kindled.
With all our sins exhausted, we have returned once more to this world;
indeed, the fruit of well-performed deeds is virtuous and adorned with manifold qualities.
The fruit of evil deeds is held to be suffering and deceptive;
thus, we shall experience both happiness and suffering amidst the perils of existence.
Like the waves of the ocean tossed by the winds of karma,
those people who are ill-disposed toward evil and who guard themselves from sins have acted rightly.
On account of that [deed], those who act unwholesomely go to hell;
but once liberated from that hell, they go to the third heaven.
For they do not remember suffering and thus again fall under the sway of sensual desires;
this mind has become hardened by pleasures and pains that swing like a pendulum.
This separation is a total obstruction; it is not found among ordinary sufferings.
One who is joined with another's wife is utterly deceived by the senses.
Under the sway of the noose of craving, a person wanders in saṃsāra;
following the dictates of the noose of craving, he wanders in saṃsāra—
from hell to the realm of hungry ghosts, and from the state of a ghost into the wombs of animals.
From the animal realm one goes to the celestial worlds, and from the celestial worlds back again to human births;
thus, wandering through various karmas, the world revolves like a wheel. (Dhs 15.56)
Though all is suffering,
they do not fall under the power of weariness, for they have come under the power of practice.
They protect the celestial realm and likewise become dispassionate toward worldly pleasures.
Wandering from pleasure to pleasure, those who roam in delusion wander through thousands of lotuses and hundreds of millions of lotuses of suffering.
Those sufferings have been experienced, yet the foolish are not distressed;
no happiness exists in the world, for it is overwhelmed by all manner of suffering.
It is the cause of suffering,
yet beings afflicted by delusion do not feel any agitation;
the fool is distressed by suffering and remains engaged in the cause of suffering.
Just as a hundredfold fruit is seen in relation to its cause, namely the seed,
so too are living beings bound by the whip of pleasure and pain, following along through the three realms of existence.
They do not go to the supreme security that is free from all suffering;
for when suffering is remembered, it then pierces the embodied being.
Furthermore, when suffering has been forgotten, beings move about free from fever;
however, the suffering of hell is always remembered by embodied beings.
Then this happiness of Kṛṣṇa remains through inference;
having understood that very [happiness], the entire world is pervaded by it.
Direct your intellect toward that which is most excellent and turn it away from faults; for life proceeds, flickering with the instability of a momentary office.
Even karmas are exhausted; therefore, one should be intent on the highest good.
The mind experiences the entire force of the heart and the whole of life.
The wise person does not fear future suffering;
therefore, a discerning person should not commit evil for the sake of a livelihood.
The multitude of people do not fear future suffering.
By this, his evil is cooked, having fallen under the power of delusive evil;
he is deluded by sinful states that are unwholesome and devoid of purity.
The deluded one goes to hell due to the power of evil;
the deluded one is led to hell where his evil ripens. He who has no fear of evil commits much evil. (Dhs 15.69)
