Burning with endless evil, he later attains hell; just as even a minute spark of fire is capable of causing a conflagration.
Those free from evil desire happiness, and others likewise; yet the unintelligent go to hell because of their evils.
Therefore, one who desires happiness must cultivate fear of sin. (Dhs 15.71)
Violence, false speech, unchastity, lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, restlessness, and association with evil friends— these lead to the arising of great suffering.
Evil is like poison and fire;
these two are indeed like poison and fire. One should protect oneself from them with great effort.
For this dharma of Māra is suffering, whereas happiness arises from the dharma on all sides.
The definition of pleasure and pain:
those who know reality understand the definition of pleasures and pains.
Truthfulness, generosity, as well as patience, constant avoidance of evil friends,
and always maintaining loving-kindness toward those who have overcome [passions]— this indeed is the path to the third heaven.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Chapter on Evil.
(16) The Chapter on Hell: Having committed evil deeds, beings who live by dishonest means [fall into] the eight fires of hell.
Listen to me regarding those states of woe to which they go after death.
Sañjīva, Kāmasūtra, Sampāta, the two Rauravas,
Tamopara, Mahācitrapatana, and Pratāpana.
Thus these eight hells have been described as difficult to escape; they are filled with those who have committed terrible deeds and are considered to cause individual torment.
The terrifying nature of the fires of hell: [The hells] have four walls and four gates, divided and measured into sections;
they are bounded by iron ramparts and are intensely tormented by iron.
The ground, made of molten iron and blazing with intense heat,
fiercely burns for many hundreds of yojanas with its own radiance.
Subduers of Kandarpa, terrible, radiant, and difficult to approach—
those [fires] of hair-raising form also say they are painful and fearsome.
Having fallen into hell, these people suffer intensely; they fall into hell with their feet upward and their faces downward—
those who speak abusively against seers who are self-restrained and ascetic.
Furthermore, they are cooked there in boiling water like balls of dough,
wailing day and night like trees shaken by the wind.
Tormented by intense sufferings, they cry out with a great roar;
pursued by the hell-guardians, they run in all directions.
Having deluded himself regarding the true goal through false views, a person shrouded by the snare of delusion and enveloped by the ocean of causal factors falls into a terrible hell.
A person whose entire wealth has been consumed by false views is the lowest of men;
thus bound, he remains in hell as a terrible cause for those who are conceited.
Those dull-witted persons who have fallen under the sway of falsehood,
all go to hell, for they have been deceived by their own minds.
O fool, you are now experiencing the fruit of that evil deed previously committed by you, which followed the lead of your own mind; you shall obtain the ultimate ripening of its result.
The minds of others are to be captivated,
and the wives of others are to be courted;
for living beings, constantly deceived by their own minds, are indeed short-lived.
You have come here solely under the power of that ripening of karma;
why do you weep, O lowest of men, having yourself committed evil deeds?
Those dull-witted men who, having committed evil deeds, pass away at death—their birth is as fruitless as seed sown in barren soil. (Dhs 16.16)
That fool who indulges in sensual pleasures, which possess little sweetness but yield bitter results, goes from darkness to deeper darkness.
O fool, what have you done by seeking the happiness of children and wife?
Deprived of the fruits of your own actions, you shall burn alone in hell.
For whom is life difficult?
That man who, being under the sway of his wife and children, performs what is difficult to do—
he goes to hell.
That evil is experienced [by the doer].
Neither wives, nor sons, nor wealth, nor friends will protect one in any way when the time of death has arrived and is present. (Dhs 16.20)
For those whose minds are afflicted and deceived by craving,
how can there be companionship for them? Why do you grieve?
You were carried away by former sense-objects and deceived by craving;
why do you weep now, O dull-witted one, having yourself committed this evil deed?
Neither fire, nor weapons, nor poison, nor standing enemies in this world afflict a person as much as one's own evil deeds do.
Just as birds dwelling in their nests depart for various directions and, rising at the proper time, take refuge in trees, so too is the meeting of living beings. (Dhs 16.24)
Having destroyed another's property and committed a transgression against the world, what evil deed does one not perform when deceived by delusion? (Dhs 16.25)
That by which one goes to supreme peace and that by which one goes to the abode of the asuras—
the cause in both cases is supreme delusion, which is the darkness even of darknesses.

The evil committed for the sake of one's family casts one into hell; brought there by the snares consisting of sons and wife, you—deceived by your own minds—have committed that very evil for their sake. (Dhs 16.27)
Friends, sons, parents, kinsmen, and relatives—
for whose sake you, dull-witted ones, have committed evil.
Surely your own self was not dear to you in your human lives,
since you, O lowest of men, committed this sin for the sake of a son.
He who does not feel remorse for the evil he previously committed goes to a terrible hell, deceived by the cause of his son.
What will the fruit of evil deeds do for your sons, what for your wives, and what for your kinsmen?
In the eternal hell, fire burns; it is that very karma which causes the torment.
Having yourself performed unwholesome karma that results in suffering, O blameless one, you now suffer in vain; deceived by delusion, you have placed a burden upon yourself.
Followed by passion and hatred, deceived by delusion,
and seeking the happiness of sons and wives, they all go toward evil.
Furthermore, being burned by fire both internal and external,
the evildoer suffers misery in hell.
All beings who have fallen under the sway of their own minds are utterly deluded;
why do you cry out in vain, O sound, when you are merely scorched by fire?
The fruit that follows from evil has been seen; now you think, "I have committed sinful deeds. O evil-minded one, do not weep for that; why do you lament in vain? (Dhs 16.36)
The fool is protected by his sins; he is protected by the impurity of his causes.
The fruit that follows from evil is seen to arise from a complex of causes and conditions.
Why was the Dharma not practiced, and why was evil not avoided?
Because of that evil, the person does not see anything beyond hell. (Dhs 16.38)
The fool who does not perceive the fruit produced by his own evil deeds will inevitably suffer the consequences; how then, O evil-minded one, will you escape them? (Dhs 16.39)
One was previously deceived by evil and is now consumed by evil;
you shall not commit further evils, and thus you will pass away without suffering.
You have committed sinful deeds and not virtuous ones in any way;
therefore, you are consumed by sin—do not set your mind upon what is unwholesome.
What is more painful than pain?
There is no suffering more painful than this: that one who pursues evil.
Therefore, do not pursue evil if you do not desire suffering. (Dhs 16.42)
The clear words of one's family members are reflected in his inner heart, yet peace is not found;
we have become objects of compassion, but there is no compassion within our own hearts. (Dhs 16.43)
Just as the manifold evil you have committed, shrouded in delusion,
now pursues you most intensely, so too do those causes [of suffering] therein.
O fool, you did not guard your virtue and accumulated much evil;
this is the fruit that has now arisen from the evil you committed.
"We are not the cause in that matter; you yourselves are indeed the cause.
Whoever performs a sinful deed, he alone is the cause of that action."
"The terrible evil that was committed by you, who were mocked by the curse of craving—that very thing now falls upon you; why do you revile us? (Dhs 16.47)
An unperformed evil does not ripen, nor can evil exist without a cause;
for whatever evil has been committed by someone, that alone ripens for him.
The sinner goes to hell;
thus you, deprived of your duties and deceived by the drinking of liquor,
have fallen into a fierce hell— why do you now grieve in vain?
You, who were devoted solely to sensual pleasures, have now come to this terrible hell;
why do you suffer so intensely even amidst such agonizing causes?
When those evils were committed by you, deluded by desire, why did you not feel abhorrence then? Why do you now suffer in remorse?
For hell has been taught to be the cause of false speech;
you have cultivated that very cause in the past, so now you lament in vain.
One does not obtain truth through wealth, nor is it attained through hardship;
therefore, having abandoned truth, you take delight in falsehoods.
The evil and harmful deeds committed by you in the past with a deluded mind—
those misdeeds (evil actions) committed by you are now ripening.
One who is liberated through the destruction of evil does not find hell; yet men who merely cry out for help are not released from it by any means whatsoever.
The doer of evil reaps the fruit himself;
why do you, O fools, cry out in vain? Deceived by your own karma, these deluded children, having been abandoned and cheated, wail pointlessly in their ignorance.
O mortal, you have been deceived by those who are harmful yet appear beneficial, and by enemies disguised as friends;
you are now departing for the great darkness.
There is no other enemy like your own evil and sinful deed;
by means of these three kinds of actions, you are led to the abode of Yama.
O fool, why were you deceived by those known as "sons"?
Why was the thought of giving and so forth not formed by them?
Deceived by delusion.
Like a snake upon the back of its enemy, he departs from this world for the next;
he is the foremost enemy of enemies, the manifestor of all evils.
Resembling poison, fire, and weapons, for you yourself have committed evil deeds; you alone shall experience the results of the actions you have performed. (Dhs 16.61)
He whose mind is always peaceful and who is not struck down by sense objects— such a state does not come to one who perceives things as they truly are.
Having heard the sound of hell, why do you cry out, O evil-minded one?
How much more so when fire shall burn you there like dry wood?
Those who have not been burned by fire are burned by their own evil deeds;
while ordinary fire may be extinguished somewhere, the fire of misdeeds is never extinguished.
Fire does not reach the end of the world, nor does a man touched by fire [perish];
for it is the fire of evil deeds that will truly consume him.
Those men who are consumed by the fire of their own evil deeds are burned in hell;
however, for those who are free from the fire of sin, there is no arising in hell.
If you always hold yourself dear, and if you fear hell, [then avoid such deeds].
Abandon your own evils, and then you will not go to suffering;
for those who follow the power of delusion constantly go toward that which is composed of evil.
"You shall reach a terrible hell; why do you shed tears?
[Therein lies] suffering, the ripening of suffering, and likewise the arrival at the end of suffering."
A well-performed deed, beautiful in its beginning, middle, and end, ripens;
in this world, no evil that you have committed can ever become a well-performed deed.
Today you shall experience the fruit of that intense ripening;
for the result is conceived as being similar to its causes and conditions, not otherwise.
Just as the cause was previously established, so shall you obtain the fruit;
as it is for you, so too for others, one should strive with effort to protect their lives.
Why were those acts of taking life committed by you, who follow after evil? For wealth is acquired by men only at the cost of the loss of life. (Dhs 16.72)
That which has been acquired by you is produced by the arising of karma;
wives are beloved to all, even more dear than one's own life.
O you who are stained by passion, why have you committed this injury against the innocent?
This supreme defilement of phenomena produces total delusion of the intellect.
You must drink the dharma-nectar,
avoiding the activity that arises from the poison of the tongue, which causes total lack of faith.
The evil deed of false speech has been avoided by you,
because you were thus devoted to these five kinds of precepts.
Therefore, do not weep before me; why do you lament in vain?
For you have been utterly deceived by those evil states that belong to the realm of the senses.
Therefore, you shall reach a great hell filled with garlands of flames;
by this fire of craving, all three worlds are set ablaze.
One must be attentive in the practice of Dharma;
having seen that the Dharma was not practiced, why do you now feel remorse?
Having heard those sweet words, which are like a temple of desire for the mind, [you should act accordingly].
When that great sin was uttered, its fruit came upon him;
having committed an evil deed, the experience of suffering for that sin is inevitable.
Why do you today suffer so piteously, distressed and wretched?
Through the exhaustion of their karma, evildoers are liberated from hell.
Sunk in lamentation many times over, they are not liberated by any means;
having performed undesirable and evil deeds, they remain under the power of disease.
The ignorant perform unwholesome deeds;
he who laments is a fool and laments in vain.
But he who understands the fruits yet to come delights in the wholesome present.
One does not cry out in hell as you are now repenting;
for the actions performed by me alone bear fruit for me.
Consumed by disease and by enemies, he subsequently fell into hell;
for the embodied being who is burnt by passion, the ground of heedlessness is inauspicious.
Bound by that noose, I have fallen into this most wretched state;
indeed, bitter is the fruit for those men who delight in wicked conduct.
"I am afflicted by ignorance; I am experiencing the fruit of my own deeds, having fallen under the power of cruel, most terrible, and sinful beings. (Dhs 16.87)
How might there be liberation?
How indeed might there be release from this ocean of suffering and saṃsāra?
This karma, which is more painful than pain itself, is being ripened by me.
I see no attainment of happiness nor any security for myself in hell;
I have fallen from the world of the living like one who has lost his way. (Dhs 16.89)
This living being, rendered helpless and surrounded by distortions,
perceives the entire atmosphere as being densely filled with garlands of flames.
The cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the earth are all without interval;
yet I, miserable, ignorant, and suffering, perceive no place of refuge.
For this king, who is scorched by the edge of a razor and led through the wilderness utterly helpless on all sides, I perceive no protector who might liberate him from this suffering. (Dhs 16.92)
Powerless, helpless, and suffering, tormented by fire and bound by the fetters of his own arms, I was led away somewhere against my will.
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor sons, nor women can protect me from this calamity; alas, they are ungrateful to me! (Dhs 16.94)
For one who practices unrighteousness, there is no refuge anywhere;
for one devoid of joy, there is neither happiness nor [peace]. (I perceive this in every way: For one bound by the noose of death, no refuge is to be found.
As if enraged, those cruel ones will appear on all sides;
all directions will be joyless and surrounded by predatory beasts.
Out of a state of mental fortitude, I would fall into hell for my transgression;
and whatever moving or stationary being I see here,
all that is indeed agitated and set ablaze by fire.
I find no refuge; I am utterly helpless on all sides.
I am sinking into a terrible darkness, like one who has lost his boat in the ocean.
I do not see the sky with its constellations, planets, and stars;
all this is inverted and enveloped in darkness.
Indeed, all five sense-faculties are completely withdrawn from everything;
yet at that time, their entire body is sawn apart by saws.
I find no refuge; desire will surely become my bond, and heaps of suffering increase on all sides, from every quarter.
Again and again, the pains arising from their bodies increase;
they grow through sufferings and are utterly helpless on all sides.
Having constantly observed that [the world] is born of karma, one should repeatedly contemplate its cause;
for the elders declare that happiness is firmly rooted in the fruits of one's own actions.
That which ought to have been done by you previously is now being considered by you later;
deceived by delusion in the past, why do you lament today?
How much more so for the evildoer who must ripen in bitter suffering?
Your suffering will arise from many causes of pain;
and there is no protection whatsoever therein, except for the exhaustion of karma.
Thus, through the destruction of truth, one who has fallen under the power of the noose of karma is led many times by the messengers of Yama to a terrible hell.
Quadrangular, with four gates, divided and measured into sections—
therein the helpless denizens of hell are cooked in manifold ways.
This result has come about because of that great amount of defilement regarding the true nature of beings which you have repeatedly spoken of with a tendency toward divisiveness. (Dhs 16.108)
Those who practice slander go to hell;
they are perpetually cast out by friends, kinsmen, and relatives.
Slander, which is detested by the virtuous, is what these people hold dear.
Therefore, you did not practice the Dharma, nor did you refrain from slander.
Having experienced the fruits of that slander, why do you lament now?
Alas! That which is seen as harshness—sharp, treacherous, elevated, and utterly devoid of the tongue’s wealth—yields such a fruit as this. (Dhs 16.111)
This being, who was supremely harsh and fell into a terrible hell, has now come to your tongue for its own misdeed; why do you lament today?
The fire consisting of hunger and thirst, arising spontaneously from the heart, increases a thousandfold and consumes the vital wind (māruta).
The distance between harsh speech and hell,

the distance between snow and fire, and the distance between Mount Meru and a mustard seed— that same distance lies between the tongue that utters such words and the blazing fire of hell. (Dhs 16.114)
The fire originating from hell is not found anywhere else;
however, the fire consisting of hunger and thirst is encountered even among the gods.
For although the hellish fire is sharp because of this cause,
it does not possess such power as the fire that arises from that [hellish being].
This result has now come upon you for that which was spoken by you with confidence—words that were disconnected, meaningless, and inconsistent in their sequence. (Dhs 16.117)
Having seen the prosperity of others, the thought arose in me, "May it be mine";
the fruit of the poison produced by that darkness has now arrived.
O lowest of men, you have been consumed by the fire of worldly activity;
having gone from one fire to another, you suffer and yet you boast.
But when you are utterly deluded by worldly activity, you are bound by this very rope for rebirth in hell; as a man, you cry out in lamentation.
Drawn by malice, you have come to a terrible hell;
through the exhaustion of karma there will be liberation, and you shall be released from hell.
The discourse on unrighteousness burns;
unrighteousness, appearing in the form of righteousness and evil in the form of virtue, consumes you.
That which was previously spoken by you burns you, not fire.
How is it that for those who have utterly destroyed reality and who do not desire the distinction between dharma and adharma,
the opening of sin has been taught as inevitably leading to evil?
The dharma that was avoided by you and the virtuous who were reviled by you—the harsh fruit of what you have earned is ripening for you today. (Dhs 16.124)
Since you are always driven by the force of delusion joined with the objects of craving,
what is the use of lamenting thus over the True Dharma and the Discipline?
He would be a constant evildoer, fallen under the power of the snare of delusion;
why do you burn with remorse and weep after having committed such a terrible deed?
For one who is always deluded regarding causes, conditions, and what is dharma and non-dharma,
you have reached a terrible hell, the most dreadful of hells.
Those who follow the sway of desire go to hell;
they do not act with what is joined to desires.
This fruit, which is the lack of flavor in well-performed karma, has now arrived.
Having wasted their merit through negligence and with minds attached to pleasure,
even gods who follow the sway of desire go to hell.
Those who revile the noble ones go to hell;
those who revile the noble ones, those who hate the results of karma,
and those who are falsely disciplined— all these, upon death, go to hell.
Those who deceive the Dharma go to hell;
those who are more wicked than a mother or a householder, as well as others who deceive the Dharma,
perform what is undesirable in this world and go to hell.

Those who delight in evil experience suffering, as do other men who are constantly attached to pleasure yet remain devoted to evil; deceived by their own minds, they go from sorrow to sorrow. (Dhs 16.132)
Blameworthy deeds cause one to fall into hell;
therefore, one should never direct the mind toward blameworthy deeds.
Even minor blameworthy deeds cause one to fall into hell.
Therefore, one should perform virtuous deeds;
one should always practice wholesome actions with a mind intent upon the welfare of others.
Thus, being ever beneficial, one becomes a dam that blocks the way to hell.
Liberation is to be pursued; this is the tenfold dharma.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Section on Hell.
(17) The Chapter on Pretas: How can there be happiness for one who does not give?
How can there be peace for one who is unsubdued? How can there be fruit for one who has not sown?
There is no light without a lamp; how can there be happiness for one who does not give?
Just as there is no peace for an embodied being regarding the objects of sight due to the absence of giving,
so too happiness is not obtained by the hungry ghosts.
The doer of evil deeds goes to the world of pretas, where, after death, those who are most base in the three worlds wander,
extremely agitated; that is the fruit produced by stinginess.
Nothing is gained by the giver, nor does there exist the destruction of what has been done;
living beings are consumers of their own karma, experiencing the fruits of their actions.
Whatever evil you have committed, those who have departed and dwell in the worlds beyond are now consumed by the fire of hunger and thirst that blazes here.
When, indeed, will the realm that brings about the arising of happiness become ours?
And when will there be liberation from this burning torment?

Deprived of the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path, one lives in nothing but suffering; though I am free from both the path and the non-path, the fruit of my actions was not known.
The fire consisting of hunger and thirst has manifested its rise unawares. (Dhs 17.7)
With faces shrouded in the darkness of afflictions, devoid of hope, and having abandoned all means of livelihood,
we live on, alas, in misery, bound by a web of skin and sinews.
There is no protector for us from all sides; alas, we have fallen into distress!
Having been born as human beings, we have been ruined by our own karma.
Why was the Dharma not practiced and accumulated in the Jewel Islands—that which always performs what is auspicious and never what is inauspicious? (Dhs 17.10)
Having ascended the steps to heaven, he proceeds with a level gaze toward those for whose sake he committed evil, greatly tormenting his mind.
By this, all those who stood to terrify you have departed;
you are bound by fierce fetters, delivered by Yama, and held under his authority.
Dragged by the rope of evil, you experience the fruit of your own deeds;
you have reached the terrible darkness of the world of Yama, which is difficult to approach.
Here you shall undergo the consequences of the wicked actions that were committed by you.
O fool, one experiences what one has done oneself;
it is never experienced by others.
Here, this person is being dragged away by a most terrifying rope of evil.
The fire of the world of hungry ghosts consists of great hunger and thirst;
indeed, the falling of fire, weapons, or poison is not so bitter as that.
The onset of the fire of hunger and thirst is so bitter that it lasts not for a moment, nor for a lava, nor for a muhūrta, nor even for a night. (Dhs 17.16)

We are beset by suffering where there might be happiness; we are constantly enveloped in misery. Having encountered what is more painful than pain itself, we have cultivated the very cause of suffering. (Dhs 17.17)
"Perhaps there might be liberation from suffering, and happiness will arise;
yet no water is seen during the festival, for the ponds are drying up. (Dhs 17.18)

If the very nature of the fruits of karma were to be destroyed, how could we continue to flow? We would become like rivers with dried-up waters, along with our mountains, forests, and groves. (Dhs 17.19)
We constantly run about on the ground, ever longing for water;
we are men whose bodies are scorched and who are afflicted by hunger and thirst. (Dhs 17.20)
We find no refuge; alas, we have fallen into a miserable calamity, beset by crows and owls with great, sharp vajra-like fangs.
Being pursued, I see no refuge that bestows happiness;
this reflection has appeared as the result of that very karma.
Just as the action was performed by us, so has this fruit arrived;
bound by the wind of karma and ripened by the thread of karma.
"There is no liberation without the exhaustion of karma; we see no escape other than the exhaustion of karma"—thus [the wise say].
For one who perceives those undesirable evils as being like fire, [there is liberation]. (Dhs 17.24)
What is the realm of the hungry ghosts (preta) like?
He does not go to the realm of the hungry ghosts, which is enveloped by the fires of hunger and thirst;
rather, the sensations arising from hell increase again and again.
We are like a mountain enveloped in garlands of flames;
that blazing mountain can be extinguished in every way only by water.
This fire of ours, resembling the ocean, is never extinguished;
at what moment did it arise, aided by the wind of craving? (Dhs 17.27)
The fire of karma consumes us, surrounding us on all sides;
we, being of evil deeds, are utterly devoid of pure dharma.
Having reached this world of pretas, deluded by the fruits of heaven,
they possess a fire consisting of hunger and thirst, as well as a second fire born of actual flame.
By their own evil deeds alone, people go to the realm of the departed as heaps of funeral mounds;
neither wives, nor sons, nor kinsmen follow them there as heaps of funeral mounds.
I have been deceived by my own mind; I have been utterly cheated by my own karma.
Abandoned by friends and kinsmen, I have reached the realm of the hungry ghosts;
there are no wives, nor friends, nor sons, nor relatives.
The examination of the fruit of evil deeds:
No other protector can save one being led away by the powerful noose of karma, just as the threefold karma is experienced by me. (Dhs 17.32)
Generosity, ethical conduct, and learning—these three have been fully proclaimed.
Whatever evil deed has been committed by me here, shrouded in the net of delusion, [may it be purified].
Liberation from the world of hungry ghosts occurs through virtuous action alone;
for whatever fruit has arisen from the karma that served as its cause—if we are released from this sinful world of hungry ghosts so difficult to escape—[it is by virtue of that]. (Dhs 17.34)
One should avoid impure and evil deeds, thinking: "I shall never again commit a sinful act in any way;
[for such acts] are hot, have hot results, and cause great suffering."
Therefore, one should avoid those evil deeds which are unwholesome in this world.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the Section on Pretas.
(18) Regarding the class of animals:
one should never commit injury against others, nor engage in devouring, mutual killing, binding, or confinement.
Having reached the state of an animal, one should therefore avoid malice toward others.
And those fools whose minds are afflicted by delusion, who are devoid of ethical conduct and generosity,
and who are deceived by craving, are born among the animal realm.
They do not distinguish between those who should be approached and those who should not, nor likewise between what is edible and what is inedible;
they exist outside the sphere of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, having cast aside both dharma and adharma.
Deluded by the aging of the five sense faculties, following the power of the noose of craving,
and utterly seized by anger and envy, such men go to the animal realm.
Mortals are afflicted by the pursuit of objects; gods are afflicted by negligence;
pretas suffer from the calamity of hunger and thirst; and hell-beings exist because of their [karmic] causes.
Who are those whose ultimate destination is the animal realm?
Those who are excessively intent on killing one another are headed for the animal realm;
thus the world is agitated by various such calamities.
One afflicted by stinginess should not commit evil;
one afflicted by stinginess toward others should not perform an evil deed.
Beings afflicted by stinginess go to the realm of hungry ghosts or among the animals.

Whose birth is fruitful? Indeed, their birth is fruitful and their intellect is undeceived—those who always possess a mind fixed on the Dharma; they are always worthy of honor by the virtuous. (Dhs 18.8)
For those who have mounted the chariot of knowledge, liberation indeed occurs;
yet thus the world, its essence consisting of the three defects and uncreated karma, wanders in a state difficult to fathom.
And he of pure being who has mounted the chariot of knowledge treats with contempt that [world].
Thus ends the eighteenth section, the Chapter on Animals.
(19) The Section on Hunger: Men afflicted by hunger perform unwholesome deeds;
thus, suffering in saṃsāra is for the most part the disease of hunger within the three realms.
Afflicted by this, sentient beings commit unwholesome deeds against themselves.
It is taught that within one's own body, fire exists in the form of hunger;
like the fire at the end of an eon, it consumes the remaining worlds as if they were trees. (Dhs 19.2)
One follows this supramundane fire as it proceeds;
one does not perceive one's own nirvāṇa even in hundreds of other eons.
Indeed, the vigor of one who is not indolent possesses such strength that it overcomes this entire triple world for the sake of food.
Various thoughts arising from human beings in this world cause delusion;
all of them exist for the sake of food within the ocean of the three realms of existence.
The indescribable suffering of one dwelling in the intermediate state, being dragged along by their karma—
the suffering of that long journey— is not capable of being fully described. (Dhs 19.6)
The suffering of one who is enveloped by the fuel of ignorance and consumed by its heat while dwelling in the womb is indeed impossible to describe.

The suffering of one who is constantly greedy for the taste of food and whose mind is perpetually fixed upon it is such that it cannot be fully described when one is so covetous of another's property.
For those of firm and corrupted minds, or whose hearts are consumed by passion,
the excessive suffering that arises is not capable of being described.
The suffering that arises when the heart is utterly ruined by constant association with those who are unpleasant and by the objects of the senses is not capable of being described.
The suffering within existence, which consists of constant seeking and is scorched by the poison of craving until death, is not capable of being fully described.
The manifold suffering born of evil friends,
which arises incessantly and produces rebirth in the miserable states, is not capable of being fully described.
The calamity that arises in the heart upon seeing what has befallen one's children and wife is a great path to the hells; it is not possible to describe it fully. (Dhs 19.13)
The suffering of one whose mind is ruined, who is tormented by hunger and thirst and consumed by fire, cannot be adequately described. (Dhs 19.14)
The sorrow born of grief for one who is constantly humiliated by friends, kinsmen, and well-wishers is such that it cannot be adequately described.
The suffering of one whose body is aged, caused by the instability of a beloved wife who has become wayward and difficult to manage— that suffering is not capable of being fully described.
The suffering that arises for one being carried away from that world by Death toward the state of non-existence (rasāt) cannot be adequately described. (Dhs 19.17)
The wise declare that through generosity one destroys the unwholesome; for whatever evil the foolish commit, and whatever leads them to an unfortunate rebirth, that they remove by means of giving.
Therefore, one should always direct the mind toward virtuous deeds and avoid all unwholesome actions;
the mind should be directed toward virtuous deeds adorned by generosity and ethical discipline.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the Section on Hunger.
(20) The Chapter on Laziness:
Through laziness comes the loss of knowledge;
laziness, as well as excessive pride, deceit, hypocrisy, and even harshness.
The stages leading to certainty have been seen, as well as the relinquishing of [false] knowledge.
Association with the unrighteous, as well as the avoidance of the righteous, and false view—these are the powerful causes of destruction. (Dhs 20.2)
Agitation at an improper place and time, not knowing what should or should not be said—
these are indeed stages of misfortune, as is excessive confidence in such matters.
Delighting in whatever is worthless and eating wherever one may find food produces a sense of insignificance in the end, as well as a lack of self-praise. (Dhs 20.4)
The loss of fortitude, the failure of memory, and conflict with the sovereign—
these are indeed those who have been overtaken by death, for cruelty resides within their minds.
One who knows the truth that actions bear no fruit, who is excluded from both merit and demerit,
and who is liberated from the virtuous, has the intention of plunging into a precipice.
Laziness, dullness, and sleep, as well as the tongue,
are declared to be the sources of hatred toward men, as is harsh speech.
Greed is the cause of contempt; excessive greed, contempt, and arrogance are restlessness.
The pursuit of sensual pleasures, devoid of the Dharma, is an illustration of delusion.
Laziness is the root of the three faults; here, laziness is said to be the root of the three faults.
Through the application of vigor, the faults arising in the mind are overcome.
For by the undertaking of vigor, the fruit is inevitably experienced;
the fruit of an action undertaken according to principle is seen for one who has realized the truth.
The fruit of this threefold karma is said to be threefold;
determined by three groups, it is like a trident that follows one through the three realms of existence.
For one who indulges in laziness there is an evil rebirth; he who serves evil, is fierce, and even practices indolence,
is a hater of the Dharma, cruel, and runs along paths that are not the way.
He who is satisfied with whatever it may be, who becomes angry at whatever it may be, and who is attached to this or that—he is called a fool. (Dhs 20.13)
Laziness,
which is the state of one's own mind swooned by the poison of negligence— that is a precipice, violent and supremely deceptive.
Those people who, in the undertaking of vigor, are free from the stain of great evil and indolence,
are enjoyers of liberation and partakers of happiness.
Laziness makes all phenomena subject to aging and death;
by that great fault, men become partakers of suffering.
And its companion is the entry of pleasure; therefore, one should avoid it, for a man pierced by it is praised by himself on all sides.
For one who is indolent, of meager merit, and whose mind is carried away by delusion, there is no auspicious destination; he is censured by all his own kin. (Dhs 20.18)
One who delights in indolence becomes sinful;
such a person associates with the sin of indolence as well as with sloth and torpor.
These are great dangers that serve to obstruct the gateway to liberation.
These are the mansions of suffering: lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, restlessness, and association with evil friends.
These are the mansions of suffering; would a wise person not guard against them?
For those who are overcome by laziness and lack the luster of spiritual exertion,
their life is like a death with gasps for breath, and even their existence is fruitless.
Men who are overcome by laziness do not truly live, even while they breathe;
for this laziness is considered to be far worse than death itself. (Dhs 20.22)
Only those who have initiated vigor cross the ocean of existence;
those who are sunk in the mire of laziness remain submerged in the expanse of suffering.
Those men who have initiated vigor have crossed over the ocean of existence.
He who is lazy and weak in vigor, and who is always devoted to evil, is dead even while living; but he who is truly dead goes to hell.
Laziness is the cause of the poverty of human beings;
those men who are poor are equal to cattle and partakers of suffering. Wretched, subsisting on the alms of others, laziness is the cause therein. (Dhs 20.25)
Generally, for those who live by usury and subsist on the wives of others,
there is an excessive longing for pleasure and a constant delight in sexual intercourse.
Those who have made a void of reality and are solely intent on food are consumed by their own minds when the time of death has arrived.
These [ascetics] endure cold and heat, as well as hunger and thirst;
they must perform bodily exertions, always maintaining their practice for the sake of dharma.
Therefore, one should not set one's mind on laziness;
one who desires virtue should not apply the mind to indolence. One who is lazy sinks perpetually in saṃsāra and is not liberated from suffering. (Dhs 20.29)
One who is possessed by stinginess is deceived by the world;
having been overcome by greed in the midst of the virtuous, he is deceived by the world.
At the end, he is either deceived or released from happiness.
Through the Dharma, liberation arises for one who is energetic, possessed of mindfulness, and always devoted to solitude;
freed from unwholesome states, he attains liberation through diligent effort.
One should certainly not direct the mind toward evil deeds,
for such a succession of sufferings exists; therefore, a sentient being should not apply the mind to evil deeds.
In this world ablaze with the fires of the three humors, one should exercise supreme peace and compassion; not toward the dead.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the Section on Laziness.
Mind, speech, and likewise action—these are the fetters of evil;
they know the ten to be hell, hungry ghosts, animals, hunger, and laziness.
Thus ends the second inspired utterance.
Then the third inspired utterance:
"Compassion, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and likewise vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and nirvana, as well as the mind and the monk— these are the ten."
(21) The Chapter on Compassion:
Compassion is like a mother, bringing about benefit;
pity toward all living beings is like a mother, bringing about benefit.
Relying upon which, persons attain supreme happiness.
A person who seeks compassion here, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
becomes worthy of worship by the virtuous and, after death, goes to heaven and rejoices there.
The inhabitants of heaven always bow down to that very person who is compassionate, ever-active, and devoted to the welfare of all beings. (Dhs 21.3)
Endowed with compassion, he goes to the world of the gods; indeed, the virtuous person who possesses compassion proceeds to the world of the gods.
That man, filled with pity, shines like the moon.
One who desires happiness should cultivate compassion;
for living beings, having relied upon it, become free from sorrow and free from suffering.
Therefore, one who desires happiness should cultivate compassion with diligent effort.
For one whose speech and body and mind are adorned with compassion, there arises an increase in fame through that very compassion.
His worlds become filled with friends and enveloped in glory.
For the wise one moistened by compassion,
for the wise one who is constantly moistened by compassion and possesses dull faculties,
and for one who exerts effort toward right view, nirvāṇa is not far away.
Adorned with compassion, they grace the world of humans as if it were a world of gods;
those who are adorned with compassion are the true gods within the human world.
Those who are poor in compassion are considered poor by the wise.
Mortals of gentle disposition are virtuous; for those mortals who possess a gentle disposition are like gold in their goodness.
They in whose minds compassion ever abides as something inexhaustible are truly noble.
Who are those devoted to the Dharma?
Those beings are constantly and always intent upon the Dharma who have had their hearts fully illuminated by the lamp of compassion.
For those whose minds are found to delight in compassion in all circumstances, the Dharma indeed never ceases, neither by night nor by day.
Compassion is a cool mind;
a mind cooled by compassion delights in the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having enjoyed incomparable happiness, it subsequently proceeds to nirvāṇa.
Compassion is indestructible wealth;
compassion is praised by the sages; compassion is a stainless lake;
compassion destroys all faults; compassion is inexhaustible treasure.
Compassion, moist with pity, is the foremost ornament of virtues and the destroyer of all faults; indeed, it attains the supreme, imperishable wealth.
Since compassion is indeed a wealth joined with the water of sweetness,
the burning heat born of anger does not arise in his heart.
Having boarded the ship of compassion, people cross the ocean of existence;
having boarded the ship of compassion, one who is devoted to joy and fortitude is not tossed about in the ocean of existence by the great force of the waves of the three defects.

Compassion is described as the definition of virtues, the non-dual and supreme ornament even without [external] ornaments, and that which is eternally beloved by the virtuous; thus it is called *kāruṇya*. (Dhs 21.17)
That person in whose heart gentleness is melted like gold shall indeed be swiftly liberated from suffering even at the end of an eon.
For one who is compassionate and whose mind has been made a fit vessel on all sides through gentleness,
blessings grow for him like rice in a field. (Dhs 21.19)
That inexhaustible treasure, deposited within the house of the mind, dispels the poverty of all embodied beings and constitutes the great high resolve of men. (Dhs 21.20)
For one of sharp faculties who is not yet tranquil, though engaged in contemplation and investigation,
suffering does not pursue him as long as he remains heedless regarding sense objects.
Always possessing a mind of loving-kindness and supreme compassion,
those who know the reality of causes and effects have emerged from the snare of suffering.
Those whose minds, free from defects, do not delight in conceptual construction,
being liberated from the fear of defects, go to the unsurpassed state.
One who is endowed with the practice of patience, possesses friends, and is fearless from any quarter,
becomes beloved in this world and later rejoices among the gods.
The jewel of compassion should always be cultivated like a mother and like a father by those people of all the worlds in whom that supreme jewel of compassion ever abides in the mind. (Dhs 21.25)
Compassion alone is the root of happiness,
and compassion is proclaimed to be the supreme root of happiness;
he in whose heart there is no compassion is proclaimed to be a miserable person.

Loving-kindness alone brings happiness; it is the one truth, the supreme Brahman, the one unsurpassed auspiciousness, the one supreme knowledge, the supreme mother, and loving-kindness alone brings happiness. (Dhs 21.27)
Only those who are non-violent are blessed;
those who are non-violent are always blessed. Right view is supremely auspicious;
this is always straight and true, as is the avoidance of all evils.
Therefore, men whose minds are stirred by compassion should cultivate the greatness of compassion,
as well as the stainless practice of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, loving-kindness, and wisdom. (Dhs 21.29)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the Chapter on Compassion.
(22) The Chapter on Giving: A Definition of Pure and Impure Giving.
[That which is] endowed with twelve virtues and free from twelve stains.
That gift is pure; the opposite of that is defiled.
Those who are devoid of generosity are indeed the lowest of men;
for gods as well as humans, wealth is the supreme power.
Devoid of generosity, the lowest of men fall at one's feet.
Stained by greed and envy, subject to the power of their children and wives,
and desiring only food, human beings go to their destruction.
In this world, giving is bestowed for the sake of liberation from the knot of greed, for the destruction of the tree of begging, and for the dissolution of the accumulation of darkness.
The giver goes to the next world; the non-giver experiences suffering. Immediately after that, the giver [reaps the fruit] as well.
Like a guide showing the path, the gift reaches the next world.
Having bathed in the water of generosity, which is stirred by the waves of ethical conduct,
people indeed reach the far shore of suffering— a shore that is vast and stainless with wisdom.
A person who desires their own welfare should kindle three lamps; these three lamps are the destroyers of faults:
generosity, ethical conduct, and likewise wisdom. These are the destroyers of faults.

Plunged into this ocean of suffering, which is discolored by craving and agitated by the waves and sea-monsters of foul-smelling discursive thoughts, these beings are indeed protected by wisdom and virtuous conduct.
Generosity is the medicine for the afflictions;
ethical discipline and wisdom are the three medicines known as the destroyers of the disease of the afflictions.
Generosity, ethical conduct, and likewise wisdom—these always bring about happiness.
The mind, which is treacherous through negligence, crooked in its intentions,
and fickle— by these three factors, beginning with ignorance, human beings are bound by fetters.
Constantly scorched by the fires of the afflictions, when this [world] is thus consumed,
one who has destroyed them through the yoga of knowledge consisting of generosity and so forth attains nirvāṇa.
Those beings whose minds are not integrated with generosity, knowledge, and ethical discipline are constantly suffering; for them, happiness does not exist.
Givers become free from the stain of stinginess;
those who suffer from the shame of not giving are deceived by the defects of their own minds. Therefore, having abandoned [such faults], one should become devoted to generosity. Dhs 22.13.
Endowed with a progressive excellence in generosity and free from the stain of stinginess,
the gods become joyful in mind and devoted to their play.
The fire consisting of hunger and thirst that runs toward the primary [element] has envy as its fruit; this has been declared by those with the wisdom of reality.
Praise of Giving:
He who gives is led to happiness and is born into happiness;
for happiness indeed arises from giving, therefore giving is praised.
Generosity that illuminates both this world and the next follows one who is departing;
and once departed, it is joined by those who are kind and auspicious through the gift of sacred mantras.
The Tathāgatas have declared this state to be non-deceptive;
and because it is non-deceptive, one should always be devoted to giving.
Now, having conquered the enemy of stinginess and having made their minds endowed with virtue, those who bestow gifts cross over the ocean of existence; they cross the ocean of existence. (Dhs 22.19)
Through three types of destruction, a gift that was performed in three ways and acquired by three means—
when thus accompanied by such destruction, its fruit has been seen by the One with Three Eyes.
What is the path that brings happiness?
Generosity should always be practiced at the outset, and ethical conduct should be attained with effort;
craving must be destroyed through wisdom—this is the path that brings happiness.
Craving is impermanent and evil; it brings harm to the world.
Without overcoming it, it is not possible to attain the highest state, the supreme good.
The consequence of non-giving is rebirth in the realms of hungry ghosts;
one should not set one's mind on non-giving, but should always delight in giving.
Due to a lack of generosity, one is tormented by hunger and thirst in the lands of the pretas.
Through generosity, the protection of ethical discipline must always be practiced;
by means of generosity, one becomes a righteous universal monarch (cakravartin).
Relying upon the ground of generosity, the wise protect their ethical discipline.
Even one who possesses virtue and knows the proper time is liberated from suffering through wisdom;
this path leading out of suffering has been praised by the bulls among sages.
Having understood this, the Great Hero should always be devoted to giving;
for even among the gods, those who do not give are considered not to possess happiness.
Now, wherever one may dwell, one becomes happy;
throughout the forest of worldly existence, mortals become partakers of happiness.
For that is indeed the fruit of giving, when it is cultivated by every conscious thought.
Even those born among animals become partakers of happiness;
the wise declare that all such pleasure is born of giving.
Whatever form the hungry ghosts take in the realm of the departed,
they experience a corresponding fruit of the gift they themselves have made.
The condition of one devoid of generosity becomes wretched;
for by that [lack of giving], embodied beings are consumed by hunger and thirst, and their austerity never yields a cooling fruit. (Dhs 22.30)
The heedless person, having previously lived in negligence and not engaging in giving and other virtues, undergoes burning at the time of death;
he is later consumed by his own mind at the moment of passing.
The fruit of giving is that one becomes beloved; through giving, one’s mind also finds satisfaction.
Later, one becomes illustrious—such is the fruit of giving.
Wherever there is always the enjoyment of giving and so forth for the mind,
in that case this is either poverty or it is protected by compassion.
Whatever is always enjoyed by the mind, and whatever is given even to the gurus—be it a beautiful grove seen as such, or perceived as mere grass—is [all subject to change]. (Dhs 22.34)
For sentient beings who are weak and constantly afflicted, giving— endowed with vision and free from conceptual constructs— is beneficial both in this world and in the next.
The fruit of giving belongs to the human realm;
having given gifts in the human realm, they go to a fortunate rebirth.
Gods are not masters of giving, for that [celestial state] is considered a land of fruition.
The majesty of karma is such that the human realm is the field of action, while the abode of the gods is the field of fruition;
all fruit is dependent upon karma, for there can be no fruit without a cause.
Who is equal to the dead? One who is devoid of meditation and study, and bereft of generosity and virtue—
even while adorned with golden bracelets, such a person, though living, is equal to the dead.
For he alone truly lives in this world who follows the Dharma;
one who is deluded regarding the Dharma is always a fool, and though living, is equal to the dead.
But the ignorant person is indeed a fool;
though covered by human skin, that fool remains an animal, whose heart has not been illuminated by the lamp of knowledge. (Dhs 22.40)
By this much alone does one become a true person: by following virtuous conduct (*śīla*).
Every man who has fallen from virtue is unworthy of praise and lacks prowess.
One devoid of generosity has the form of a hungry ghost;
one devoid of generosity is negligent, a doer of evil, and of unsteady senses.
He should not be known as a mortal; this is a departed spirit possessing a physical form.
One devoid of knowledge is as good as dead; one who is bereft of wisdom and virtuous conduct, and abandoned by the jewel of generosity, is called "dead" even while living. (Dhs 22.43)
Who is a god?
A person who possesses generosity, ethical conduct, austerity, meditation, energy, mindfulness, and concentration;
such a person is honored by other men and even by the gods.
A man endowed with virtues is worthy of veneration, while one devoid of virtues is equal to a beast;
he who knows the rules regarding virtue and vice is called a god.
Whose life is fruitful? His life is well-lived whose mind is established in renunciation;
for a life devoid of renunciation is not considered true living. (Dhs 22.46)
Giving is always the bringer of happiness for beings born into the five realms of existence through their own karma;
like a mother and like a father, giving is seen as always bringing happiness.
Those who delight in giving are liberated from the perils of existence;
having established themselves on this ground, a sentient being should delight in giving.
Those who always delight in generosity and ethical discipline are liberated from the perils of existence. (Dhs 22.48)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the Section on Generosity.
(23) The Chapter on Virtue:
Virtue shines like the sun;
virtue is the supreme among riches, just as the sun is the foremost among luminous bodies.
Leaving behind wealth, one departs; virtue remains as if standing before one.
Through ethical discipline one goes to the realm of the Thirty-three, or indeed to the sphere of meditative absorption;
there is no light equal to ethical discipline in this world and in the next.
By this cause, one who desires heaven attains heaven;
therefore, having abandoned misconduct, one should always practice good conduct.
Generosity cultivated through volition and ethical conduct well-guarded lead one to the realm of the gods, endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Only through well-guarded ethical conduct can happiness be attained;
neither mother, nor father, nor wealth, nor beloved ones, nor kinsmen can provide such happiness.
He is seen in such a way that his moral conduct is well-guarded.
The virtuous person attains happiness;
virtue is protection here and in the hereafter, and virtue is the supreme refuge in this world.
The virtuous person always attains happiness upon happiness.
Those people who practice generosity and ethical conduct, who act virtuously,
go to the abode of the gods, fashioned by their own karma.
Virtue is an inexhaustible treasure, and the happiness of virtue is inconceivable;
for those who are superior in virtue always dwell in happiness.
Let the wise person guard their moral conduct, for it is like a vehicle that brings three kinds of happiness:
praise, good reputation, and gain; and after death, one rejoices in heaven.
The virtuous person attains nirvāṇa;
for that man who cultivates virtue alone proceeds happily to the cessation [of suffering] where death is not found. (Dhs 23.10)
In this beginningless saṃsāra, which is shrouded by craving, delusion, and the like, virtuous conduct is ever-present as a light; therefore, let one's conduct be stainless.
Virtue is a wealth that cannot be stolen by kings, thieves, water, or other such forces;
therefore, virtue should always be cultivated, and immorality is to be condemned.
For a person who delights in ethical discipline stands near to nirvāṇa;
the person endowed with virtue is fortunate, and one endowed with virtue is also worthy of service.
Virtue shines like the sun, while misconduct is indeed censurable;
virtue is stainless, free from the wilderness [of afflictions], free from fever, and devoid of longing.
The wise person, constantly nourished by ethical discipline, certainly reaches a long life that leads to the city of Nirvana, as praised by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
Those devoid of ethical discipline are equal to beasts;
yet one protected by ethical discipline has no fear at the time of death. Ethical discipline is auspicious in the beginning and the end, and it brings about all forms of happiness.
A person endowed with virtue is blessed; one who delights in immorality is a beast.
Men devoid of ethical conduct do not reach the shore; they do not discern what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. Therefore, one should practice ethical conduct. (Dhs 23.17)
Those who are covered by the garment of moral conduct are considered truly covered;
but those who are devoid of moral conduct are naked, equal to beasts.
The virtuous person goes to heaven; the virtuous person goes to heaven as if to a garden.
There, the virtuous person regards it as their own kinsmen.
According to valid cognition.
Those people who are pure in conduct and observance of moral discipline, endowed with virtuous qualities,
and who perform good deeds, go to the world of the gods.
The virtues of a virtuous person who always refrains from desiring sensual pleasures increase, nourished by their morality;
his virtues flourish, being sustained by that very morality.
Virtue is the staircase to heaven;
virtue is the most precious and supreme [asset] both in this world and in the next.
Therefore, having abandoned the three qualities of nature, one should always practice virtue alone.
For that virtuous conduct, endowed with purity, is pleasing to the gods; it is a protection, highly cultivated, supremely auspicious, and leads one to the next world.
If one who possesses virtue were to know what kind of fruit such virtue yields, [he would never abandon it].
Taking up a very sharp weapon, one should cut away from oneself that which is like a blade—blameful and devoid of true happiness. (Dhs 23.25)
The fruit of ethical conduct has been demonstrated by the Sugata;
the stainless fruit of ethical conduct has been demonstrated by the Sugata.
It is praised at the beginning, likewise in the middle, and it is praised indeed at the end.
The fruit of ethical discipline is vast, a supreme happiness arising from happiness;
the practice of virtue is the highest bliss, whereas the pursuit of wealth is not like that.
Men may be deprived of wealth, but never of their moral conduct;
because of that, a person grieves, or else he shines forth distinctively.
Therefore, the virtuous, whose conduct is auspicious, go toward that which is praised by the best of sages as leading everywhere; it is like a pleasure grove,
a supreme mine of happiness for them, equal to the world of the gods.
One should practice ethical conduct for the sake of going to heaven;
for one who has well-cultivated ethical conduct, even if it were consumed many times over, the fruit that ripens is heaven. Therefore, one should practice ethical conduct.
Ethical conduct is the staircase to heaven and the source of happiness and liberation;
for a person devoid of ethical conduct does not flourish in happiness anywhere.
One who possesses ethical discipline obtains incalculable happiness through the pure and ever-pervading water of morality;
having bathed therein, people proceed to the world of the gods and to nirvāṇa.
Those who are endowed with divine garlands, ornaments, and celestial pleasures.
He rejoices in the celestial abode; all that is caused by his merit, and his countless pleasures increase at all times.
A person who follows moral conduct obtains everything;
practicing virtue and always truthful, he is honored and remains unconquered.
Ethical conduct, which bestows manifold happiness, should be practiced;
by virtue of goodness, a mortal shines and is always honored by kings.
A mortal shines through goodness; therefore, one should practice ethical conduct. (Dhs 23.35)
One should practice ethical conduct that produces manifold happiness and provides all forms of consolation; one should perform good deeds and avoid evil actions.
Those who practice generosity and morality with their minds intent upon the heavenly realms—
their virtue is defiled, like rice mixed with poison.
Even for various kinds of ethical conduct that have been guarded many times,
the ripening of the result of those virtuous deeds matures among the gods.
Having always bathed in the waters of ethical conduct— which are both serene and abundant— human beings go to the gods and to ultimate happiness.
Those who are always generous and virtuous, self-controlled, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
endowed with wisdom, and whose minds are filled with loving-kindness— they have gone to a state equal to that of the gods.

Those wise ones who have destroyed their faults, who are active in virtuous deeds, adorned with the jewel of ethical discipline, and who possess compassion for all sentient beings, dwell among the worlds of the gods.
Resembling pure gold, with all stains and impurities blown away,
those wise ones are firmly engaged in right action within the worlds of the gods.
Those who possess compassion for all beings, who desire the welfare of all beings,
and who are detached from all evil— such as these have their dwelling in the abode of the gods.
Those who, being discerning, guard their ethical discipline day after day,
for them there is indeed happiness manifoldly day after day.
Mounted upon the steed of ethical discipline, men who contemplate reality travel to the abode of the gods; mounted upon the steed of ethical discipline,
they go many times to that celestial realm filled with delights.
Whatever play there is in the celestial abodes and whatever unsurpassed happiness exists—
that has been declared by the Tathāgatas to be the fruit of the entirety of ethical discipline.
The happiness of the gods arises solely from moral conduct;
that all the deities sport, adorned with divine garlands and ornaments and decorated with celestial garments, is entirely caused by their wholesome deeds.
Those gods who delight in heaven, which is adorned with delightful groves of lotuses and water-lilies and beautified by forests and gardens— all that is the fruit born of merit.
When the stainless gods, adorned with divine jewels, stand as if in space and shine forth, that is the great fruit of virtuous conduct.
That the gods delight in beautiful, variegated, and flowering forests,
as well as upon mountain ridges, is the fruit born of their virtuous conduct.
Just as mortals enter their own homes free from distress,
so do men who practice virtuous conduct proceed to the third heaven.
This is the best and most excellent way to live: the preservation of ethical discipline;
for among all forms of death, the abandonment of ethical discipline is the ultimate death.
Always considering these qualities and even one's own dear self as incomparable,
one should practice virtue and well-guarded conduct, and avoid immorality. (Dhs 23.53)
One who practices virtue, is ever self-controlled, patient, and of noble vision,
ascends as if by a staircase and proceeds to the presence of bliss.
With morality as a raft, the fruit is the crossing over of saṃsāra; indeed, the happiness of morality ripens in the worlds of the gods.
And with morality as a raft, they cross over from saṃsāra.
Those of firm mind who are purified by the water of ethical conduct and have attained self-mastery,
them the gods here worship with flowers made of Jāmbūnada gold.
Those whose minds are not easily led astray and who are constantly adorned with virtuous conduct go to the abode of the gods, where there is infinite happiness.
Men who perform virtuous deeds go from happiness to even greater happiness;
nurtured by their moral conduct, they sport in the abodes of the gods.
Having ascended the staircase of ethical discipline, people go to a happy rebirth;
having ascended the staircase of ethical discipline and being further strengthened by wisdom,
they reach a happy rebirth through wisdom as their ultimate refuge.
This cool happiness has arisen for that virtue which was protected with a perfectly serene mind.
The transformation of virtue is the giver of happiness;
for one who has well-guarded and repeatedly cultivated virtue,
having become happy through that transformation, one attains nirvāṇa.
One protects morality through skillful means and leads morality toward association [with the noble ones];
therefore, morality should always be protected, for its transformation is cooling.
When the time of death has arrived, one who possesses ethical discipline is fearless from any quarter;
there is no protection for me against an evil rebirth, for ethical discipline is indeed the supreme protection.
For one of reprehensible conduct, the result is reprehensible;
he whose conduct is like a film of glass or cloud, being of reprehensible conduct, that man is born as one who is reprehensible. (Dhs 23.64)
One devoid of ethical conduct becomes deluded and does not even go to heaven;
for it is by the root of ethical conduct that embodied beings obtain this happiness in the celestial realms.
Yet, if craving is not extinguished, one later suffers remorse.
Therefore, for one who possesses virtue, virtue alone is always preeminent;
a foolish man devoid of virtue does not ascend to heaven.
This divine happiness, which resembles the fivefold sensual pleasures that is being enjoyed here,
is indeed the great fruit obtained by one whose virtue is pure.
The brilliance of this gold, which rivals Mount Meru,
does not equal even a sixteenth part of the brilliance of the light of one’s own virtuous conduct.
Possessing ever-shining virtues and the luster of gold refined from its ore,
the wise go to the third heaven by means of their own karma.
The fruit of the threefold morality is likewise threefold; for indeed,
the fruit of the three types of morality— whether inferior, middling, or distinguished— is seen to be inferior, middling, and superior respectively.
Ethical conduct free from negligence and augmented by heedfulness is seen to always bestow happiness; this is the established nature of reality.
The splendor of a thousand suns is utterly surpassed by the stainless radiance born of ethical discipline that belongs to embodied beings;
that radiance shall not be equaled even by a thousand suns joined together.
That best of men who guards the seven kinds of delightful ethical conduct enjoys the fruit as taught by the Sugata.
Without the practice of ethical conduct, people do not go to heaven;
by relying upon ethical conduct and being intent on right view,
those who practice austerities go from the world of mortals to the celestial realm without difficulty.
That morality which is cool to the touch and remains cooling even upon its maturation—
yet which the ever-deluded person neglects— he later comes to regret.
Through sevenfold morality, proximity to the gods is attained;
this sevenfold morality is auspicious and a state free from contradiction. A person protected by morality goes into the presence of the gods. (Dhs 23.76)
Just as a bird with firm wings attains a beautiful fruit and wards off the rain with its feathers,
so too a man who is firm in his virtues is fit for the world of the gods.
Merely hearing of that virtue is more delightful than the delightful;
the person who practices it, the doer, obtains the beautiful fruit of that virtue.
Whether a deity or a human, one who takes refuge in the heart with the jewels of generosity, ethical discipline, and austerity attains the supreme state.
Men devoid of virtue are hollow both within and without;
for those who desire the fruits of cyclic existence, the true Dharma is not pleasing.
Those men who possess essence both within and without are firm in reality;
they are practitioners of the Dharma, peaceful, and seekers of the welfare of other beings.
The fragrance of those possessed of virtue is unsurpassed; it is not the scent of the *ketakī*, the *campaka* flower, the *tamālaka*, or the *nāgara* incense.
Just as fragrances are carried by the wind,
so too does the unsurpassed fragrance of those possessed of virtue spread.
Immorality must always be avoided;
therefore, morality should always be practiced by those whose wealth consists of generosity, knowledge, and austerity.
Immorality should always be shunned like poison, a weapon, fire, or a sword. (Dhs 23.83)
Through virtue alone one attains happiness;
thus well-guarded virtue leads men to a favorable rebirth.
Indeed, without virtue no one attains a state of happiness.
One should always practice ethical conduct that is similar to the qualities of the gods;
therefore, regarding ethical conduct as the very quality of the gods, one should always practice it alone.
Indeed, there is no other protection in this world equal to ethical conduct.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, the Chapter on Ethical Conduct.
(24) Chapter on Forbearance: A man is truly adorned by the ornament of patience; one who is adorned with forbearance lives adorned, not by other riches.
Without wealth, one never attains patience in any way whatsoever.
A patient person becomes dear to all embodied beings; he is constantly honored by the gods. Therefore, O scorcher of foes, patience is supreme.
The patient person is honored everywhere;
the patient person is free from all faults of anger.
Such a person is eternally honored by fame, both in this world and in the next.
The wealth of patience is the most supreme;
patience is wealth that increases both ethical conduct and wisdom.
Other forms of wealth are praised by the Teacher, yet they do not lead to benefit in any way whatsoever.
Only the patient person is honored by the virtuous;
he is constantly honored by the virtuous and is honored by fame as well.
Since every patient person is thus esteemed, one should therefore be devoted to forbearance.
Forgiveness alone is the remedy for the poison of anger;
patience is considered the supreme medicine for this poison of anger.
Anger, when not destroyed by patience, arises only for one's own ruin.
For the foolish who are overcome by ignorance and lack of discipline,
patience— which reveals the path— performs a task that is contrary [to their nature].
Only those who possess patience are truly wealthy in this world;
for those who wander through the five realms of existence, destitute of the wealth of Dharma,
it is those whose substance consists of forbearance who are remembered as the wealthy in the world.
O Khula, just as the virtuous have declared, men cross over the impassable wilderness of accumulated darkness by means of patience and firm resolve.
For those who have lost their way in the study of the True Dharma, patience is the supreme guide;
for those terrified by the fear of the miserable realms, patience is said to be no fear at all.
For human beings, patience brings happiness;
it always brings happiness to people and is the destroyer of suffering. It constantly leads to security and produces the quality of trustworthiness. (Dhs 24.11)
The auspicious heroine is indeed blessed, for she is free from all that is inauspicious;
she is the guide to liberation for men and the destroyer of the fear of saṃsāra.
Patience destroys the fires of hell and serves as a staircase to heaven;
it serves as a staircase to heaven and destroys the fires of hell. It protects one from the world of hungry ghosts (preta) and likewise from the animal realm (tiryagyoni).
Patience is a lamp for the nectar of the true path; it is always full of multitudes of virtues and brings auspiciousness to embodied beings.
Therefore, when excellent happiness is attained, one should practice patience with diligent effort.
Like a mother to the entire world, she is a lamp for the nectar of the true path.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Forbearance.
(25) Chapter on Diligence: Undertakings that are consistent with place and action succeed for one who is situated in the proper place and time, and whose conduct is appropriate for hospitality.
The entire fruit belongs to that vigor which is undertaken according to the proper method.
Devoid of logic, instruction, and proper action, and abandoned by righteousness,
multitudes of undertakings fail when they are bereft of vigor.
Those who have initiated vigor attain liberation;
through meditation and the vigor thus initiated, the wise go to liberation.
Like one cast from existence, they proceed to the world of the gods.
Whatever undertakings are begun by men who are energetic and strong, those very tasks become successful and expansive.
Those goals that are accomplished in the supramundane and those that are esteemed in the worlds are achieved through vigor; indeed, those devoid of vigor never attain them at all.
A person of weak vigor, long since devoid of enthusiasm, and abandoned by the true Dharma,
enters the world like the moon defiled by a stain.
Vigor bestows the supreme goal through the Noble Eightfold Path, for one who is not protected by mere knowledge;
vigor with great enthusiasm proceeds to the supreme goal. (Dhs 25.7)
Awakening is attained through vigor;
awakening is attained through vigor, and likewise the great earth [is moved] by one's own vigor.
Arhatship is attained by those possessed of vigor; therefore, there is no state equal to fire.
One should apply the mind to the undertaking of vigor for the sake of attaining the highest state;

therefore, considering the gods as virtues, the person of vigor, with senses restrained, should direct the mind toward the undertaking of vigor, for there is nothing that vigor cannot accomplish. (Dhs 25.9)
The person who seeks vigor, possesses mindfulness, and is devoted to wisdom,
goes to the unsurpassed state that is free from old age and death.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Diligence.
(26) The Chapter on Meditation: Who is at ease?
One whose mind is forever unattached and who constantly dwells in meditation.
For one whose mind is ever pure and who delights in one-pointed concentration.
For one whose mind is one-pointed, faults are not obstructive;
liberated from the fear of faults, such a person is called "established in well-being."
A mind that delights in one-pointedness pursues solitude;
liberated from all discursive thought, it is called "established in itself."
He describes one-pointedness of mind:
For one whose mind is constant, peaceful, and always delights in Nirvāṇa,
there are no defects born of the senses that serve as causes for rebirth.
Whatever happiness is produced by meditation and whatever [happiness] is born of concentration—
all that mind of the embodied being becomes one-pointed in intellect.

The ascetic enjoys supramundane happiness; whatever joy arises in the heart of an ascetic who finds delight in solitude is a bliss difficult to comprehend, and is not considered worldly pleasure. (Dhs 26.6)
What kind of mind attains peace?
A mind that delights in one-pointedness and is indeed formed by purity, being completely liberated from the web of defects, attains peace. (Dhs 26.7)
With a mind constantly and single-pointedly focused, and with the five sense faculties restrained, the wise person destroys the fire of craving with the water of knowledge; indeed,
he extinguishes that which has been greatly increased by the fire of craving with the water of knowledge.
For him who is liberated from craving, purified, and seeking happiness,
the state that is indeed inexhaustible and imperishable stands before him.
The path leading to the city of Nirvana is crooked with discursive thoughts; wherever the mind may arise,
it should be held steady by means of that concentration which is joined to a single object of focus.
Therefore, this is the supreme path leading to the city of Nirvana.
This is the supreme fruit of restraining the mind: having devoured the mind, one may destroy the host of enemies;
for by thoroughly subduing this mind, [one achieves victory].
He knows through the firm states born of meditative concentration.
The bliss born of meditation is incomparable;
those excellent men established therein—possessing faith and being wise—go to the supreme state, free from sorrow and with all taints destroyed. (Dhs 26.12)
For the wise man who is free from poison, contented, and without malice, the bliss born of meditation shines forth; how could there be any other comparison for it?

The supreme state is attained through meditations; this is the essence for wise yogins who have reached the further shore. Having heard this regarding the mind, they proceed to the immutable state. (Dhs 26.14)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, the Section on Meditation.
(27) The Chapter on Wisdom:
Wisdom is like a mother, acting for one's benefit;
wisdom that follows the Dharma is augmented by vigor.
Endowed with the power of concentration, she is like a mother, acting for the benefit [of all beings].

Wisdom protects one from the five states of existence; for it truly rescues all persons from the five states of existence. Neither mother nor father follows one who departs for those realms. (Dhs 27.2)
Having ascended the peak of wisdom, which is adorned by the mountain caves of ethical discipline,
one who is decorated with knowledge beholds all these defects of existence.
One crosses the ocean of existence by means of concentration when the senses find that state beyond the objects of the senses;
then, through concentration, one shall cross the sea of existence by means of knowledge.
Through generosity, ethical conduct, austerity, and meditation, knowledge alone is said to be supreme;
for when there is knowledge leading to liberation, both knowledge and ethical conduct bring about happiness.
Wisdom is the eighth path taught by the Tathāgata; it is seen as the supreme among all visions and is declared to be perfectly stainless.
Among all paths, the eighth path is proclaimed by the Tathāgatas to be auspicious.
The power of wisdom is the most supreme of all;
among the four truths, two are proclaimed as foremost.
Indeed, the power of wisdom is always seen here as the highest for the foolish.
The path of birth must be severed by the weapon of knowledge; like an unassailable creeper, it must be cut by the sharp weapon of knowledge.
The multitudes of faults must be destroyed, and the path of birth must be severed.
There is no kinsman higher than knowledge;
knowledge is the supreme nectar and the highest treasury of all that is auspicious.
There is no kinsman greater than knowledge, and there is no wealth more excellent than knowledge.
One should serve wisdom endowed with knowledge and virtue; one should always serve the virtuous who are aged, free from passion, devoid of longing, and who point out the path of reality.
