One should tear apart the afflictions and other obstacles with the weapon of wisdom,
using the sharp vajra of wisdom through the power of great awakening; mounted upon the chariot of Mahāyoga, one should utterly shatter the afflictions and the rest.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on Wisdom.
(28) The Chapter on Nirvana:
The path to nirvana is indeed the destruction of the afflictions;
the wise declare that beyond the destruction of the afflictions lies supreme bliss.
This is the path leading to Nirvana, as taught by those who perceive reality.
The Tathāgatas describe that eternal state as the one they delight in,
wherein there is neither birth nor death, and where the arising of suffering does not exist.
For one who is liberated, vigilant, peaceful, dwelling in the forest,
free from greed, and heroic, there are the manifestations of nirvāṇa.
For one who is heedful regarding sense objects, who has abandoned both friend and foe, and who is free from the craving for existence, nirvāṇa is attained before long;
for one who is heedful regarding sense objects, nirvāṇa is not far off.

One who performs virtuous deeds, who is intent on wholesome actions, who dwells in loving-kindness and compassion, and who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, attains nirvāṇa; for such a person, nirvāṇa is not far off.
One who is free from laziness quickly attains nirvāṇa; for one who knows the method for the destruction of the afflictions, even though they possess selflessness,
and because they are liberated from laziness, nirvāṇa is not far off.
For one whose senses are subdued, who is peaceful, who knows the method of the Four Noble Truths, and who practices for the destruction of the three defects, Nirvana is very near;
for one whose senses are subdued and who is peaceful, Nirvana is not far away.
The sage who is liberated from the snares of pleasure and pain is called one who has gone to the further shore;
he whose mind is not struck by the snares consisting of pleasure and pain is free from faults and fear, and is called a sage who has gone to the further shore.
The person who seeks what is auspicious, who fears the lower realms, and who abandons the power of negligence, attains nirvāṇa;
performing good deeds and seeking the auspicious, he attains nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on Nirvāṇa.
(29) The Chapter on the Path:
The lay follower of the fourfold Noble Ones goes to the further shore; those four truths are auspicious.
Having clearly perceived that these [states] are well-cultivated,
the wise and well-reflecting one is liberated from the fears of birth and old age, and, being tranquil, reaches the further shore.

One who is attached to sensual pleasures and bound by the enjoyments of existence becomes devoid of reflection; he whose intellect is distracted, being attached to sensual pleasures and bound by the enjoyments of existence,
is fettered by bonds consisting of desire.
One is not liberated from the fears of birth and old age.
He who perceives happiness within the ocean of existence, yet contemplates this vast suffering at its end,
does not feel weariness toward the oceans of existence.
Struck by the arrows of desire, that fool indeed goes to a miserable state even in hell.
Having abandoned internal security and happiness,
why indeed do fools delight in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures?
They do not realize that the intense fear of death, blazing like a fire, is approaching.
What has been said by those who show the path of reality?
"This self is impermanent, suffering, empty, and devoid of an agent;
such is saṃsāra, as declared by the Buddhas, the revealers of the path of reality. (Dhs 29.5)
Therefore, all this knowledge of reality should be understood in brief:
that which is liberated from both the knower and the known; a third state is not perceived.
Who is the knower of the method of reality?
It is he who knows the method of reaching the further shore, who understands the reality of the sixteen aspects,
who indeed knows the method of the upward movement, and who is skilled in the reality of patience.
Only one who knows reality enters into the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he who is the sole knower of the Dharma in the world, the knower of reality immediately following [the path].
In whatever manner he should enter into that *dharmatā*:
It does not waver.
One who is free from the two means and repeatedly destroys what has been lost—
the hero whose course of evil is destroyed— is called a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
The streams of unwholesome states that lead toward evil are withered;
they are scorched by the fire of liberation, and thus one becomes a stream-enterer.
That which is born of pliancy is said to have great fruit; it brings liberation from saṃsāra.
The happiness of the exhaustion of craving is seen as truly productive of bliss.
Who is always happy? One whom craving does not bind and who is not mocked by discursive thoughts;
having reached the further shore of existence, such a person is happy at all times.
The fourfold noble path arises from mutual fruition;
arising from mutual fruition, it proceeds everywhere.
That very cause should be known as the fourfold noble path.
A person who has realized the Noble Truths certainly exists;
for the world, resounding with attachment to sense objects, wanders like a wheel.
What is the supreme path?
That path is the best teacher, which is the auspicious path that has been taught;
by means of that path, the ancients [attained] the eternal.
The wise have departed.
Only one who has gone for refuge to the Three Jewels lives happily; his life is well-lived, he whose mind is established in wisdom.
Indeed, a life devoid of wisdom cannot be called a life at all.
The life of one whose mind is established in the Dharma is truly lived;
for a life devoid of the Dharma cannot be considered true life.
A life well-lived would be that of one whose mind is established in the Saṅgha;
for a life devoid of the Saṅgha cannot truly be called a life.
For whom is life well-lived? Life would be well-lived for one whose mind is established in truth;
for a life devoid of truth cannot truly be called life. (Dhs 29.19)
The life of one whose mind is established on the Path is truly lived;
for a life devoid of the Path cannot be considered true living.
He whose mind is constantly fixed on proceeding toward Nirvana is liberated from defects alone; he is not a god who sports for his own pleasure.
What kind of play brings forth happiness?
That play which pervades existence for one whose mind is always one-pointed—that is the play that brings forth happiness; it is not a play that produces passion.
By what path is the auspicious state attained?
Just as one who is self-controlled finds the truths such as happiness here, so too does the Supreme Person reach the secure and auspicious state. (Dhs 29.23)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Path.
(30) The Chapter on Monks:
A monk is a mirror who shows the way to the world;
he who does not harm living beings, who knows his friends, is ever-inexhaustible.
The world regards him as one who looks upon all beings as its own father.
The wise one, constantly abstaining from taking what is not given, having conquered the senses,
with his bodily actions fully stilled,
has crossed over the transition into rebirth.
She is not found even in a painting, nor is she beheld by the eye;
one whose desire is destroyed, who has seen the truth, and is liberated—such a person is said to be like her.
Regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, free from sorrow, and composed in mind— one who is not touched by the serpents of the afflictions shall attain certain happiness.
Who is the monk who exists?
He for whom gain and loss are the same as profit and loss, and who is likewise equanimous toward pleasure and pain—he indeed is called a monk. (Dhs 30.5)
One who has abandoned both friend and foe, whose mind is equanimous, who has conquered the senses,
and who does not fear sense objects— such a person should be known as a true ascetic.
One who hates sense objects attains nirvāṇa;
for the wise person, free from distress, hates sense objects because of their inherent instability.
For him, nirvāṇa—as taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One—is not far off.
Knowing the truth of arising and passing away, possessing right view and free from greed,
he departs from saṃsāra like the Himavat mountain, having become one whose causes for bondage are extinguished.
For one who consumes food and clothing with equal craving, grass and sandalwood are indeed the same;
he is not at all afflicted by the craving for silk garments.
Content with gain and honor, and content even with a bed of grass—
he who views gain and honor as he would fire, he truly sees.
The monastic qualities taught by the Buddha are carried by one who is not swept away by sense objects, nor is he carried off by the river of grass;
knowing the reality of the fruit of his own actions, such a person is a monk as taught by the Buddha.
He who does not grieve for the past, who has indeed lost all longing through his intellect,
and who is engaged in present activity— his intellect is not defiled.
He whose mind is set upon nirvāṇa and remains constantly fixed on the Dharma does not wander in saṃsāra, being fully enveloped by pure qualities.
For one whose mind is not turbid by the fire-like power of knowledge,
and for whom sense objects are like wood, no suffering exists.
The sage who has his senses under control, who follows the mastery of his senses, and who is not carried away by the objects of the senses— he is like a touchstone for men.
That sage whose mind is well-increased by virtue, who is patient and pleasant to behold, gladdens the hearts of men like the moon.
A monk who delights in the dawn-red [robes], who is not attached to the upper stories of mansions,
and who is content with a rag from a dust heap, should be devoted to alms-gathering.
Peaceful, self-controlled, and wise— meaning one who knows the reality of pleasure and pain—
he travels the supreme path, having gone upon which he does not grieve.
With a straight mind, constantly devoted to meditation,
and free from both major and minor defilements,
that yogi stands upon the path of truth.
He who overcomes all sensory afflictions, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings,
who is peaceful, whose senses are subdued, and who is established in his own self— such a person is a true mendicant.
Mounted upon the chariot of the six sense-faculties, warding off the enemy of passion,
he who is steadfast in wisdom and active in practice attains the state of peace.
Dwelling in the forest, contented, living on the ground, and concentrated in mind,
one shakes off evil states just as the wind disperses clouds from the sky.
Whether his bodily actions are auspicious or he is devoted to virtuous conduct,
one who perceives reality and is skilled in action destroys the means of Māra.
A compassionate monk stands on the path to nirvāṇa; when passion has ceased, his virtuous mind, free from attachment, is not afflicted.
Abounding in loving-kindness and compassion, the monk remains established in the way of deliverance.
He for whom forms and other sense objects are not accepted as causes of bondage attains supreme peace, having gone where one no longer grieves.
One who knows the reality of causes and conditions, who has reached certainty regarding subtle matters,
and who delights in the stream of liberation, is never stained by craving.
He who does not take up unwholesome karma and is always devoted to wholesome karma—
such a one becomes a yogi whose course is as pure as the rays of the moon.
Burning away evil states of being like fire consuming dry fuel, he shines resplendent in the three worlds, freed from sin and devoid of suffering.
But he whose mind is set on liberation and not at all on cyclic existence,
he is not bound in saṃsāra, like a bird released in the sky.
One who knows the reality of the arising of sensation, who has reached certainty regarding the fruit of sensation—he should be known as liberated; he is a knower of reality and a speaker of truth.
Nevertheless, these experiences of pleasure and pain do not defile him with the pleasant or the unpleasant;
he who perceives cyclic existence as ablaze is considered a yogi by the wise.
What kind of person is a bhikṣu?
One who is always of undeluded mind and constantly devoted to the Dharma, delighting in the conduct of a bhikṣu— such a one is a bhikṣu.
There is no satiety in beholding the virtuous; one finds delight in seeing them.
Such a person becomes a monk who has emerged from the defilements of the household life.
Not beholding dance or song, and looking instead upon the truth,
such a monk is well-guarded even in cremation grounds.
Taking only one supreme morsel of food on a day and desiring nothing else,
such a monk is content with filling only one-third of his stomach.
He who rejects the finest garments and delights in rag-robes from dust heaps,
and whose conduct is like that of one liberated— such a person is a true monk.
He who undertakes actions without being devoid of hope, and who neither suppresses nor desists from those actions— such a one is a true monk.
Freed from the extremes of bodily existence, devoid of the darkness of delusion,
and unstained by unwholesome qualities— one such as this is a true bhikṣu.
Not brought by any underlying tendencies, free from all underlying tendencies,
and liberated from all underlying tendencies— such is the monk.
Standing before the city of Nirvāṇa by means of the noble eightfold path—this indeed is the true nature of all goals; such a one is a bhikṣu.
With senses stilled, firm in intellect, and free from the ripening of desire,
such a monk has a mind established in one-pointed concentration.
A monk who knows the transition between the stages, who demonstrates the reality of the stages,
and who knows what is higher and lower regarding the stages— such a one is a true monk.
Such a monk comes to know all phenomena— both those that arise and those that do not— as they truly occur through causes and conditions, in accordance with the proper method.
A celibate student who knows the proper seasons, who is free from sloth and torpor, who is alert and diligent on the ground— such a one becomes a true monk.
One who abides in tranquility and insight, who delights in the four dhyānas,
and who finds joy in the *ālaya*— such a one is a true monk.
Like the shadow that always follows a bird in the sky,
such is the monk who lives in accordance with the true Dharma.

A monk who is such as this— one who destroys the primary and secondary afflictions, who views all things with equanimity, who is endowed with virtue, and who knows the method for inhalation and exhalation— is truly a bhikṣu.
One who knows the sequence of the rules, who is a knower of yoga, a seer of reality,
and who knows the method for crossing from this shore to the further shore— such a one is a true monk.
He who does not rejoice in delights and does not fear in the face of dangers, being liberated from joy, fear, and agitation— such a one is a true mendicant.
One who knows the reality of birth and death, who is honored by gods and asuras,
and who understands the higher and lower states of beings— such a person becomes a true monk.
Rejoicing in nothing more than his outer robe, he does not delight in accumulations;
such is the monk who is of few desires and lives the holy life.
He who always strives for meditation at the foot of a solitary tree,
detached from gain and honor— such a one is a true monk.
One who possesses equanimity and compassion, whose passion is free from the defects that obstruct liberation, and who has utterly consumed all traces of defilement— such a person is a true monk.
Nor for the sake of seeing monks who are weak in vigor and indolent;
such is the monk who is not devoted to other practices.
A monk who delights in indolence does not deserve what is wholesome; indeed,
such a monk who enjoys beds and seats has been described by the Buddha as one who,
delighting in indolence, does not deserve what is wholesome.
For laziness is indeed the root-ripening of the afflictions;
for one who possesses it, most terrible suffering proceeds within saṃsāra.
For one who possesses indolence, the Dharma does not exist;
he is called a "monk" (bhikṣu) by virtue of his robes alone. (Dhs 30.57)
Such a person is not a bhikṣu;
he who finds no delight in teaching nor protects [himself] quickly through meditation, becomes a bhikṣu merely by outward appearance alone. (Dhs 30.58)
There is no such monk who delights in monasteries but does not delight in the sphere of the Dharma, whose mind is greedy for women and liquor.
He whose mind is constantly inclined toward various evil deeds— such a monk has been described by the Buddhas as one who does not enjoy his own proper domain.
It is better to consume the venom of a poisonous serpent or even molten copper than to eat the sinful food consumed by those of utterly depraved character.
For he who is not worthy of alms is not fit for alms;
he whose defilements have been gathered together like snakes dwelling in their holes.
That monk should subsist on alms-food and not be intent on looking at women;
he should rather make himself a hostage for the injury inflicted by the axe [of worldly existence].
How is that monk to be recognized as one who defiles the Jewel of the Saṅgha? He is a monk whose nature is defined by evil qualities—
he for whom gain and honor are desired, and for whom sensual objects are esteemed.
He is neither a mendicant nor a householder; he is one who longs for the sight of women, who eats the food provided by royal servants, and is likewise a drunkard and prone to anger.
Indeed, a monk who relies on worldly expedients and dwells at the gates of kings always deceives his donors with his mind;
he is as agitated among householders as forest-dwelling elephants are among men.

Therefore, those who have become peaceful and have taken refuge in the Jewel abandon their sons and wives; yet, driven by envy, they gather together and nourish only those very people [who remain attached].
Having abandoned the faults and [cultivated] the greatness of the qualities of a monk, that monk who knows the reality of vision,
who understands the reality of the aggregates such as form, always strives for liberation. (Dhs 30.68)
Delighting in the awakening to the Dharma and dwelling in the delight of meditative absorption,
one shall attain the imperishable state through the realization of the true nature of reality.
One who constantly delights in loving-kindness, is ever-diligent in the sphere of the Dharma,
and knows the reality of the characteristics of reality— such a one is a true monk.
But he whose mind is properly directed and is not struck down by desire and anger—he should be known as a monk; one who is otherwise is the opposite.
Firm toward all beings, peaceful, and free from all attachments,
liberated from all bonds— one who knows reality becomes a true monk.
He whose consciousness is not struck by the objects of action, who is stainless like gold, and who is contented—he is called a monk. (Dhs 30.73)
He whose mind incurs no stain regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant, who knows the method for subduing mental constructions, and who is free from all evil— [he is liberated].
One whose conduct is untainted by others, who is virtuous, has conquered the senses,
possesses undiminished strength, and is wise— such a person is a true monk.
He whose mind is always delighted in the study of the scriptures and in the understanding of their meaning,
and who is not attached to food and drink— that monk is one whose mind is peaceful.
One whose mind finds delight dwelling in forests and wildernesses, or in cemeteries upon a bed of grass— that one is a true bhikṣu.
A monk who knows the true nature of the actions of the defilements, who understands their results through logical deduction,
and who knows the reality of causes and conditions, shall be free from all impurity.

The monk who has destroyed the wilderness of sin, who has eliminated faults, conquered his senses, understands the process of rebirth, and whose mind is peaceful and mindful—[he is liberated]. (Dhs 30.79)
He who does not exalt himself when his heart is gladdened, nor becomes angry at being censured,
and who possesses a depth equal to the ocean— he is called a monk endowed with yoga.
One who is independent, firm-minded, a speaker of subtle truths, free from greed, one who speaks of desirelessness, equanimous, and skillful— that monk is said to be peaceful.
The knower of reality who [abandons] the causes leading to the desire realm, and likewise those in the form realm and the formless realms,
is called a monk by the Teacher.
He who is never attached to worldly talk regarding the destruction of enemies and faults,
and for whom sense objects are like poison— he is declared a monk by the wise.
He whose mind is always pure regarding sensual desires—
that monk, with a liberated mind, is freed from the bonds of saṃsāra.
One who is fit for the practice of meditation and study, from whom laziness is far removed,
and who acts for the benefit of sentient beings, is called a forest-dwelling monk (āraṇyaka).
He whose intellect consists of answering questions with inspired eloquence and who has conquered his senses—such a person should be known as Dharma; the opposite is equal to straw.

What kind of monk is praised in the Buddha’s teaching? He who, possessing physical and mental vigor, is never weary; he should be known as one who performs all duties and is devoted to the Saṅgha. (Dhs 30.87)
He who acts neither for the sake of others, nor for the sake of greed, nor for the sake of fame,
but whose mind is intent on the affairs of the Saṅgha, is liberated from all bonds.
He whose mind is not set on heaven, nor on gain or fame,
but performs every action for the sake of Nirvana— he is called a monk who has entered the stream.
Constantly abstaining from evil deeds, always delighting in virtuous practices, and avoiding association with evil friends— such a one shall be a monk in the teaching of the Buddha.
For one whose mind is cultivated in loving-kindness, who is skillful and upright in heart,
and who delights in the precepts of training, nirvāṇa is not far away.
For one whose nature is subject to old age and death, who turns away from cyclic existence,
and who is not heedless even in meditative absorption, nirvāṇa is not far off.
For one who knows the method of impermanence, who acts with emptiness as their guide,
and who knows the method for the excellence of meditation, nirvāṇa is not far off.
This monk is a wise man, yet he is a foremost thief;
unrestrained within, he sheds the essence of the inner apartments while remaining concealed by his outer robe.
A monk who is empty of the Dharma and Vinaya will surely partake in suffering; just as a heap made of effort is entirely pithless and weak,
so too does one who merely calls himself a monk wander about empty and false.
That hell-bound person of immoral conduct, excluded from the Jewel of the Saṅgha,
is led to hell after the dissolution of the body, deceived by his own mind.
Deceived from the Dharma and Vinaya, he goes there by his own karma;
stained and bound by darkness, he will become a partaker of suffering.
One who is unclothed, O Śubhadhama, naked, and loathed by the virtuous,
is led to a terrible hell, just like one who has been cast out from the Dharma.
An accumulation of what is unwholesome is an unobstructed gateway to suffering;
it is called the intense bondage of saṃsāra, namely, immorality.
He who is consumed by non-restraint is utterly consumed by fire;
for him whose restraint is exhausted, downfall is certain.
Even a wicked monk goes to hell;
yet, by remaining mentally restrained and conducting himself according to proper rules, he acts as one who observes the vows.
However, by embarking upon deluded conduct, he prepares himself for hell.
The unwholesome increases for him day and night in every way,
he whose jewel of virtuous conduct has been obstructed by immorality.
For one who is devoid of Dharma, empty, and enveloped by darkness, there exists non-restraint; such a person is not fit for purity.
The noose consisting of non-restraint is defiled and shunned by the virtuous;
it drags down those of immoral conduct, the most wicked who are devoid of ethical discipline.
Association with non-restraint, immoral conduct, and evil deeds—
these are messengers of hell and servants of sensual desires.
For one who is unrestrained, fickle,
and especially devoted to evil deeds, hell is not far off.
Do these fools not understand that the fruit of actions is commensurate with the action?
They are utterly deluded by their wicked minds and their foolishness.
Day by day increase the rivers of evil, difficult to approach,
turbulent with garlands of waves of suffering, and carrying away the most sinful people.
Neither birth nor mental composure is easy for those men who lack moral conduct or who are devoid of pure virtues.
Dharma is the exceedingly lofty and auspicious path;
that exceedingly lofty and auspicious path is called "Dharma.
Having attained it, a human being swiftly proceeds to the imperishable state.
Therefore, those who are capable of establishing themselves free from reproach and who find happiness in the constant service of their vows—for them no suffering exists;
for this [suffering] is supreme when it arises from immorality, which defiles human beings. (Dhs 30.111)
Those who have fallen away from the stages of training are destined for hell;
knowing this, a person undertakes every form of restraint.
A monk who possesses virtuous qualities attains nirvāṇa before long;
for restraint is indeed a bridge across the entire ocean of existence,
belonging to one whose livelihood is pure, who is purified, and whose conduct is tranquil.
For one who meditates, who is fully liberated, who bears the burden, who is heedful, and who dwells in cemeteries and forests, nirvāṇa is not far away.
For one who constantly sleeps upon the ground, nirvāṇa is not far off;
[he experiences] a single, worn-out shoulder-droop while reclining on a bed of dust.
Contentment with fruits and roots is the happiness of one born of awakening;
for one liberated from sensual desires, contentment is indeed superior to anything else.
For the Protector whose mind is completely liberated and who is free from deceit and impurity, nirvāṇa is not far off, nor is even a speck of dust.
For one whose mind is equal to space, nirvāṇa is not far off;
the course of worldly existence should be understood as being composed of many bound states.
The nose is the gateway to the practice of celibacy that leads to the state of Nirvana and the end of suffering;
yet it is constantly indulged by common people who are devoid of moral discipline.
That [craving] must be constantly abandoned by meditators who perceive reality;
it is the root of weakness and the destroyer of mental attention.
It is the destroyer of celibacy, the revealer of hell,
the bringer of downfall from the path to heaven, and the drier up of the ocean of suffering.
She is the messenger of the realm of hungry ghosts, one who causes falling into the animal womb;
by name she is Saṅgaṇikā, the service that is the mother of bondage in saṃsāra.
Indeed, those incapable of meditation and study must always be shunned by monks;
for one who is devoid of meditation and study is always delighting in signs.
The duty of another is fraught with fear;
it is abandoned by the virtuous for the sake of proceeding without sin.
He who, having forsaken his own duty, takes delight in the duties of others [is lost].
One who has fallen away from the two-fold Dharma is destined for ruin,
like one who abandons his own home and dwells in the houses of others' courtesans.
O wise one, he who has become full of doubt and proud of his own learning merely due to the desire of worldly people always incurs insignificance and quickly goes to his destruction.
Having abandoned his own duty, he conducts himself according to the duties of others;
the intention of one who lives off the emblems of another is fixed upon unrighteousness.
This preta, smeared with the knowledge of grass, is cooked among the sinful;
having established himself in a state that is the end of his reputation, he persists in evil deeds.
He is not called a monk here;
he is seen as perpetually fallen from the end of the teaching. Free from desire for sensual activities and devoid of delight, he is one who has truly gone forth.
A monk who has initiated vigor, is contented, and is meditative is so described here.
One who is attached to sensual pleasures, constantly engaged in eating and recreation, and though clothed in saffron robes, is intoxicated by worldly desires— he is not called a monk here.
He who interprets omens,
who calculates the movements of the stars,
and who is intent on royal service— even if diligent therein— is not called a monk here.
By performing medical treatments, as well as composing scriptures and engaging in a confused daily routine, a mendicant perishes.
A monk who hates meditation and study, who delights in social company,
and who pursues greed, honor, and gain, goes to ruin.
The monk who is attached to gold and minerals, who delights in many friends, and who covets gains from others, falls away from the Teaching.
One who is free from attachment to asceticism, does not serve a multitude of sinful acts,
and is content with even a little flour and water— that mendicant is considered "harsh."
Who is the pure monk?
He who abandons all sense-objects that have come his way, which are like a blazing fire;
with faults completely purified, he is called here a pure monk, like a gem.
One whose self is purified internally and externally, adorned with knowledge and other virtues,
and who possesses ritual action through the garment of ethical discipline and faith, is called a bhikṣu.
He who has transcended the nature of greed, who stands as immovable as Mount Meru,
who is beloved by the whole world, peaceful, and has reached the further shore— he is called a bhikṣu.
Dwelling for three nights anywhere, reclining on a seat of kusha grass,
and frequenting mountain caves— such a one is called a liberated monk.
One who fears evil, avoids contact with the world, is restrained and well-restrained,
who cultivates wisdom, is steadfast and peaceful, and dwells alone— such a one is called a monk.
One who is steadfast, speaks kindly, avoids evil companions,
is incapable of worldly activities, and is liberated is here called a monk.
Service to a king and service to speech characterized by base passions are censurable for a mendicant dwelling in the forest;
such service to speech of base passion is a livelihood like that of a thief who preys upon death.
For a monk who serves a king is not one to be served even by the gods;
he is a servant of great impurity, for he is mixed with the intoxication of violence.
Service to a king does not befit a monk who is stainless, free from affliction, and devoid of desire;
for one who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, service to a king is not fitting.
A monk dwelling in forests, wildernesses, and cremation grounds, by ponds, on mountain slopes, or in remote regions beyond the village, shines with splendor.
A monk who dwells in forests, jungles, or cremation grounds, yet does not serve the king,
is devoid of meditation and study, and subsists on solid food,
should be known as no monk at all— his mind being equal to that of a *piśāca*.
For the wise proclaim that stainless happiness arises from meditative absorption;
there is no other happiness whatsoever in the world like that happiness.
Having abandoned that supreme bliss of meditative concentration, the lowest of men— the fool who delights in sensory flavors— is ruined by his own delusion.
For one who is perpetually distracted by sense objects and whose mind is constantly fixed upon them,
unwholesome states increase, which lead to degradation in the next world.
A monk who knows himself attains nirvāṇa; likewise, one who is humble in his vehicle and inquires of his guru,
and a monk who possesses diligent energy, attains nirvāṇa.
A monk who knows himself and is free from pride speaks only as much as he has heard; such a one is a knower of reality.
He who is free from honor and dishonor, who is discerning regarding what is the path and what is not the path,
and who knows the method for the welfare of himself and others— that monk is said to be contented.
Whence can there be peace for the proud?
For one who is arrogant, cruel-minded, fickle, and of little intelligence—
who is devoted to gain and honor— whence will peace ever arise?
For one who is endowed with pure conduct, who dwells within the sphere of wisdom,
and who fears the defects of cyclic existence, the life of renunciation is considered fruitful.
He whose intellect does not abandon [the notions of] intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature,
nor [the notions of] action and its non-ripening, and likewise the path and the non-path— [he is one who has transcended them].
A monk who is attached to dwelling finds no happiness;
for one devoid of right conduct, who is indifferent to both pleasure and pain, a monk attached to dwelling is viewed by others as a mere child. (Dhs 30.156)
Like a blade of grass, he becomes light and falls away from his own true purpose;
the monk who dwells in a forest that has been despoiled loses his very foundation.
The mind does not engage at all in the duties of meditation and study;
a monk who is intent on gathering crowds is ruined by his dwelling.
The life of one whose mind is distracted by accumulation wastes away;
it consumes his own vital essence, yet he does not attain true life.

Who goes to a miserable rebirth? It is the monk who, though he has done nothing that would cause him to experience happiness elsewhere, is ruined by his dwelling and intent upon gathering crowds of people.
He constantly accumulates evils; by means of those, he goes to a miserable rebirth.
The greatness of the dharma of asceticism is considered fruitful for an embodied being who is free from desire and devoid of hope,
and who is liberated from all attachments.
For those who constantly dwell in meditation among the trees in mountain caves,
auspicious knowledge that is free from immoral conduct becomes serene.
Whose life is fruitful? That mendicant who is liberated from all attachments and is not deceived by sense objects— he should be known as fruitless, like a fire with dry fuel.
Praise for a monk who delights in nirvāṇa:
For that monk who, being pure in soul, delights in nirvāṇa out of fear of the ocean of worldly existence, he is a true monk; never by mere residence [in robes] alone. (Dhs 30.164)
Craving alone is the cause of misfortune;
those who are subject to greed and delusion are always subject to craving.
For those bound by the fetters of craving, there is neither this world nor the next.
One who knows the Dharma does not fall into an evil rebirth,
for his mind is always unattached to false actions; one who knows the Dharma and is impartial does not go to an evil rebirth.
Who is called a sage?
He whose mind is never stained by the mire of faults,
who dwells delighting in solitude, and who is free from longing— he is called a sage.
One who is liberated, whose conduct is stainless, from whom impurities and defilements have turned away,
and who is freed from all sense objects— he is called a forest-dwelling sage.
One who does not fall into despondency due to worldly conditions in any way,
whose wisdom remains equanimous toward pleasure and pain, and who is stainless, is called a sage.
Contentment is the supreme dharma; one who is constantly free from desire,
free from affliction, living with austerity, and pure is here called a sage.
One who does not form attachments wherever he goes,
who wanders alone with firm resolve and is dedicated to practice, is called a sage.
One who knows the true nature of the fruits of all actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
and who has abandoned both the auspicious and the inauspicious, is called a sage in this world.
One who is diligent in destroying faults and whose course is always directed toward desire is known as a sage;
one who knows the truth of arising and passing away is called a wise muni.
One who knows the proper place and time, the foremost among those who teach non-duality, who has conquered the senses,
and who is terrified of the fear of cyclic existence— such a person is called a peaceful sage.
Which monk attains nirvāṇa?
The monk who has gone to dwell alone, whose five sense faculties are withdrawn,
and who knows the reality of the characteristics of the body, attains nirvāṇa.
The energetic monk, truthful in speech and ever free from faults,
attains nirvāṇa as one reaches a garden for recreation.
Become one whose nature is virtuous;
when the afflictions are burnt away, we too are burnt, just as a forest is consumed by fire.
Those who are devoted to virtuous qualities are not stained by the enjoyment of sensual desires.
People who are constantly eager for gain and always devoted to their own kin become perpetual deceivers through illusion.
Those fools who are deceived by illusion [are far] from the path of the Dharma.
The mind should be directed toward virtuous action; therein, in the delightful forests, the mind finds delight.
Those who are free from passion find joy there, but not those who seek after sensual desires.
But he who delights in talk, who is addicted to the thirst for sense objects,
will not go to the peaceful city, nor does he perceive death.
Become a proponent of non-duality,
you whose mind is eternally and utterly tranquil, who is constantly devoted to meditation,
who is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, and whose sphere of experience is forever non-dual.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the Chapter on the Bhikṣus.
Compassion, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, as well as vigor,
meditative concentration, wisdom, nirvana, the mind, and the monk— these are your ten [qualities].
Thus ends the third inspired utterance.
Now follows the fourth inspired utterance: "Endowed with the merits of celestial bliss and the praises of King Mitra,
this compendium is embraced by the extensive mindfulness of the True Dharma."
(31) The Chapter on Merit:
Praise of Merit. Meritorious deeds are delightful; their fruit is supremely auspicious.
Therefore, perform meritorious deeds; there is no wealth equal to merit.
Merit is an inexhaustible treasure; merit is the unsurpassed jewel;
merit is like a lamp, and it is always like a mother and a father. (Dhs 31.2)
Having performed merit, the gods have gone [to heaven]; merit leads one to a happy rebirth.
Having performed merit in this world, men indeed rejoice in the third heaven.
Merit is supreme happiness;
for those who possess an abundance of merit become men who are always happy.
Therefore, perform meritorious deeds; there is no happiness equal to merit.
Having performed merit, the gods have gone [to heaven]; merit is always seen as the cause for one who holds merit dear as wealth. Therefore, merit is the supreme happiness.
Without merit, happiness is impossible;
merit is seen to be eternally supreme and follows one like a shadow.
Therefore, there is no happiness higher than merit; without merit, there is no happiness.
There is a distinction between the fruits of merit and demerit;
even gods who have transcended merit fall again, following the consequences of their good deeds. The world is the fruit of both merit and demerit; therefore, one should practice merit. (Dhs 31.7)
For those who revile merit, who are devoid of virtue, undisciplined, and constantly destined for evil rebirths—how could happiness be seen in them? It would be like [finding] ghee in sand. (Dhs 31.8)
Deceived by wealth and deluded, deprived of merit, no happiness exists for them; for them, there is only unsurpassed suffering.
By the power of merit, one goes to the world of the gods;
for this is the result of well-performed deeds for the embodied being.
Through the ripening of that karma, one is born in the heavenly worlds.
He who cherishes his own self and whose mind is established in happiness—
let him perform great merit for the sake of rebirth in the world of the gods.
A person who practices the Dharma indeed attains happiness;
for a person practicing the Dharma attains happiness after happiness,
and being stainless, they very swiftly attain supreme peace.
Therefore, perform meritorious deeds that are eternally conducive to spiritual accumulation.
The doer of merit enjoys imperishable happiness; the virtuous one, ever self-controlled, attains the eternal state. Many meritorious deeds are to be performed with delight. (Dhs 31.13)
The diversity of merit and the worthiness of adopting the Dharma:
for merit performed in diverse ways ripens in diverse ways,
throughout the world of living beings, in whom dharma and adharma predominate.
Since the Dharma is a protection here on earth, one should therefore delight in the Dharma.
The unrighteous man who, having abandoned the Dharma, delights in evil deeds,
suffers constant misery, for he is consumed by his own misdeeds. (Dhs 31.15)
One should direct the mind toward the Dharma as long as death has not arrived; as long as there is time for complete reflection,
one should apply the mind to the Dharma, and thus tranquility will arise.
He who teaches the Dharma to others out of a desire for their welfare, acting as a benefactor to others, goes to the city of Nirvana;
he is indeed both mother and father, the guide to the city of Nirvana.
That teacher who teaches the priceless, excellent speech of the Master, being uniquely devoted to the supreme good,
is a knower of the path to the ultimate destination and becomes a protector for embodied beings.
Indeed, there is no price that can be set for a single well-spoken word of the Teacher.
The distinction between common property and the property of the Dharma does not find its footing: that which is peaceful is not obtained through wealth;
common property is seen as such, whereas the Dharma is not a bond for the intellect.
The substance of Dharma remains unimpaired, whereas the material wealth of men perishes; indeed, the substance of Dharma never perishes at all.
While thousands of internal [treasures] perish, a single instance of Dharma follows one even beyond death.
Wealth does not follow even a single step of one who departs;
their riches are lost through kings, thieves, water, and fire.
But that wealth which consists of Dharma cannot be taken away by any means whatsoever.
Therefore, one should be devoted to the Dharma;
for after enjoying manifold happiness even in a short time, a fall from that state will inevitably occur. Thus, one should be devoted to the Dharma.
Dharma alone is the supreme protection; dharma alone is the ultimate refuge.
This world proceeds according to dharma, and even death occurs through the power of adharma.
Praise for those who practice the Dharma: Better is the Dharma; the practitioner of Dharma practices the Dharma alone.
He attains happiness after happiness and does not behold suffering. (Dhs 31.24)
Censure of the Unrighteous:
When a person who practices unrighteousness indulges in unrighteousness, he then experiences suffering again and again in the hells. (Dhs 31.25)
The greatness of Nirvāṇa:
even for one who has repeatedly cultivated faith in the Three Jewels,
the fruit is Nirvāṇa, rather than merely living on in previous heavenly realms.
One must perform meritorious deeds by oneself;
merit is created by oneself and attained by oneself.
Whether it be happiness or suffering, it is experienced by oneself alone.
The power of merit of one who possesses virtue proceeds incessantly like the current of a river;
for him whose mind delights in virtue, the power of merit is vast.
For whomsoever dharma does not please, the fruit of his existence is [unfortunate];
for dharma leads one who practices dharma, endowed with happiness, to heaven.
Without dharma, a person goes to hell;
indeed, this alone is sufficient: the preservation of dharma.
For without dharma, a person runs toward the hells.
Death is better than the reviling of the Dharma;
for death would indeed be better than the reviling of the Dharma.
Deprived of the Dharma, the world would wander forever in saṃsāra.
For one devoid of Dharma, life consists of suffering; for one whose eye of Dharma is lost and whose mind is overcome by delusion,
this perceived happiness is seen to be in vain, just as another [perceives it] upon seeing it.
The sprout of Dharma does not grow in the field of the mind of one who lacks consciousness,
even if their intellect is intent on the practice of Dharma and dedicated to the cultivation of ethical conduct.
Through auspiciousness that is thoroughly purified and cultivated with diligence,
they go to that peaceful state where suffering is not found.
One who is under the control of the senses does not overcome Māra;
likewise, he who remains under the sway of the senses and their objects is bound by all fetters and does not overcome Māra.
Unstained by evil dharmas, he remains established in his own nature;
unstained by evil dharmas, he possesses a golden luster even when destitute.
Having escaped the wilderness of existence, he becomes secure in every respect.
Through the worship of the Buddha and others, one attains nirvāṇa—
those for whom the Buddha is always highly esteemed, for whom the Dharma is their sphere of activity,
who are intent on serving the feet of their teachers, and who have faith in karmic actions.
Through constant worship of the Three Jewels, one's virtuous intellect becomes perfectly pure;
and through honoring one's parents, who are those traveling toward the city of Nirvana, [the same is attained].
The qualities of the nature of renunciation have been proclaimed for all;
through the practice of celibacy, they bring about the highest of all forms of happiness.
The gift of Dharma is the most excellent of all gifts;
the gift of Dharma is proclaimed as the supreme gift.
Among all endeavors, meditative concentration is always superior, by means of which one attains nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost of the world— above, below, and across— which is composed of manifold karmas;
the Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost among all phenomena, the seer of reality.
Among the classes of beings, the most excellent is said to be the peaceful one within the multitude of those seeking wealth;
from that field arises threefold merit, consisting of virtue, suffering, or both.
The preceptor should always be honored as equal to one's mother and father;
he opens the eye for the purpose of bringing [truth] within the range of perception.
Objects of the senses are considered devoid of happiness,
or rather, they are always seen as ungraspable by the Sage who perceives reality;
for these stages of pleasure are indeed considered to be objects devoid of true happiness.
If one thus performs pure dharma that reveals the path, his happiness shall be eternal; there is no such happiness even in the realms of the gods.
In other states of existence, merit stands behind embodied beings;
therefore, men should always summon and cultivate it with effort.
He who perceives with the eye of a Buddha the danger that lies in the future is wise and ever steadfast; the one who is excessively fearful due to ignorance is a fool.
Seeing the fear born of misfortune, the wise person perceives the Path;
for when an obstacle has arisen, he is not afflicted by despondency.
Then, one of deluded mind constantly indulges only in sense objects;
deluded by those objects, he is later consumed by remorse.
As long as this entire life proceeds toward knowledge without obstacle, perform meritorious deeds; for those who have failed to perform merit, there is only suffering. (Dhs 31.50)
Merits come to an end and life passes away swiftly;
therefore, O gods in Tuṣita, you must exert yourselves in the gathering of the Dharma.
For that man who, struck by negligence, abandons the Dharma and does not accumulate merits, suffers even later on.
As long as old age has not arrived, nor disease together with death, so long should meritorious deeds be performed; do not suffer later.
For one who has not accumulated merit and is struck down by negligence, suffering in hell is the result; indeed, negligence shall destroy you.
What is the purpose of life for him, what is the use of his fortunes, and what is the use of his kinsmen, who,
having attained the full strength of his senses, is not always devoted to Dharma?
Day after day, one should apply the mind to the accumulation of dharma,
as well as to abstaining from evils and beholding the virtuous.
He who, having obtained this birth as a god through his virtue, is deluded by sensual desires and does not accumulate merits, does not transcend cyclic existence.
Those who always delight in the Dharma are worthy of homage; they take pleasure in the undertaking of wisdom and are adorned with the jewel of ethical conduct.
For those who are afraid of sensual passion are esteemed as gods among the gods.
For those who are always devoted to the Dharma are indeed ever to be honored as gods;
but those who are constantly attached to worldly existence have all gone to their destruction.
Having reached this great bridge of Dharma, which spans from this shore to the further shore,
he who does not cross over quickly is never liberated from existence.
The auspicious never perishes;
through qualities that follow after the auspicious, the auspicious always comes to be.
Even in thousands of millions of eons, the auspicious never perishes.
For the sake of attaining merit, those things that ought to be done must be performed: ethical conduct has been constantly maintained, wisdom has been cultivated,
and generosity has been given without exhaustion, becoming natural to one's very being.
Virtues should always be cultivated;
by the three [practices] beginning with generosity, the three defects of men are destroyed.
Therefore, having abandoned the defects, virtues should be pursued with diligent effort.
Through knowledge, worldly suffering perishes;
through association with those of virtuous character and diligent application to knowledge,
the suffering born of existence perishes, just as darkness is dispelled by the rays of the sun.
Beloved by the gods, he is honored by the deities;
having reached another birth, he also swiftly attains nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, the Section on Merit.
(32) Those who walk upon the path of the Sugata are a class of gods; men are equal to deities on those paths which were taught by the Sage, the seer of reality, in his treatise.
For those men, esteemed by the gods, have indeed set forth by means of them.

The Buddhas have declared that the path to heaven consists of the truth taught by the Sugata, as well as generosity, loving-kindness toward sentient beings, protection, pleasant speech, right view, and a pure mind. Dhs 32.2.
Endowed with pure qualities and possessed of a pure mind,
one who has light as his ultimate goal goes from happiness to even greater happiness.
Just as a lamp filled with light [is illuminated] by another light,
so indeed does one who has departed from this world reach the supreme worlds.
One who possesses proper conduct shall go into the presence of the gods—
whose mind is always pure and stainless like a gem— he,
being peaceful, free from the sense of "mine," and wise, shall go into the presence of the gods.
He whose mind is endowed with virtue through meditation, ethical conduct, and concentration— that wise one, resembling refined gold, shall go into the presence of the gods.
Abstaining from taking life and devoted to compassion for all beings,
as well as being sympathetic toward the flow of the seasons, one shall go to the presence of the gods.
One who is learned, who has abandoned cruel deeds in all the world,
and who is unstained by sinful qualities, shall go into the presence of the gods.
He for whom gold is like grass and for whom sensual desires are like poison—
that wise one who has abandoned desires shall go into the presence of the gods.
One whose mind is not drawn away by desires for sense objects— the causes of passion—
throughout the wilderness of existence, shall go into the presence of the gods.
Lineages that were initially divided, he who— possessing friends and kinsmen—
makes closely united, shall go into the presence of the gods.
He whose dwelling is established in the intellect, and whose intellect is not attached to anything, is a conqueror of enemies; with a purified self, he shall go into the presence of the gods.
He whose bodily actions are praiseworthy, who has desisted from evil and is happy,
being free from sensual desires and meditative, shall go to the presence of the gods.
Freed from evil friends and devoid of the poison of craving,
one who is not bound by the snares of fear for women shall go into the presence of the gods.
One who speaks with diligence regarding the Dharma, who possesses generosity, ethical conduct, and meditative concentration,
and who is constantly exerted and firm in intellect, shall go to the presence of the gods.
He who has severed the bonds of attachment as one cuts a snare with a sword,
being freed from all fetters and self-mastered, shall go into the presence of the gods.
Through the ripening of virtuous karma, there is birth in the world of the gods;
those beings who, having become human, conduct themselves in a way that brings about good deeds,
are born in the world of the gods as a result of that ripening of karma.
Only those who rely on the path of Dharma are truly strong; among humans, the gods are strong by virtue of their power, and among the gods, humans are strong.
Those who are established upon the path of the True Dharma possess mutual strength.
There are three realms of misfortune:
for the gods, a good rebirth consists of mortals; for mortals, a good rebirth consists of gods.
These three realms of misfortune are devoid of virtuous karma.
All happiness depends on the Dharma;
all happiness depends on the Dharma; for liberation indeed depends on the Dharma.
The Dharma remains awake among those who sleep; the Dharma is indeed the supreme refuge.
By the gods the asuras were conquered;
by righteousness unrighteousness was defeated; by truth the liar was overcome;
and by wisdom delusion was dispelled—for thus indeed were the asuras conquered by the gods.
Those actions are indeed the stairway to the heavenly realm where happiness arises;
for by abandoning their human birth, men go to the heavenly realm where happiness arises.
Through restraint of speech, the wise enjoy the happiness of the third heaven;
the fourfold discipline of speech is indeed threefold and fivefold.
Having ascended the seven steps, the wise go to the third heaven.
And sporting with the divine radiance born from their own bodies,
they take delight in the heavenly realm, gladdened by their own karma.
Virtue alone is the cause of purity for those who dwell in constant fragrance and always abide in happiness.
Whatever virtue the gods possess in their divine abode, that indeed is the cause.
That the gods are surrounded by apsarases and are as radiant as the sun and the moon throughout the divine realms— all that has its cause in merit.
Whatever is desired comes to pass, and once it has come to pass, it does not perish;
and as long as the auspicious continues, it is always rooted in the auspicious.
One who practices virtue attains equality with the gods; one who always practices virtue, is generous, and delights in compassion for all beings—
being ever joined with the loving-kindness of giving— attains equality with the gods.
One who abstains from taking life, is devoted to compassion for all beings,
and whose livelihood and actions are right, shall go to the assembly of the gods.
He finds no pleasure in taking what is not given, and his mind is always intent on generosity; with his senses stilled and his intellect wise, he attains association with the gods.
He who is liberated from false desires, who always delights in the true path,
and who longs for nirvāṇa— being stainless, he shall go into the presence of the gods.
For that which causes dejection in a joyful man becomes insignificant for the wise one who abstains from intoxicants; such a steadfast person shall go into the presence of the gods.
One who is free from negligence attains happiness; for that deity which is the vital breath finds no pleasure in indulging in negligence.
From happiness one attains happiness, and one realizes liberation.
That bliss which ends with destruction is called Nirvana; it is eternal.
Having attained that, the supreme persons shine resplendent within the celestial palaces.
Mount Meru is higher than the high; therefore, happiness is always high.
A living being who is disciplined by virtue shall conquer the gods of the Akaniṣṭha realm.
How can there be satisfaction in that which is faultless, especially in the world of the gods?
Why does one always obtain such extreme happiness among the deities?
Who experiences happiness?
One consumed by the fire of craving does not experience happiness;
likewise, one consumed by [the fire of] evil deeds does not experience happiness.
Having performed threefold good deeds of three kinds and with three causes,
one obtains this supreme fruit, great and possessing three qualities, abiding in the three realms.
Those who were devoted to non-violence and generosity, dedicated to the true Dharma,
and endowed with truth, patience, and self-control, have ascended to the third heaven.
Endowed with divine ornaments and adorned with celestial garlands,
whatever auspicious acts the gods of divine intellect perform, that is indeed auspicious.
That great happiness of the gods which remains free from deficiency or excess— this very result, characterized by deficiency and mediocrity, is seen to belong to merit.
The doer of merit goes to the world of the gods;
for as much merit as has been performed by an embodied being,
for that long is his happiness ripened in the celestial realms.
The preservation of ethical discipline is essential;
welcome to you, O noble one!
You have performed a virtuous deed.
This fruit has come to him because he guarded his ethical conduct in seven ways.
Delight yourself with the gods upon the forests, groves, and mountains, and in the groves of lotus-pools;
delight yourself upon the golden rooftops of the palaces.
Always accompanied by the deities.
Delight yourself together with the deities in forests, groves, and mountains, upon the peaks of lapis lazuli, and among the many forested hills.
Delight together with the deities amidst the lovely wish-fulfilling trees, by the rivers and springs, and upon the broad streams.
Delight together with the deities upon mountains endowed with flowing rivers and the like, by streams, and in cities of great significance.
Delight together with the deities in the sprouts of fragrant sandalwood, in groves of blue lotuses, and in the delightful abodes of the yakṣas.
Delight yourself with the deities upon the various regions of the earth, at its borders, in jewel-mines and forests, and in delightful celestial palaces.
Dancing to the fivefold musical ensemble that gladdens the mind, rejoice eternally in happiness together with the deities.
Having purified the seed of virtue through various moral conducts,
sport with the various divine pleasures as you truly deserve.
That the gods, garlanded with radiance, rejoice in various pleasures is seen to be the fruit of merit, especially that which is stainless.
That the gods sport manifoldly with these various pleasures is not due to us; rather, the cause therein is what was performed in the past.
The god, honored and sustained among the gods, always enjoys all the gabled palaces, which are variegated with diverse works of art.
For one who is liberated from the three bonds, protected by the five,
and who has transcended the single dharma, the world of the gods is exalted.
For those men whose minds are joyful, their clear conduct becomes concentrated as they arrive at the abode of the gods, bearing witness to the fruits of their own karma.
The fruit of well-performed deeds is happiness higher and higher; such indeed is the nature of merit.
For the gods in heaven enjoy that which follows from their previous deeds.
These various trees stand as witnesses to all actions;
the wise declare that they speak of them constantly and with perfect accuracy.
Fortune bears fruit everywhere through whatever ripening of karma; wherever a person is reborn, they experience the auspicious or inauspicious results of their own past actions.
By virtuous action, a living being is always born among the gods;
by auspicious karma, a creature is constantly reborn among the gods.
Likewise, by unwholesome action, the lowest of men fall into hell.
Those who lust, being passionately attached to the pleasant and the unpleasant, do not understand death; those who lust, deluded by desire,
do not realize that death will inevitably come to pass.
This ripening of the auspicious and inauspicious which is perceived among the trees—
these beings do not desist from pleasure, for their minds are deluded by such happiness.
Having performed good deeds, humans go among the gods;
having performed the threefold good deed and cultivated it in seven ways,
and having slain the enemies numbering three, humans go among the gods.

Who would go into the presence of the gods? He who does not find fault with the hardships of ritual action, nor feels aversion toward joy— he, pure and free from aversion, has gone into the presence of the gods.
Having censured this great abode of suffering, namely stinginess,
and having given equally the three kinds of gifts, he has gone to the presence of the gods.
Having constantly protected the affection of living beings out of compassion,
always possessing a mind of loving-kindness and being self-controlled, he has gone to the presence of the gods.
Having given away wealth that was not given and having bestowed joy everywhere,
one whose mind is cultivated by volition shall go to the presence of the gods.
Regarding the wives of others as one’s own mother, the one who contemplates the true meaning of reality,
unstained by sinful dharmas, shall go to the presence of the gods.
That which is produced from the fire-drill of the tongue for the sake of pleasing one's own mind is called false speech; by abandoning it, one shall go to a happy rebirth.
Having always abandoned slander and the state that causes harm through unkindness, one who possesses a gentle radiance and a gentle mind shall go into the presence of the gods.
The wise one always avoids harsh speech as if it were an enemy;
possessing a mind of gentle radiance, he constantly moves toward all favorable rebirths.
He on whose tongue-tip neither unrighteousness has occurred nor will it ever occur,
and who always knows the truth regarding evil times, shall go into the presence of the gods.
The steadfast one who has protected this morality taught by the Buddha in its sevenfold form,
knowing the true nature of morality, shall go into the presence of the gods.
Who is truly successful and a knower of dharma?
Having obtained this birth, which is subject to the power of various karmas and shared even with the gods,
he who does not practice dharma is later tormented by remorse.
This grove, delightful with its gardens and bowers, its creeper-arbors and pavilions, is the fruit born of auspicious deeds;
whatever variety exists in the world, all that is the fruit born of auspicious deeds.
In whatever manner a beautiful deed has been performed,
its corresponding fruit is seen to follow that very person in such a way.
The gods perceive directly the happiness—whether inferior, middling, or superior—that results for each person exactly according to how they practiced their conduct. Dhs 32.77.
Through evil deeds, the fruit born of suffering arises;
yet the gods, wearing diverse guises, utterly deluded and subject to the power of delusion,
do not perceive the great terror with their minds because they are so infatuated with its destruction.
Delighting in various sensual pleasures and desiring various fruits,
those asuras of deluded minds do not perform meritorious deeds.
Who are those devoted to passion?
Those for whom the fruit is a dear mind, yet whose intellect finds no delight in virtuous conduct;
they abandon the lamp and are intent upon the light of passion.
Those who know the reality of cause and effect become happy; those who, through the similarity of cause and effect, desire the most excellent gods, they—
knowing the reality of cause and effect— become partakers of happiness.
Liberation comes from knowledge alone;
without a seed there is no fruit, and without a lamp, whence can there be light?
Without moral conduct, whence can there be heaven, and without knowledge, whence can there be liberation? (Dhs 32.82)
What is the happiness of the wise one? It is the happiness of that liberated one who is free from longing, the protector,
whose craving for sensual desire has been relinquished, and who is free from the sense of "mine."
Happiness indeed arises from good deeds; yet all this happiness born of karma is to be known as tainted.
That which is not desired [by the wise] is remembered as entirely stainless.
The description of the world of the gods,
which encompasses the entirety of one's desires both within and without (in every respect),
is a realm of universal light, ever-luminous, and frequented by hosts of deities.
This excellent mountain shines like a ruby,
abounding in water and surrounded by lotus ponds.
Delightful with its forests and groves, frequented by deer and birds, this mountain—
its interior filled with caverns— has risen up, piercing the sky.
Where is it served by the deities?
It is constantly served by deities adorned with divine garlands,
and on all sides by deities preeminent in dance and song.
As if impelled by the fivefold musical ensemble,
he appears as the head of all, most magnificent, and encircled on every side with a garland of light.
By means of well-performed, auspicious, and truly superior karma,
they rely upon which the hosts of gods sport everywhere.
Who go to heaven?
Those who are endowed with generosity and morality, who are mature, whose minds are always fixed upon that [virtue],
and who are ever self-controlled— those people go to heaven.
Those people whose minds are withdrawn and who are peaceful go to heaven;
those whose minds are eternally tranquil are beyond the reach of their enemies.
Those people who are free from passion and free from delusion go to heaven;
[but] where the means of attainment is afflicted by intense becoming and non-becoming.
Those wise ones whose minds are well-tamed are the people who go to heaven.

Those who proceed slowly along the path of truth, who partake of happiness as it comes, and who know the method for distinguishing the essential from the non-essential, are people destined for heaven.
Those embodied beings who do not guard their own minds within saṃsāra,
yet are constantly delighted in nirvāṇa— those people go to heaven.
Those people who meditate at the foot of a tree, in a cremation ground, or likewise in a mountain cave,
with their minds fixed on sentient beings, go to heaven.
Those who know the proper measure, who know the right place and time, who have avoided evil friends,
and who possess a mind of loving-kindness— those people go to heaven.
Those people who take no delight in bathing or in the sight [of women], who go to solitary places, and who are tranquil, go to heaven. They are not led astray by the waters of passion.
Those people who constantly perceive the body as arising from impurity moment by moment,
and who understand the rules for what should and should not be done, go to heaven.
Those who perceive the true nature of phenomena as diverse yet equal do not remain in cyclic existence; such people go to heaven.
Those people who perceive sensation— which arises in many ways and ends in the middle reality— and do not cling to it, are destined for heaven.
Those whose minds always understand that [the world] is like an illusion, momentary, and like a city of the Gandharvas, are people who go to heaven.
Those people who know the reality of the single characteristic, who themselves understand the absence of characteristics,
and whose minds are free from passion for nirvāṇa, go to heaven.
Those who view the wives of others as their own mother and all living beings as their own father,
and who perceive danger in the world— those people go to heaven.
Those who always abide in the category of emptiness, who speak kindly to sentient beings,
who are free from cruelty, and whose minds are possessed of supernatural power— such people go to heaven.
Those people who regard all the wealth of others as equal to wood, grass, or clods of earth,
and who are content with their own minds, are destined for heaven.
Those for whom the light of laziness is not desired, neither by night nor by day,
and who dwell in constant application— they are the people who go to heaven.
Those fortunate people who always avoid remorse, sloth and torpor, and especially indolence, are destined for heaven.
Those people who have purified their immorality in many ways through the five gates,
and who always contract [the causes of] suffering, are destined for heaven.
Those wise people who understand the fourfold grasping and likewise perceive the truths, those people possessing wisdom go to heaven.
Those people who always perceive suffering, the ripening of suffering, and the mind that dwells upon sufferings as they truly are, go to heaven.
Those who, even when fallen into intense calamity,
do not abandon the Dharma,
and who are peaceful and intent upon the Dharma— those people go to heaven.
Those people who wear white, bright garments as well as rags from dust heaps,
and who are always devoted to alms-food, go to heaven.
Free from punishment, with peaceful minds, constantly dwelling in meditation, and all devoted to the state beyond action— those people go to heaven.
Whether food is refined or unrefined, they remain content with whatever comes according to their desire;
such people do not become angry and are destined for heaven.
Those people who are content with white, bright clothing as well as rags from dust heaps, and who are likewise restrained in their conduct, go to heaven.
Whether on a bed, on the ground, or on the roof of a palace, those people who are neither distressed nor elated go to heaven.
Those people who perceive in truth that action which has entered the range of the eye and pertains to the future life are the ones who go to heaven.
Those people who, upon hearing what is unpleasant or even pleasant, remain undisturbed in mind due to intense composure, are liberated and destined for heaven.
Those people who withdraw all six sense faculties as well as their objects, and do not let them run wild, are destined for heaven.
Those fortunate people who, being free from mental agitation, perceive all actions exactly as they are performed in their true nature without distinction, are destined for heaven.
Those people who, with steadfast minds, [reflect upon] the ripening of actions performed, always fear suffering here in this world; they are destined for heaven.
All those people who constantly perform these highly significant acts, even though they cause suffering, according to the prescribed rules, are destined for heaven.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the Section on Devas.
(33) The Chapter on Happiness: An Investigation into the Nature of Happiness.
Those who delight in the unsurpassed blisses attained through meditative concentration—
May they possess happiness exactly as it is, which reveals the city of Nirvana.
New pleasure and pain strike down the old;
for the god, this old [state] is struck down by the new alone.
Just as wood mixed with smoke, or rice mixed with excrement,
so too all this pleasure is not understood to be devoid of self-nature.
That is true happiness for those who go toward the city of Nirvāṇa— the happiness of those free from craving, who dwell in absolute bliss,
who are without delusion or passion, and who proceed toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
Even among those pure pleasures that have no beginning or end, that [other] pleasure is the true one for those whose minds are entirely free from longing and desire that follow after craving.
For one whose mind is fully restrained, who is entirely devoid of self,
yet remains unconfused regarding what ought and ought not to be done, happiness is ever present.
Who is the most excellent, who is happy?
He by whom Nandana—the cause of saṃsāra—has been struck down externally;
he is the steadfast one, the one who has gone to the further shore, the most excellent, and the happy one, for he is established in nirvāṇa.
That which is conjoined with passion and hatred is not true happiness for those who thirst;
that which is free from passion and the like is considered pure happiness. (Dhs 33.8)
Where does craving not cause affliction?
Having attained the world of the gods, that deity who does not treat others with contempt goes from happiness to further happiness, where craving no longer causes affliction. (Dhs 33.9)
That final happiness is the highest good wherein death is not found;
for one not bound by the snares of death, no happiness exists anywhere.
That pleasure which gives rise to desire is not considered true happiness by the wise.
Wherein one who is liberated from desire finds that which is the highest happiness beyond all pleasure;
for such happiness produces the ultimate good, just as rice mixed with milk produces nourishment.
Where there is liberation from craving, like rice mixed with water;
just as carnivorous scavengers rush into a lotus grove [thinking it meat].
Thus, in peaceful forests, those who act unwholesomely do not shine;
in one place there is a lovely, tranquil forest, while in another there are gods who are heedless.
Who attains supreme happiness? It is one who is free from thirst and liberated from suffering—the Protector whose bliss is unlike anything else, just as cool light is not like the sun. (Dhs 33.14)
Compared to that, this happiness of worldly pleasure is not even reckoned as happiness for one who meditates,
remains ever vigilant, and is forever liberated from evil.
That is happiness, that is supreme bliss; this is not the view of those possessed by craving.
This forest, frequented by sages, has been cultivated through well-spoken teachings.
O best of gods, you ought not to indulge in the host of passions;
for this happiness of yours is certainly not eternal.
That supreme, peaceful happiness is cultivated by those free from craving;
they have abandoned this forest and gone to the highest state.
Upon attaining which there is the total severance of all suffering—
those who have not been liberated from the holy life (brahmacarya) are deceived by a mere lip-service to moral conduct.
For monks, dwelling in the forest alone brings happiness;
they ought not to frequent even a beautiful, peaceful forest that is well-spoken of, if it is not itself peaceful and cultivated.
He delights in a virtuous sphere of experience.
The mind of those who act out of passion does not find delight in the forest retreat;
a mind agitated by passion finds no stability in the forests.
Who is the supreme person?
He whose mind is always undeluded regarding the three worlds as being in his own hand;
that best of men finds delight and peace in the forest.
The forest should be resorted to for the sake of happiness;
yet he who is crooked with the passion of the age and is constantly enveloped by lust and other defilements does not find peace at all in the tranquil forest that brings such bliss.
But for those who are constantly engaged in meditation in the forest with their minds, the forest is always delightful; it is not so for those who pursue passion.
A mind cultivated in the forests does not become agitated in cities;
therefore, the forest should always be resorted to, while the city is never praised.
For a person enveloped by passion and other afflictions is distracted within the city;
yet the forest, though once agitated and crooked with delusion, becomes clear once more.
Therefore, the forest is supremely peaceful, a great abode for yogis;
it should be resorted to by one whose mind is free from attachment, for it is devoid of all defilement.
Do not find delight even in that joy which resides in the heart of a yogin whose senses and mind are perfectly tranquil;
that joy is beyond the power of a thousand [ordinary] men.
It will come to pass.
That delight which is seen in those who meditate, which always leads to purification,
is never seen even among those who constantly indulge in passion.
That delight which is under the sway of desire always gives rise to suffering;
but that joy which arises from the power of the afflictions is not eternal.
Who attains the state of supreme excellence? It is the life led by men in the forests that is truly excellent,
for it is said that the state of supreme excellence is indeed dependent upon that.
With a mind well-accumulated in the Dharma and as if protected by it,
one attains a state that is well-seen, wherein no fault is found.
For those whose minds are constantly distracted and who are not devoted to the Dharma,
this happiness passes away in vain and does not return.

Those wise ones who know reality do not perceive suffering; those steadfast ones who understand the true nature of the world’s existence find no suffering in that which is impermanent, painful, and empty.
The practice of the dharma of happiness and the cultivation of knowledge,
non-violence, and truthful speech— these too are established as being exclusively [the path].
Who goes to heaven?
Those people who have transcended a single [worldly] dharma, who are not deceived by unrighteousness, and who are endowed with the characteristics of the three states, go to heaven.
The nature of pleasure is impermanent, characterized by arising and passing away, for it is born of karma.
That pleasure is tainted (sāsrava); it has never existed, nor will it ever exist eternally.
That is true happiness for the embodied being who is free from craving and devoid of passion;
indeed, liberation belongs to one who stands on the further shore of the burning afflictions.
Whatever happiness is associated with outflows is considered entirely momentary;
that which is liberated from the bondage of passion is all unwavering bliss.
Those who do not cast away suffering through pleasure, and for whom there is no attachment to pleasure,
are liberated from both suffering and pleasure and proceed toward the bliss of Nirvana.
Those fools who always seek happiness through improper means will never obtain it, just as one might seek oil from sand.
Even with a hundred desires of the mind, a wise person cannot bring about that happiness by thought alone, just as even Śakra cannot undo the great fruit of karma that has been performed.
One should practice the Dharma for the sake of happiness;
for he whose mind is happy becomes a follower of the true Dharma.
This desire for liberation from sufferings is what directs the mind toward the Dharma.
Neither pleasure nor the threefold suffering is seen to be without a cause;
since pleasure and suffering exist as distinct entities, one should therefore practice virtuous deeds.
This pleasure is not always praised; it is unstable and destructive, mixed with the poison of craving like rice mixed with venom.
