That happiness alone is praised by the virtuous wherein death is not found,
where there is no separation from the beloved and no encounter with the unpleasant.
What kind of pleasure gives rise to suffering?
This pleasure consisting of women is fashioned for the sake of suffering;
it is seen as the seed that causes rebirth in the hells.
How can that which generates suffering be considered pleasure?
By the power of its transformation, it should be known as even more painful than pain.
This happiness that is enjoyed perishes with time,
just as the rays of the sun vanish when it has set, along with its companions.
He whose mind does not undergo transformation through pleasure or pain is wise; having gone to the world of the gods, he attains further happiness.
One enjoys ancient happiness, yet performs inferior deeds;
when ancient merit has decayed, one does not realize it at the time of death.
All happiness is impermanent; this intense pleasure seen here, born of mind, speech, and desire,
is impermanent and will soon come to destruction.
All happiness in the ocean of existence is like a bubble on the surface of water, resembling a mirage, and as unstable as a flickering wave; it ends in downfall.
Irremediable and treacherous, bringing fear to all living beings,
this King Death rushes forward with the force of a whirlwind.
Having destroyed all happiness and having destroyed his very life,
he will lead the world elsewhere, away from the sphere of karmic intentionality.
That which is exceedingly pleasant for humans is indeed reckoned as happiness;
however, that which will not result in any future happiness is not reckoned as such at all.
But whatever happiness exists in the present that is free from the poison of craving— indeed,
all conditioned power is impermanent, suffering, and devoid of self.
Worldly pleasure is not true happiness; that pleasure which exists in the three worlds is not praised by those who see reality.
Considering this, how can the gods be free from the fever of suffering?
This terrible time has arrived and passes swiftly,
which will consume all the gods like fire consumes dry fuel.
Let all pass by in happiness; let the mind be set upon what is beneficial.
Lest there be regret later when the time of death arrives during the practice of yoga.
The happiness born of karma that is liberated [from it] remains unstable throughout thousands of future births;
who could know this [world] to be like a wave?
The fool is unstable.
Who is satisfied by pleasure?
A fool is not satiated by pleasures, just as fire is not satiated by wood;
therefore, [pleasure]...
For one who is attached, there is ultimate happiness.
For one who is free from the defects of poison, who perceives the faults of desire,
who is meditative and vigilant, there is that happiness which is untainted.
Having attained that [Dharma], one becomes happy; the happiness born of worldly existence does not compare to it.
Just as poison mixed with a binding agent [is lethal], so too is the arising of the happiness of worldly dharma.
Those free from desire attain happiness; therefore, for those who are constantly attached to that pleasure and ever in search of sensual desires, there arise manifold forms of suffering.
Therefore, desire does not arise.
By means of knowledge alone do the senses turn away from their own objects;
it is not possible to achieve mastery over the senses regarding the sphere of sense-objects.
Indeed, it is by means of knowledge that the senses are turned away from their own objects. (Dhs 33.66)
Only fools wander through the five realms of existence;
fools of dull intellect are constantly attached to suffering as happiness.
Deluded by their inversions, they continue to roam within the five realms of existence.
Where does pleasure become like suffering?
That which is seen as ultimate pleasure is called true pleasure;
where there would be the ripening of suffering, that pleasure is indeed suffering itself.
The non-committal of evil alone is happiness; the wise person wards off future suffering.
Suffering is born from the cause of evil; the non-committal of evil is happiness.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the Section on Happiness.
(34) Who is the circle of friends? He who restrains one from evil is a friend; that friend is called a true friend who is a friend in the afterlife.
He who turns one away from evil and also protects one from calamity.
That which one constantly causes to enter [one's heart] is beneficial for the future life;
that is a friend to human beings, not a friend who commits evil.
Faults and virtues arise from association: from contact with the foul, only foulness is produced.
That which is not foul cannot, by contact with the foul, become foul. (Dhs 34.3)
For whatever kind of association a person always forms,
by reason of that fault he is seen to become similar— whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
That which is auspicious does not cause suffering;
a person seeking what is auspicious never practices anything inauspicious.
Therefore, he attains happiness, for the auspicious is not a cause of suffering.
The characteristics of virtues and faults:
virtues are seen to arise from association, and faults likewise originate from association;
this definition of virtues and faults is said to be born of their own nature.
For he who constantly associates with the virtuous becomes endowed with fame, whereas the lowest of men quickly falls away from fortune due to association with the wicked.
This is the fruit of association with the virtuous:
that which is essential should always be practiced— namely, the constant avoidance of the unwholesome,
dwelling always with the good, and the shunning of the wicked.
The wise person should eliminate faults and cultivate the increase of virtues;
he should make good friends and turn away from indolence.
A wise person should not make a friend who is arrogant or lazy, who is constantly suspicious of everything, or who is stained by evil and exceedingly cruel.
A wise person should cultivate friendship with one who is industrious, gentle by nature, virtuous, free from faults, possessed of right view, and steadfast.
One should not have an evil friend; one should have a person of supreme character.
For one who associates with the supreme, there shall be no fear of faults.
Who undergoes degradation? That embodied being whose beauty, sovereignty, lineage, and so forth are shattered;
even an outcaste does not look upon him as he departs, for he is a source of terror.
A man who is ever haughty, whose senses are agitated by negligence,
incurs contempt in this world and is cooked in hells after death.
Those men who, for the sake of pride in their physical form and power, commit evil deeds—
their karma is not easily pacified;
after death, they are cooked in states of suffering.
Those who possess forms, power, noble lineage, and wealth do not partake of reality;
being fools with minds fixed on what is not reality, they do not cross the ocean of existence.
A family endowed with wisdom, virtue, and other such qualities is excellent;
yet whatever wealth this family possesses, and whatever other happiness is desired—all these are impermanent. Therefore, one should not place one's trust in them.
The wise do not go to a state of virtue that is devoid of knowledge and ethical conduct;
those who possess both knowledge and ethical conduct are established in a great family.
Those wise ones, born of noble lineage and self-controlled, practice pure conduct; indeed, such conduct is most wonderful.
Those who are endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, austerity, meditation, truthfulness, sovereignty, and valor,
and who are not devoid of the Dharma, are truly of noble birth.
For one devoid of sovereignty and knowledge, there is neither noble lineage nor true association;
therefore, a lineage consists of knowledge, and that which lacks knowledge is not a lineage at all.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Friends.
(35) The Chapter on Advice to Kings:
A righteous king goes to heaven, while his subjects, seeing him, follow the Dharma and conquer their senses.
That king, righteous and wise, [strives] for rebirth in the heavenly world.
Who is the king free from greed? He who, being restrained, enjoys the tax at the proper time and in accordance with dharma—
he is the king free from greed who becomes the lord of the Yāmas.
A king who possesses a true nature characterized by forbearance and pleasant speech, yet maintains [proper restraint over] anger, joy, and other emotions—
he shall protect this earth and indeed attain preeminence in the world. (Dhs 35.3)
The faith of one who is impartial is not destroyed by a friend;
such a person, honored in the assembly of kings, is fit for the world of the gods.
The high-souled one who perceives the bound, who is devoted to the worship of the Guru,
who is free from greed and firm in intellect, shall go into the presence of the gods.
He who does not harm living beings— that which was given by his ancestors in the past and that which they teach to the gods— is reborn among the deities.
Always skillful in generosity and morality, speaking the Dharma and having conquered his senses, he,
considering the entire earth as noble, is honored in the world of the gods.
He does not uphold what is unrighteous and protects those who are righteous;
purified by his virtuous conduct, he shall go to the presence of the gods.
The king, whose mind is stainless and who is steadfast, does not fall under the sway of women and always dwells among the virtuous; he is thus destined for rebirth in the realm of the gods.
One who does not grasp at every word is beloved by virtuous people;
like one who has drunk the nectar of truth and seen reality, he flourishes as if drawn upward.
Who is the lord of the Yāma gods?
He who abandons greed for wealth and shall not acquire riches;
freed from the stain of greed, he shall become the lord of the Yāma gods. (Dhs 35.11)
Even by means of false views, he who is intent on perceiving the female nature is indeed pure and stainless; he shall become the lord of the Yāma deities.
Who is a king dear to the gods?
One who is wise, ever devoted to moral conduct, and constant in generosity;
having conquered the entire earth, such a one shall become dear to the gods after death.
But the speech of one who is dear [to the virtuous] is supreme, creating a festival of praise;
having gladdened the earth, it leads at last to rebirth as a god.
He whose speech is non-deceptive and as immovable as Mount Meru has ascended the staircase of truth and gone into the presence of the gods.
That king who indeed causes the sudden decline or increase of living beings dwells in the world of the gods, honored by the supreme deities.
He who knows the true nature of the various types of humans and understands their strengths and weaknesses,
being endowed with both wisdom and power, shall become the lord of the Yāma gods.
Whatever is called the "state of the three realms" and the "Three Jewels" here,
the king who honors that is reborn among the gods.
He who perceives the appointed time for all beings and is devoted to their welfare is remembered as the Lord of the Gods, the Auspicious One of the Forest of All-Goodness.
Freed from the stain of censure and devoid of the fault of attachment,
he who is fully honored as the object of knowledge is certainly a god indeed.
Who goes to heaven?
One who is free from the fault of laziness and is always firm in valor;
having destroyed the flood of defects, he is born in the heavens after death.
Surrounded by good friends, a king becomes a lord of the gods; he whose friends are always active in performing beneficial deeds—
that king, completely surrounded by such friends, shall become a lord of the gods.
One who does not associate with the wicked and is free from verbal abuse shall immediately be liberated from poison and become a lord of the gods.
He does not protect against the destruction of anger and joy, nor does he guard against sins;
yet, cleansed from the mire of evil, he is always the sovereign of the world of the gods.
One who is always attached to food and drink is not capable [of spiritual progress];
however, the wise person who perceives the pure Dharma shall attain superiority.
Who attains the supreme state?
He who reflects with right reflection and abides within the teachings.
Just as one goes to the third heaven by beholding the source of phenomena (dharmodaya).
He who practices the Dharma with urgency, rather than procrastinating within saṃsāra,
being thus freed from procrastination, proceeds to the supreme state.

The king who protects his subjects through righteousness attains the happiness of heaven; indeed, that righteous one of praised soul who constantly protects his subjects is honored in the world of the gods.
These ten wholesome qualities have been taught here by the Seer of Reality;
he who practices these qualities shall attain the sovereignty of the gods.
Demonstrating causes and conditions, as well as what is the path and what is not the path,
that wise one is freed from the stain of views and has attained superiority.
With what qualities endowed does a king who worships the deities become the sovereign of the gods, just as a lord of the earth [becomes so] during the day?
Having worshipped the gods, he shall further become the sovereign of the gods.
With an untroubled mind, serene and faithful toward his wife, and contented with his own spouse, one shall become a lord of the gods.
Who is virtuous?
He who is not overcome by the sense objects that carry away all the foolish;
such a virtuous person, protected by constant virtue, goes to heaven.
He who constantly associates with those who are very righteous and avoid ignorance,
and who contemplates the true Dharma, attains happiness in the assembly of the gods.
He whose mind remains composed even while engaged in activities that captivate the conversation of his attendants,
being constantly protected by virtue, is virtuous and goes to heaven.
A king who possesses the true Dharma is indeed a lord of the earth; by protecting this Dharma through righteous conduct,
that lord of the earth rules the entire world and becomes a sovereign of the Yāma gods.
Even a servant shines when serving a king devoted to virtuous deeds; when the monarch is endowed with excellent qualities,
the person attains purity like the autumn moon in the sky.
Who is a king equal to a god? Those who understand causes, targets, and methods, who are not mutually contradictory,
who properly carry out the interests of their master, have come under the sway of the gods.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, "Instruction to the King."
(36) Chapter on Praise: Praise of the Buddha.
To the one who is the supreme Veda among all beings, the kinsman to all sentient beings—[I offer praise].
To the caravan leader of the true path, who severs the bonds of worldly existence.
Homage to the one with the eye of perfect knowledge, who dispels various divergent views, who releases one from all doubt, and who establishes one in right view. Dhs 36.2.
Homage to the one who has become the constellations, who shatters all calamities, who purifies the impurities of the three humors, and who causes all seeds and fruits to grow.
Homage to the one who possesses the supreme treasury of all wisdom, who bestows the pinnacle of all meditative absorptions,
the noble one who is the highest of all jewels, and who reveals the supreme tethering post.
This is that peaceful image of the world-destroyer, the solitary scorcher, which is seen as the opener of liberation.
The person whose mind is peaceful who constantly honors this [teaching] is liberated from the fear of cyclic existence and attains cessation.
This is the peaceful state, this is the delightful; this is called the ultimate, which he who teaches the city of Nirvana proclaims as the Dharma.
Relying upon his word, those whose prowess depends on the Supreme Person constantly draw near to that state which brings infinite bliss.
Having first ascended this [path], those persons who contemplate reality cross over the terrible ocean of existence, the flood of the three worlds.
This is the eye of the world, for it provides vision in every direction;
this is the supreme light, that light which arises from the ultimate source.

The King of Speech indeed purifies the minds of living beings throughout the end of an eon, which have been defiled by the impurities of passion and other such stains in men, by means of the great waters of knowledge.
That state which has not been seen by any of the heretics, even those with the hand of knowledge,
has been revealed by you to humanity through stainless words.
This people, who were supremely negligent and without a protector, has been delivered by you;
having yourself crossed over and reached the further shore, O Protector, you deliver them from the destruction of evil.
You alone are established for the benefit of the entire world;
you alone, O Supreme Person, exist solely for the welfare of those who are malevolent.
In this beginningless saṃsāra, you have purified the afflictions of men with your words, just as darkness is dispelled at the rising of the sun.
Inexhaustible regarding all phenomena, you are the great creator of the light of knowledge;
you alone, O Lord of the World, are an ocean of supramundane virtues.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the Section on Praise.
Endowed with the merits, divine pleasures, and praises of kings by friends,
this compendium has been composed through the expansion of the mindfulness of the True Dharma.
Thus ends the fourth udāna.
"Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, and also their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa."
Having attained merit that dispels the afflictions of mantras and possesses the power and glory of the Victor,
he understands through truthful words the world as long as it remains agitated and confounded by those devoted to mere logic.
This was extracted by the monk Avalokitasiṃha from the most excellent of sūtras, the vast, profound, and great ocean-like [Vaipulya].

Thus concludes the Dharma-discourse named "The Compendium of Dharma" (Dharmasamuccaya), belonging to Vākyavidya Vipulārjana, who is free from the inauspiciousness of delusion and other such afflictions.
Thus may it be auspicious.
